Because jwave runs in JAX, the simulation is fully differentiable. This is not exposed through the PRESTUS wrapper but is available by calling run_jwave_sim.py directly or extending it. All of the examples below use jwave and jax directly in Python; no MATLAB changes are needed.

Sensitivity map: gradient of focal pressure with respect to every voxel's speed of sound. Cost: one reverse-mode pass, equivalent to a single forward simulation, regardless of grid size.

import jax
from jwave import simulate_wave_propagation

def focal_pressure(sound_speed):
    result = simulate_wave_propagation(domain, medium_with(sound_speed), source, ...)
    return result.pressure[focus_idx].real

grad_fn = jax.grad(focal_pressure)
sensitivity = grad_fn(medium.sound_speed)   # same shape as the grid

Phase optimisation: optimise per-element drive phases to maximise focal pressure.

phases = jax.grad(lambda phi: -focal_pressure_from_phases(phi))(initial_phases)

Full-waveform inversion (FWI): estimate skull acoustic properties from measured transmissions.

loss = lambda sos: jnp.mean((simulate_pressure(sos) - measured_pressure) ** 2)
sos_estimated = jax.scipy.optimize.minimize(loss, sos_init, method='BFGS')

items.title: k-Wave
items.text:
k-Wave is the default solver for the acoustic and the thermal simulation and is installed with PRESTUS. Its implementation (simulation.code_type) decides whether a run uses the CPU or the GPU, through MATLAB or a C++ binary. The elastic skull model changes the physics instead: it adds shear waves in the skull, which fluid skull models omit and which lowered the intracranial pressure in ex vivo measurements; in PRESTUS it is a draft and not yet validated.

On this page:

  • Solver Implementations (code_type): CPU or GPU, MATLAB or C++, and building the binaries.
  • Elastic Skull Model (Shear Waves): configuration, skull elastic properties, limitations and cost.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To choose simulation.code_type for your hardware, or to model shear waves in the skull.
  • Before you start: Nothing; k-Wave is installed with PRESTUS. The C++ variants need the k-Wave binaries.

items.title: Solver Implementations (code_type)
items.text:
simulation.code_type selects the k-Wave implementation. This mainly affects the acoustic simulation; with either GPU variant, thermal simulations also use GPU acceleration (if k-Wave 1.4.1 is provided).

code_type Implementation Requirements matlab_cpu kspaceFirstOrder3D / kspaceFirstOrder2D / kspaceFirstOrderAS in MATLAB none matlab_gpu MATLAB with GPU acceleration via DataCast Parallel Computing Toolbox cpp_cpu kspaceFirstOrder3DC wraps the C++ binary kspaceFirstOrder-OMP The binary from k-Wave downloads cpp_gpu kspaceFirstOrder3DG wraps the C++/CUDA binary kspaceFirstOrder-CUDA, offloading computation to NVIDIA GPUs A CUDA-capable Nvidia GPU and the binary from k-Wave downloads cpp_mlx kspaceFirstOrder3DG wraps the C++/MLX binary kspaceFirstOrder-MLX, offloading computation to the Apple Silicon GPU An Apple Silicon Mac (macOS 14 or later) and the binary with mlx.metallib, built as described below Compiling the CUDA binary for your GPU

To use C++ with GPU support you may need to recompile the binary for your GPU version (for example the A100 GPUs on the Donders HPC).

  • Download the Linux C++/CUDA source files (version 1.3; the C++ code is versioned separately from the k-Wave 1.4.1 MATLAB toolbox). This includes the Makefile to compile the binary.
  • Follow the compilation instructions by TU Delft. Include your GPU type in the Makefile.
  • Example scripts for compiling binaries on the Donders HPC are in PRESTUS/examples/hpc_compile...
  • For the Donders HPC, a precompiled binary is available here.
  • Place the updated binary into PRESTUS/external/k-Wave/binaries/
Building the MLX binary (macOS)

cpp_mlx is experimental and has not been validated on a PRESTUS head simulation. It runs the acoustic simulation on the Apple GPU; thermal simulations run on the CPU. Axisymmetric grids fall back to matlab_cpu, and kwave_elastic runs with matlab_cpu, because the port has no solver for either.

The binary is the MLX port of the k-Wave CUDA solver by S. Pichardo (kspacefirstorder-unified, pull request 31). Building it needs CMake and Xcode with the Metal Toolchain (xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain).

git clone --branch MLX-k-Wave-binary https://github.com/ProteusMRIgHIFU/kspacefirstorder-unified.git
cd kspacefirstorder-unified
cmake -S repos/kspaceFirstOrder-mlx-darwin -B build/mlx-darwin \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=14.0 -DKWAVE_BUNDLE_DEPS=ON
cmake --build build/mlx-darwin --parallel

Copy kspaceFirstOrder-MLX and mlx.metallib from build/mlx-darwin into PRESTUS/external/k-wave/k-Wave/binaries/. The two files must stay side by side, because the binary loads mlx.metallib from its own folder.

items.title: Elastic Skull Model (Shear Waves)
items.text:
acoustic_backend: kwave_elastic runs k-Wave's pstdElastic3D / pstdElastic2D instead of kspaceFirstOrder*, so the skull supports shear as well as compressional waves. The motivation is Gao et al. (2026), who compared fluid and elastic k-Wave skull models against hydrophone scans through an ex vivo skull at normal and 40° incidence for shallow (cortical) foci. In those scans the fluid skull model overestimated the intracranial pressure by ~40 % on average and the −6 dB focal area by up to 170 %. The elastic model was also less sensitive to small transducer position errors.

Status: draft. Not yet validated in PRESTUS against measurements or the ITRUSST benchmarks.

items.title: Elastic Model Settings
items.text:
acoustic_backend: kwave_elastic
simulation:
  code_type: matlab_gpu      # cpp_* is overridden to matlab_* (no C++/CUDA elastic solver)
grid:
  axisymmetric: 0            # not supported
elastic:                     # defaults shown; see doc_parameters.md
  shear_mapping: pichardo    # pichardo | off
  shear_density_min: 1200
  poisson_min: 0.1
  alpha_coeff_shear: 43.63   # dB/(cm MHz^y)
  alpha_power_shear: 1.662
  alpha_coeff_long: 27.31    # dB/(cm MHz^y)
  alpha_power_long: 1.722
  long_attenuation: elastic

Compressional speed and density come from the usual medium setup (layer values or pseudo-CT mapping). The shear speed and the two attenuations follow Pichardo et al. (2017), the viscoelastic model behind BabelBrain, evaluated at the transducer's fundamental frequency. Expect the elastic model to be most reliable at low frequencies: Pichardo et al. found good agreement at 270 kHz (delay error 5 % of a wavelength) but only global agreement at 836 kHz (17 %), where trabecular scattering degraded the spatial prediction of an isotropic model.

Skull elastic properties

Pichardo et al. (2017) fitted shear speed and attenuation to transcranial scans at 40° incidence (10 locations, 3 formalin-fixed skulls, 270 and 836 kHz). Every value is evaluated at the transducer's fundamental frequency f0:

Property Pichardo et al. 2017 PRESTUS default at f0 Shear speed cS = 0.458·ρ + 545.52 (270 kHz); cS = 0.386·ρ + 815.51 (836 kHz) slope and intercept interpolated linearly in f. At 500 kHz: 0.429·ρ + 655.2, i.e. 1448 m/s at ρ = 1850 (cortical layer), 1384 m/s at ρ = 1700 (trabecular layer). Extrapolated, with a warning, outside 270–836 kHz Shear attenuation 57 Np/m (270 kHz), 373 Np/m (836 kHz), one value for the whole skull power law through both points: 43.63 dB/(cm·MHz^1.662); 0.68 Np/cm at 300 kHz, 1.59 Np/cm at 500 kHz Longitudinal attenuation 33 Np/m (270 kHz), 231 Np/m (836 kHz), from Pichardo et al. 2011; the shear values were fitted with these power law through both points: 27.31 dB/(cm·MHz^1.722); 0.40 Np/cm at 300 kHz, 0.95 Np/cm at 500 kHz

The shear-speed fits are BabelBrain's DensityToSSoSPichardo before averaging: BabelBrain uses their mean over the two frequencies (0.422·ρ + 680.5).

Why the skull longitudinal attenuation is replaced. The shear attenuation was fitted together with this longitudinal attenuation, so the pair is used as a set. The fluid/pCT skull values are fits for a fluid model, which have to absorb mode-conversion losses into the longitudinal attenuation. Set long_attenuation: medium to keep them anyway. The sources disagree by about 2×: Gao et al. (2026) used 0.5 Np/cm at 500 kHz with the same k-Wave solver (Pichardo pair: 0.95; PRESTUS fluid default 13.3 dB/(cm·MHz): 0.77).

Poisson-ratio floor. Combining a density-based shear speed with a density-based compressional speed can give unphysical bone. For example, the Gao et al. shear mapping with the k-Plan cL mapping gives ν ≈ 0 at ρ ≈ 1300 kg/m³; BabelBrain disables shear on its CT path for this reason. The Pichardo mapping is better behaved, but at ρ = 1200 kg/m³ it still gives ν from 0.17 (250 kHz) down to ≈0 (836 kHz), because cS rises with frequency while cL does not. poisson_min caps cS in those voxels and the run log reports how many.

Resolution. The slowest shear wave sets the grid requirement. A warning is issued below min_ppw_shear (6; Gao et al. used 6.6 with k-Wave, Pichardo et al. 8 with 4th-order FDTD). At 0.5 mm, 300 kHz gives ≈7.4 points per wavelength for cS = 1105 m/s (ρ = 1200); 500 kHz needs ≈0.39 mm.

How the elastic run differs from the fluid run Step Fluid kwave kwave_elastic Medium sound_speed, density, alpha_coeff/alpha_power the same maps, plus sound_speed_shear and alpha_coeff_shear in the skull and (by default) elastic.alpha_coeff_long as skull longitudinal attenuation (medium_elastic_properties, called from acoustic_wrapper with the final density map and skull masks) Absorption power law, alpha_power (remapped to y = 2 by fit_alpha_power) Kelvin-Voigt, fixed y = 2; every coefficient is rescaled so the attenuation at the source frequency is exact Source pressure source p_mask, p equivalent normal-stress source s_mask = p_mask, sxx = syy = szz = −p. k-Wave scales both by 2·dt·c0/dx and records p = −(sxx+syy+szz)/3, so the injected pressure is the same Solver kspaceFirstOrder3D/2D/AS, MATLAB or C++ pstdElastic3D/2D, MATLAB CPU or GPU (DataCast) Free-water baseline fluid solver same elastic solver (cS = 0), so ISPPA scaling uses one forward model

The fluid kwave_medium returned to the pipeline is unchanged; thermal simulation, NIfTI export and the report use it as for a fluid run. With simulation.debug: 1, the shear speed and shear absorption grids are written to debug/medium/matrix_*_shear*.nii.gz.

items.title: Elastic Model Limitations and Cost
items.text:
• Compute and memory: pstdElastic3D holds ≈65–75 single-precision arrays of the padded grid (split stress and velocity fields, staggered material maps, derivatives), i.e. ≈0.27–0.30 GB per million voxels, or ≈26–30 GB for a 512×512×384 padded grid. Runtime is several times that of the C++/CUDA fluid solver (MATLAB time loop, ~3× the FFT work); Gao et al. report ~15 min for 320×256×384 on an RTX 3090 at CFL 0.3. Keep grid.source_cfl ≤ 0.3; the PRESTUS default 0.15 is conservative.
  • Not supported: axisymmetric grids and C++/CUDA binaries. Nonlinearity (BonA) is not passed to the elastic solver.
  • Property uncertainty: the shear properties come from few ex vivo skulls (Pichardo et al. 2017: 3 formalin-fixed skulls plus 1 for validation; Gao et al. 2026: 1 skull). Gao et al. note that no single property set fits all incidence angles, so treat absolute values with caution.
  • Caches: the acoustic result cache is not keyed on the backend. Use a distinct io.output_affix when comparing kwave and kwave_elastic runs.
References
  • Gao, Y., et al. Influence of shear waves on transcranial ultrasound propagation in cortical brain regions. IEEE Trans. Biomed. Eng. 73(3):1298–1306 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1109/TBME.2025.3603836
  • Pichardo, S., et al. A viscoelastic model for the prediction of transcranial ultrasound propagation: application for the estimation of shear acoustic properties in the human skull. Phys. Med. Biol. 62(17):6938 (2017). https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6560/aa7ccc
  • White, P. J., Clement, G. T., & Hynynen, K. Longitudinal and shear mode ultrasound propagation in human skull bone. Ultrasound Med. Biol. 32(7):1085–1096 (2006). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultrasmedbio.2006.03.015

items.title: Limited Acoustic FOV
items.text:
A full acoustic simulation on a whole-head grid is slow and memory-intensive when only the focal zone and near field matter. The acoustic FOV crops the acoustic domain (k-Wave, BabelBrain or jwave) to a beam-axis-aligned box before the simulation and back-projects the result onto the full grid afterwards. A box that misses part of the beam or the focus gives a wrong field, so its size has to enclose both.

On this page:

  • Quick Start: the two keys that switch the FOV on.
  • FOV Box Geometry: where the box starts and how auto sizes it.
  • Choosing FOV Dimensions: what too small and too large boxes do, with starting values.
  • Thermal Grid: why the thermal simulation keeps the full grid by default.
  • Multi-Transducer Setups: FOV boxes for coherent, async and independent runs.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Optional: for large grids, fine resolutions or many runs.
  • Before you start: A working head simulation to compare against.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text:
Add the following keys to your study YAML (or set them on the parameters struct before calling prestus_pipeline_start):

grid:
  acoustic_fov_diameter_mm: 60   # lateral width [mm], centred on the focus
  acoustic_fov_length_mm:  120   # axial depth [mm], starting at the transducer

Choose values that enclose the focal zone and any near-field region of interest. The pipeline prints the resulting sub-grid dimensions and offset at runtime, so you can check the crop before a full run.

items.title: FOV Box Geometry
items.text:
The FOV is a rectangular box in the beam-axis-aligned acoustic grid:

Dimension Extent Anchor Axial (beam axis, z in transducer_axis mode) acoustic_fov_length_mm starts at the bowl apex (trans_pos) Lateral (x, y) acoustic_fov_diameter_mm (full width) centred on the focal point

The axial start sits at the bowl apex rather than at the focus, so the whole near field between transducer and focus is captured; this matters for skull heating metrics. The axial end should extend at least a few wavelengths beyond the focus to avoid boundary artefacts from the PML. acoustic_fov_length_mm: 'auto' sets the length to the apex-to-focus distance (trans_pos to focus_pos) plus grid.z_beyond_focus_mm (default 40 mm); acoustic_fov_diameter_mm: 'auto' uses the outer element diameter of transducer(1). The box is clamped to the full acoustic grid. If acoustic_fov_length_mm is too short for the focus to fall inside, a warning is raised; increase acoustic_fov_length_mm.

items.title: Choosing FOV Dimensions
items.text:
Parameter Too small Too large acoustic_fov_length_mm Focus outside FOV: warning, clamped focal position, incorrect simulation No harm; wastes grid voxels acoustic_fov_diameter_mm Lateral beam clipped, boundary reflections near focus No harm; wastes grid voxels

Recommended starting values for a single-element transducer at a ~70 mm depth:

acoustic_fov_diameter_mm: 60    # 3–4× the −6 dB beam diameter at focus
acoustic_fov_length_mm:  120    # bowl apex–focus distance + 40 mm (grid.z_beyond_focus_mm default)

At 2 mm resolution this box is roughly 30 × 30 × 60 voxels (54 k), compared with a whole-head grid of 256 × 216 × 192 mm (the benchmark grid; 128 × 108 × 96 voxels, 1.3 M): a ~96 % reduction in voxel count. Print the actual reduction at runtime:

fprintf('FOV: [%s]  full: [%s]  reduction: %.1f %%\n', ...
    num2str(parameters.grid.dims), num2str(full_ac_dims), ...
    100*(1 - prod(parameters.grid.dims)/prod(full_ac_dims)));

items.title: Thermal Grid
items.text: Thermal conduction has a much longer spatial scale than the acoustic focal zone. Heat deposited at the focus diffuses into surrounding tissue over the sonication duration. Cropping the thermal domain would suppress heat loss to surrounding tissue (overestimating the peak temperature rise), miss heating of non-target structures just outside the FOV (such as the skull surface), and give incorrect boundary conditions at the crop edges. By default (grid.thermal_use_acoustic_fov: 0) the thermal stage therefore restores the full grid and back-projects the acoustic field onto it. With grid.thermal_use_acoustic_fov: 1, the thermal simulation runs inside the acoustic FOV box instead; this is faster, but the cooling boundary is less accurate. For faster thermal simulations, use grid.thermal_resolution_mm (coarser grid) or grid.thermal_fov_mm (explicit thermal crop, for prototyping only; see the caveat in doc_parameters.md).

items.title: Multi-Transducer Setups
items.text:
The FOV works in both multi-transducer couplings (details):

  • Coherent (all transducers in one run): the FOV box is the union of one box per transducer, each around that transducer's own beam axis, and every transducer's position is moved into the FOV grid. 'auto' is resolved per transducer.
  • Async (transducer_coupling: async): each transducer's acoustic run has its own FOV box; combine_async_intensity back-projects each field onto its full grid before combining, in shared and per_transducer grid mode.

Coherent fields can also be built from per-transducer limited-FOV runs by adding their complex fields (io.save_p_complex, superpose_complex_fields); the sum is complete only where the FOV boxes overlap.

For independent limited-FOV acoustic runs outside async mode, combine them with assemble_limited_fov_fields before thermal:

assemble_limited_fov_fields( ...
    {'sub-001_layered_results_t1.mat', 'sub-001_layered_results_t2.mat'}, ...
    'sub-001_layered_results_combined.mat', ...
    [target_t1_wcm2, target_t2_wcm2]);

The assembler back-projects each sub-grid onto the shared full acoustic grid, sums the intensities incoherently, and writes a combined cache that the thermal pipeline reads as a normal full-grid result. See doc_multitransducer.md for the full multi-transducer workflow.

Pipeline stages, cache and functions Stage Effect Medium setup (Stage 4) Full-grid state is saved before the crop. FOV crop acoustic_grid_fov crops kwave_medium, medium_masks, segmentation, trans_pos, focus_pos, and parameters.grid.dims to the sub-grid. Source/sensor setup (Stage 5) kgrid and the source matrix are built on the sub-grid. Acoustic simulation (Stage 6) k-Wave runs on the sub-grid; sensor_data.p_max_all is sub-grid sized. Acoustic analysis and NIfTI export (Stage 7) Analysis runs on the sub-grid; outputs are back-projected to the full grid before NIfTI writing, so the spatial location is correct. Thermal setup (Stage 8) Full-grid state is restored. sensor_data.p_max_all is back-projected to the full grid via fov_backproject_volume. kgrid is rebuilt from the full-grid parameters via thermal_grid_setup. With grid.thermal_use_acoustic_fov: 1, the FOV sub-grid is kept and only the T1 ↔ grid affines are shifted by the crop offset. Thermal simulation and analysis (Stages 8–9) Runs on the full grid, or on the FOV sub-grid with grid.thermal_use_acoustic_fov: 1.

The acoustic cache (.mat file) stores the sub-grid pressure field together with the crop metadata (acoustic_provenance.fov_offset_ac and acoustic_provenance.full_ac_dims). This keeps the cache small and lets assemble_limited_fov_fields back-project and combine multiple limited-FOV results from independent transducer placements.

Function Role acoustic_grid_fov Crops medium, masks and positions to the FOV sub-grid; returns the crop offset. fov_backproject_volume Zero-pads a FOV-sized array back to a given full-grid size. assemble_limited_fov_fields Back-projects and incoherently combines N limited-FOV acoustic caches for multi-transducer thermal simulation. thermal_grid_setup Rebuilds kgrid and resamples medium/masks for the thermal stage, on the full acoustic grid or, with grid.thermal_use_acoustic_fov: 1, on the FOV sub-grid.

items.title: Medium Properties
items.text:
The medium sets the sound speed, density and attenuation the simulated wave travels through, and the thermal properties that govern heating. Whether you simulate free water or a head, and which tissue properties you assume, therefore shapes the predicted focus, intensity and temperature rise. This page shows how to choose the medium and which tissue properties PRESTUS assumes by default.

On this page:

  • Choosing the Medium: the water, layered and phantom media and what each needs.
  • Default Tissue Properties: the acoustic and thermal defaults per tissue, and how much of the attenuation heats the tissue.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To choose between a free-water and a head simulation, or to change tissue properties (e.g. for a more conservative estimate).
  • Before you start: Nothing; the defaults apply until you change them.

items.title: Choosing the Medium
items.text:
Set simulation.medium to one of three values:

Medium What is simulated Needs water The transducer in homogeneous water, placed at the inner edge of the requested PML layer. Free-water specifications and measurements refer to this. No images layered A head built from the SimNIBS segmentation. With the default layers and a charm segmentation: water (including CSF), brain, skin, cortical skull bone and trabecular skull bone; the default skull layer has no charm label and is dropped. See Layer mapping and smoothing. The skull can instead take voxel-wise properties from a (pseudo-)CT. T1 (and T2/UTE), SimNIBS phantom A designed test object. The segmentation file is mapped onto medium masks without rotation, cropping or other preprocessing. A final_tissues.nii.gz in a (dummy) SimNIBS output folder 
simulation:
  medium: layered

Which layers a layered simulation contains is set under layers. A layer whose segmentation label is missing is dropped from the run. The HTML report lists the layers that were modelled and their properties.

A phantom NIfTI holds artificial layers of a SimNIBS segmentation. It covers the simulation domain only: the PML is added outside the grid. Its voxels must be isotropic. The phantom medium accepts the same layers flexibility as layered, but applies no image processing, so 2D phantoms are a quick way to benchmark or debug.

items.title: Default Tissue Properties
items.text:
The properties below apply in a full layered simulation. They are set under medium_properties in config_default.yaml (Parameters) and can be changed per tissue in your study config, for example for a more conservative estimate of intensity or heating. The defaults follow the literature and commercially available tools; they are not ground truth. The uncertainty mode runs the ITRUSST bounds for you.

Tissue Density [kg/m³] Sound speed [m/s] Attenuation coefficient [dB/(cm·MHz^y)] Attenuation power law (y) Thermal conductivity [W/(m·K)] Specific heat [J/(kg·K)] Perfusion [mL/min/kg] Absorption fraction Equivalent absorption coefficient [dB/(cm·MHz^y)] Water 994 1500 0.00217 2 0.6 4178 0 1 0.00217 Brain 1046 1546 0.59 1.2 0.51 3630 559 1 0.59 Skin 1090 1610 0.4 1 0.37 3391 106 1 0.4 Skull (single layer) 1850 2800 13.3 1 0.32 1793 20 0.28 3.78 Skull (cortical) 1850 2800 13.3 1 0.32 1313 10 0.28 3.78 Skull (trabecular) 1700 2300 13.3 1 0.32 2274 30 0.28 3.78

The defaults set absorption_fraction; absorption_coeff stays empty. The last column is the coefficient to set instead (for skull, the Pinton et al. value from which the fraction 0.28 is rounded).

# example: a more conservative skull for heating
medium_properties:
  skull_cortical:
    absorption_fraction: 0.5

items.title: Absorption Fraction for Heating
items.text:
For thermal simulations, PRESTUS uses only part of the attenuation as absorbed energy in the bioheat equation. Each tissue sets either absorption_fraction (a fraction of alpha_coeff) or absorption_coeff (a coefficient in dB/(cm·MHz^y) used directly); setting one empties the other (Heat deposition).

The skull default of 0.28 lies between the BabelBrain default (16 %) and the k-Plan default (100 %). More measurements are needed to narrow the uncertainty about how much acoustic energy the skull absorbs.

Where the skull absorption fraction comes from

The bulk attenuation coefficient includes contributions from both longitudinal and shear waves. Longitudinal waves contribute most (about 80 %, Wang et al., 2018) to absorption and heating in the skull (Pinton et al., 2012; White et al., 2006). For longitudinal and shear waves, absorption values of 2.7 dB/(cm·MHz) and 5.4 dB/(cm·MHz) have been reported (Pinton et al., 2012), with a bulk attenuation of 13.3 dB/(cm·MHz). PRESTUS therefore assumes absorption fraction = (longitudinal absorption + 0.2 × shear absorption) / bulk attenuation = (2.7 + 0.2 × 5.4) / 13.3 = 0.28. The equivalent absorption_coeff is 2.7 + 0.2 × 5.4 = 3.78 dB/(cm·MHz).

References
  • Pinton, G., Aubry, J., Bossy, E., Muller, M., Pernot, M., & Tanter, M. Attenuation, scattering, and absorption of ultrasound in the skull bone. Med Phys 39, 299–307 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1118/1.3668316
  • Wang, X.-D., Lin, W.-J., Su, C., & Wang, X.-M. Influence of mode conversions in the skull on transcranial focused ultrasound and temperature fields utilizing the wave field separation method: A numerical study. Chin Phys B 27, 024302 (2018). https://doi.org/10.1088/1674-1056/27/2/024302
  • White, P. J., Clement, G. T., & Hynynen, K. Longitudinal and shear mode ultrasound propagation in human skull bone. Ultrasound Med Biol 32, 1085–1096 (2006). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultrasmedbio.2006.03.015

items.title: Modules
items.text:
A run segments the head, places the transducer and simulates acoustics and heating, and segmentation alone can take an hour or more. Each stage of prestus_pipeline is switched on or off with a modules.* flag in the config. This allows partial runs: re-running only the analysis after changing output thresholds, or stopping after segmentation before committing to a full simulation.

On this page:

  • Common partial-run patterns: the settings for frequent partial runs.
  • Pipeline stages: the stage order and the flag of each stage.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To run only part of the pipeline, e.g. segmentation first, or heating on top of an earlier acoustic run.
  • Before you start: Nothing.

items.title: Common Partial-Run Patterns
items.text:
Goal Settings Run SimNIBS segmentation only modules.segmentation_only = 1 Reuse a heuristic / PlanTUS / TUS_entry placement Nothing to set: placement.reuse: auto reuses a recorded run whose settings match; always requires one. See Starting from earlier stage outputs Thermal simulation (or analysis) on a completed acoustic run path.acoustic_input: <earlier run>/nii/sub-XXX_<medium>_T1w<affix>_pressure.nii.gz; keep the other modules on (grid and medium take seconds to a minute). The map is rescaled to transducer.target_isppa_wcm2 from its sidecar Regenerate analysis outputs from the acoustic cache run_acoustic_sims = 0, run_heating_sims = 0 (the acoustic stage then loads cache/…_results….mat, which the earlier run only wrote with io.save_acoustic_matrices: 1). Without that cache, use path.acoustic_input as above Skip free-water reference modules.run_posthoc_water_sims = 0 Run thermal at a specific free-water ISPPA transducer.target_isppa_wcm2: 30 (with modules.run_water_baseline: auto, the free-water baseline runs when the target needs it); see ISPPA targeting Report the field at the simulated drive (elem_p_amp) transducer.target_isppa_wcm2: [] Run thermal at multiple ISPPAs (parallel jobs) transducer.target_isppa_wcm2: [10, 20, 30, 50] triggers multi-ISPPA mode; see Multi-intensity sweeps Simulate two or more transducers asynchronously simulation.transducer_coupling: async with multiple transducer entries; see Multi-transducer Always record the free-water baseline modules.run_water_baseline: 1 (auto, the default, runs it only when a target needs it) Generate a cross-subject group report modules.generate_group_report = 1 (or run prestus_group_report_start manually); see Group HTML report Run many subjects with per-subject settings study.manifest + prestus_study_start(config); see Study setup

Note

Downstream modules depend on outputs from upstream ones. Within-run caches in cache/ are reused subject to io.overwrite_files, and a reused grid or medium cache must match the current settings (Cache reuse checks). The grid, medium and acoustic caches are only written when io.save_grid_cache, io.save_medium_cache and io.save_acoustic_matrices (or io.save_matrices) are on; by default they are not. If a stage is switched off and its cache does not exist, the stage does not stop the run: the grid and medium stages continue with empty results, and the acoustic and thermal stages report that no results are available and skip their analysis. To start a run from the results of an earlier one, use its stage outputs instead (Starting from earlier stage outputs).

items.title: Pipeline Stages
items.text:
prestus_pipeline_start decides where a run executes (local MATLAB or an HPC job) and hands uncertainty, pose-workflow, async multi-transducer and multi-ISPPA runs to their own pipelines (pose workflow: Time Reversal). prestus_pipeline then runs the stages below. How PRESTUS works describes what each stage reads, writes and caches.

Stage diagram 
load_parameters                 toolbox default → project default → study config (+ overrides)
      │
prestus_pipeline_start          platform: matlab | slurm | qsub;  special modes, in this order:
      │                           simulation.uncertainty = 1           → uncertainty_pipeline
      │                           time_reversal.pose_workflow.enabled  → pose_workflow_pipeline
      │                           async coupling                       → async_transducer_pipeline
      │                           target_isppa_wcm2 is a vector        → multi_isppa_pipeline
      │
prestus_pipeline
      │  special modes (run instead of the stages below):
      │    simulation.uncertainty = 1          → uncertainty_pipeline
      │    target_isppa_wcm2 is a vector       → multi_isppa_pipeline
      │    time_reversal.pose_workflow.enabled → pose_workflow_pipeline
      │    modules.combine_async = 1           → combine_async_intensity
      ▼
[1 segmentation]        SimNIBS charm (layered media only)
      │                 modules.segmentation_only = 1 → stop here
      ▼
[2 placement]           modules.run_transducer_placement
      │                 placement.mode → trans_pos / focus_pos in T1 voxels
      ▼
[3 grid]                modules.run_grid_setup              (grid cache)
      │                 reorient, crop, smooth the head; positions → grid voxels
      ▼
[4 medium]              modules.run_medium_setup            (medium cache)
      │                 tissue labels / pseudo-CT → acoustic & thermal properties
      │                 NIfTI export of masks and property maps
      ▼
[  acoustic FOV crop]   grid.acoustic_fov_*  (optional sub-grid for the acoustic run)
      ▼
[5 source]              modules.run_source_setup
      │                 kWaveArray / mask source, sensor, CFL check
      ▼
[  free-water baseline] modules.run_water_baseline (auto | 1 | 0)
      │                 free-water ISPPA of the current drive, for target_isppa_wcm2 scaling
      ▼
[  time reversal]       time_reversal.enabled  (refocusing phases, aberration report, pose search; skipped with BabelBrain)
      │                 time_reversal.only = 1 → stop here (no water baseline either)
      ▼
[6 acoustic]            modules.run_acoustic_sims           (acoustic cache)
      │                 k-Wave / jwave / BabelBrain, or a prior pressure map (path.acoustic_input);
      │                 field scaled to target_isppa_wcm2; dry-run backends stop here
      ▼
[7 acoustic analysis]   modules.run_acoustic_analysis
      │                 Isppa, MI, focal metrics → CSV; NIfTI (modules.run_nifti_creation);
      │                 targeting accuracy (modules.run_targeting_analysis)
      │                 BabelBrain input export (io.export_babelbrain)
      ▼
[8 thermal]             modules.run_heating_sims
      │                 k-Wave diffusion or BabelBrain BHTE over the timing protocol
      ▼
[9 thermal analysis]    modules.run_thermal_analysis
      │                 peak temperature, CEM43 → CSV; NIfTI
      ▼
[10 reports]            modules.generate_report / generate_group_report /
      │                 multi_isppa_report / uncertainty_report
      ▼
[11 post-hoc water]     modules.run_posthoc_water_sims  (one water run per transducer)
      ▼
[12 sequential]         options.sequential_configs  (follow-up run on the same medium)

items.title: Multi-ISPPA Mode
items.text:
Heating and safety metrics depend on the intensity a study applies, and choosing one often means comparing several candidates. In the linear regime the pressure field scales with the square root of intensity, so this mode runs the acoustic simulation once and scales it to each target before a separate thermal simulation. The scaling holds only below the onset of nonlinear effects; at very high targets the scaled field may not be valid.

On this page:

  • Configuration: giving several target intensities.
  • Output files: per-target files and the summary report.
  • Validity of post-hoc scaling: when one acoustic result can serve every target.
  • Resuming a partial run: re-running a partial sweep, stages and HPC options.
  • Combining with uncertainty mode: running a sweep for each uncertainty variant.
  • Combining with async transducers: per-transducer targets and sweeps.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To compare heating and safety metrics across candidate intensities without repeating the acoustic simulation.
  • Before you start: A study config whose single-intensity run works; targets within the linear regime (below roughly 50–100 W/cm² free-water).

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Give transducer.target_isppa_wcm2 more than one value:

transducer:
  target_isppa_wcm2: [10, 20, 30, 50]   # W/cm²; triggers multi-ISPPA mode
  elem_p_amp: ...
  # ... other transducer fields

PRESTUS then runs one acoustic simulation, caches it, and runs the thermal analysis at each requested intensity, each with its own output files and HTML report, plus a summary report. The free-water baseline that the scaling needs runs automatically (modules.run_water_baseline: auto, the default); see ISPPA targeting. In the Nexus, Sweep… next to the target ISPPA (Transducer tab) edits the list.

Note

The older form calibration.target_isppa_wcm2 is still accepted and is moved to transducer(1).target_isppa_wcm2 at load time with a deprecation warning.

items.title: Output Files
items.text:
Each thermal stage writes output under its own affix. For target_isppa_wcm2: [10, 30]:

sub-001_layered_desc-isppa010.csv
sub-001_layered_report_desc-isppa010.html
sub-001_layered_desc-isppa030.csv
sub-001_layered_report_desc-isppa030.html
sub-001_layered_desc-multiIsppa_report.html   ← summary

items.title: Validity of Post-Hoc Scaling
items.text:
The acoustic simulation (k-Wave skull propagation) is the expensive step. In the linear acoustic regime the pressure field scales as \(p \propto \sqrt{I}\), so one acoustic result serves every target. Linear scaling is valid when:

  • the acoustic simulation was run in the linear regime (target amplitudes below the onset of nonlinear harmonic generation, roughly < 50–100 W/cm² free-water for typical TUS setups);
  • the spatial pressure pattern is the same at all target intensities (guaranteed in the linear regime);
  • the thermal simulation uses the scaled pressure as input (the pipeline scales sensor_data.p_max_all before thermal_simulation is called).

A warning is printed if the scale factor relative to the baseline exceeds 4× or falls below 0.25×. Large scale factors mean the baseline and target are far apart in amplitude; at very high targets, nonlinear effects may invalidate the scaled field.

items.title: Resuming a Partial Run
items.text:
Each stage checks for its sentinel output file before submitting (HPC) or running (MATLAB). Re-running prestus_pipeline_start with the same config resumes a partially completed run; completed stages are skipped. With io.overwrite_files: always (default), only the acoustic stage resumes from its cache; thermal and summary stages always re-run. force re-runs every stage. See Overwrite behaviour.

Pipeline stages and HPC options 
[Stage 1]   Acoustic simulation + water baseline
            Runs once at the configured elem_p_amp.
            Saves sensor_data + acoustic_provenance.freefield_isppa_wcm2.
            No thermal simulation.

[Stage 2…N] Thermal analysis: one job per target_isppa_wcm2
            Loads cached acoustic results.
            Scales p_max_all by sqrt(target / baseline).
            Runs thermal simulation and analysis.
            Writes output files with affix _desc-isppaNNN (NNN = integer W/cm²).
            Generates per-target HTML report.

[Stage N+1] Summary report (optional, default: on)
            Aggregates results across all target intensities.

On HPC (SLURM/qsub), stages 2…N are submitted in parallel with an afterok dependency on stage 1. The summary depends on all thermal jobs.

Pass an options struct to prestus_pipeline_start to control per-stage resources:

options.acoustic_timelimit  = '08:00:00';   % wall time for stage 1
options.thermal_timelimit   = '02:00:00';   % wall time per thermal job
options.summary_timelimit   = '00:30:00';   % wall time for summary
options.acoustic_memorylimit = 80;           % GB for stage 1
options.thermal_memorylimit  = 40;           % GB per thermal job
options.generate_summary_report = false;     % skip summary stage

items.title: Combining with Uncertainty Mode
items.text:
Multi-ISPPA mode and uncertainty mode compose. When both simulation.uncertainty = true and transducer.target_isppa_wcm2 is a vector, uncertainty is the outer mode and each variant runs its own multi-ISPPA pipeline:

Stage 1    preproc / source setup                      (shared)
Variants   default, Temp-H, Temp-L, Trans-H, Trans-L, each:  (after stage 1)
             acoustic + free-water baseline
             thermal: one job per target               (_desc-temphigh_desc-isppa030 …;
                                                        none for Trans-H/L)
             multi-ISPPA summary
Stage 7    uncertainty report: one per target          (after every variant job)

Affixes compose: the variant affix (_desc-temphigh) prefixes the per-target affix, yielding _desc-temphigh_desc-isppa030. Each target gets an uncertainty report comparing the five variants at that intensity, e.g. sub-001_layered_desc-uncertainty_report_desc-isppa030.html (with the base io.output_affix before the target suffix when one is set). No report aggregates across intensities. See doc_uncertainty.md.

items.title: Combining with Async Transducers
items.text:
When simulation.transducer_coupling = 'async' and multiple transducers are defined, each transducer carries its own target_isppa_wcm2. The async pipeline scales each transducer's pressure field independently before summing intensities incoherently. If any transducer has a vector target, one combine+thermal pair is run per sweep point. See doc_multitransducer.md.

See also: doc_calibration.md, doc_uncertainty.md, doc_modules.md

items.title: Multi-Transducer Modelling
items.text:
When several transducers sonicate the same head, the exposure depends on how their fields combine, which a run per transducer does not capture. PRESTUS simulates them in one layered setup: transducers that fire together (coherent) add as complex pressures and interfere, while for transducers that fire in separate windows (async) acoustic safety metrics take the per-voxel maximum of the fields and heating uses the sum of their intensities.

On this page:

  • Configuration: listing transducers and choosing how they fire.
  • Grid setup: how the grid is aligned and cropped around several beams.
  • ISPPA targets: per-transducer free-water targets and their baselines.
  • Complex pressure field: saving fields and superposing them afterwards at any relative phase.
  • Partial acoustic FOV: limited fields of view with several transducers.
  • Known limitations: what refers to the first transducer only, and unsupported setups.
  • Subpages: async firing in separate windows.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Bilateral or dual-site stimulation, or any protocol with more than one transducer on the head.
  • Before you start: A layered (skull) simulation in a 3-D grid; one equipment entry and placement per transducer.

Experimental support

See this pull request for examples.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
List several transducers in a layered simulation:

transducer:
  - name: right
    serial: IS_PCD15473_01001
    combo: {ds_serial: IGT_32_ch_comb_10_ch}
    # ... trans_pos, focus_pos, focal_distance_ep

  - name: left
    serial: IS_PCD15473_01001
    combo: {ds_serial: IGT_32_ch_comb_10_ch}
    # ...

simulation.transducer_coupling sets how the transducers fire:

Firing Setting Simultaneously, same frequency, known phase coherent (default): one k-Wave run with all sources active; the fields interfere. All transducers must share the fundamental frequency (a warning is issued otherwise). In separate, non-overlapping windows async: see Async Multi-Transducer Mode. In sequence, or with partial overlap Use Sequential Simulations: carry each heating run's temperature and CEM43 maps into the next via adopted_heatmap / adopted_cem43. This assumes the acoustic fields do not overlap in time.

In the Nexus, Multi-transducer coupling (Sonication tab, shown once the config has more than one transducer) selects the row above, and Target free-water Isppa is set per transducer on the Transducer tab. The card can show an analytic prediction of both forms: the at-target intensity when the beams add independently and its range over their relative phase when coherent, and free-water maps of both in the beams' plane. The maps use Gaussian focal spots from each transducer's aperture and focal distance, with no skull and no side lobes; they guide the choice and do not replace the simulation.

items.title: Grid Alignment
items.text:
The default focal_axis mode rotates the grid so that the mean beam axis of all transducers aligns with z. Beams are averaged as axes, not directions, so opposed (bilateral) beams do not cancel: z bisects their two axes. Each beam off z is drawn obliquely on the grid, which costs accuracy at coarse resolution (for async runs, see async_grid_mode: per_transducer).

grid:
  mode: 'focal_axis'   # default; omit to get the same behaviour

With three or more transducers whose axes are too spread to average (mean-axis norm below grid.focal_axis_min_norm, default 0.5), focal_axis falls back to transducer(1)'s axis and warns.

To align the grid to transducer(1)'s focal axis instead, set transducer_axis. ras_plus keeps the RAS+ orientation without rotation (isotropic rescaling only), so every beam is oblique; it does not work with grid.axisymmetric. See Preprocessing: Orientation for the mode table. In the Nexus, Placement ▸ Transducers shows the grid z axis and each beam's tilt for the chosen mode.

items.title: Grid Cropping
items.text: The grid is cropped to the bounding box that encloses the CSF-expanded head tissue and the bowl geometry of every transducer. See Preprocessing: Cropping.

items.title: ISPPA Targets
items.text:
transducer(k).target_isppa_wcm2 is the free-water ISPPA of transducer k alone, for every coupling mode. Each transducer has its own drive (elem_p_amp), so the target rescales that transducer's drive, not the combined field.

simulation:
  transducer_coupling: coherent
transducer:
  - name: left
    serial: IS_PCD15473_01001
    target_isppa_wcm2: 20     # left transducer alone: 20 W/cm² in free water
  - name: right
    serial: IS_PCD15473_01003
    target_isppa_wcm2: 40     # right transducer alone: 40 W/cm²
Coupling How the targets are applied Sweeps (vector targets) coherent Before the simulation (coherent_drive_calibration): each transducer's elem_p_amp is multiplied by √(target / baseline), where baseline is the free-water ISPPA of that transducer alone at its configured drive. The combined field is simulated at these drives and not rescaled afterwards. Not available. Errors (prestus:isppa:coherentSweep); run one config per point, or use async. async After the per-transducer simulations: each field is scaled to its own target in combine_async_intensity, then combined. Yes: one acoustic run per transducer, one combine + thermal pair per sweep point (see Async Multi-Transducer Mode).

Coherent baseline. The rule is the same as for one transducer (ISPPA targeting). If the target matches the transducer's calibration ISPPA (tx_calibration.isppa_wcm2) within 1 %, the calibration is the baseline. Otherwise PRESTUS simulates that transducer alone in water (others at zero amplitude, same grid). With N transducers that is up to N extra free-water simulations. A transducer with target_isppa_wcm2: [] keeps its configured drive.

Provenance and cache checks

The result records targets, baselines, their source and the drive scale in acoustic_provenance.coherent_drive. The combined free-water ISPPA (both firing) is reported but is not a target. A coherent cache without coherent_drive is refused when targets are set (prestus:isppa:coherentWithoutDriveCalibration): re-run its acoustic simulation. path.acoustic_input cannot be rescaled per transducer and errors when targets are set.

items.title: Complex Pressure Field
items.text:
io:
  save_p_complex: true

This writes sub-XXX_<medium>_p_complex<affix>.mat with the complex amplitude at the fundamental on the simulation grid, at the simulated drive level, before ISPPA rescaling. Propagation in PRESTUS is linear, so fields simulated one at a time can be summed. superpose_complex_fields does this on one shared grid, back-projecting limited-FOV fields:

out = superpose_complex_fields({'.../sub-001_layered_p_complex_trans-01.mat', ...
                                '.../sub-001_layered_p_complex_trans-02.mat'});
out.p_coherent    % |p1 + p2|          coherent (simultaneous) firing
out.p_incoherent  % sqrt(|p1|^2+|p2|^2) async heat source
out.p_max         % max(|p1|, |p2|)    async peak pressure
out = superpose_complex_fields(files, Weights=[1, exp(1i*pi/2)]);   % relative phase of transducer 2

One async run (async_grid_mode: shared) with io.save_p_complex: true therefore also gives the coherent field for any relative amplitude and phase, without another simulation. Fields on different grids (per_transducer mode) and fields at different frequencies are not combined. Storing p_complex takes a lot of memory on fine grids.

File contents
  • p_complex: complex amplitude at the fundamental on the simulation grid (the acoustic FOV sub-grid with a limited FOV), at the simulated drive level, before ISPPA rescaling. The phase refers to t = 0 of the simulation, when every source starts.
  • p_complex_info: phase_reference ('simulation_t0'), freq_hz, record_t0_s, dt_s, drive_level ('simulated'), grid_dims, and fov_offset_ac / full_ac_dims with a limited FOV.

Files without p_complex_info are accepted only all together, with a warning (valid only for runs with the same time step and length).

items.title: Partial Acoustic FOV
items.text:
A limited acoustic FOV (grid.acoustic_fov_diameter_mm, grid.acoustic_fov_length_mm) works with several transducers:

  • Coherent: the FOV box is the union of one box per transducer, each enclosing a cylinder of the FOV diameter along that transducer's beam axis. 'auto' is resolved per transducer (its outer element diameter; its focal depth + grid.z_beyond_focus_mm). For opposite transducers the union spans most of the head, so the saving is mostly lateral.
  • Async: each transducer's run gets its own FOV box. Fields are back-projected onto their full grid before combining, in both grid modes. Partial-FOV and full-grid caches can be mixed.
  • Complex superposition: each field is zero outside its own box, so the sum is complete only where boxes overlap (out.coverage counts the fields per voxel). Make the boxes cover the region around both foci.

The Nexus placement viewer draws every transducer's FOV box.

items.title: Known Limitations
items.text:
• Simulations without a skull or layered setup (e.g. medium: water) only model the first transducer.
  • kWaveArray mode supports multiple transducers only in non-axisymmetric mode (grid.axisymmetric = 1 is single-transducer). Matrix-type transducers in kWaveArray mode assume a +Z beam axis; see Transducer geometry.
  • Different carrier frequencies: time step and PPW (source_sensor_setup) use the highest frequency; Mechanical Index (acoustic_analysis) uses the lowest frequency, which never underestimates MI = p / √f; with io.save_p_complex: true, one *_p_complex_<freq>Hz.mat is written per frequency.
  • Exit-plane metrics (real_focal_distance_ep_mm, real_focal_distance_bowl_mm, max_Isppa_after_exit_plane) refer to the first transducer only.
  • Focal-plane heating plots show only the first transducer's focal plane. Always inspect the 3D maxT and CEM43 NIfTI volumes for a complete safety assessment.
  • Post-hoc water-only simulations are not implemented for multiple transducers.
  • The PRESTUS BabelBrain backend (acoustic_backend / thermal_backend: babelbrain) supports one transducer per run. Multi-transducer runs need kwave or jwave with thermal_backend: kwave. See BabelBrain: Geometry limits.
Comparison with BabelBrain

BabelBrain models one transducer per simulation. It treats several foci of one phased array as time-multiplexed, like PRESTUS async mode: the safety field is the per-voxel maximum of the pressure amplitudes (CalculateFieldProcess.py), and the thermal simulation switches between the spots' fields by duty-cycle share (BHTEMultiplePressureFields in ThermalModeling/CalculateTemperatureEffects.py). It does not add complex fields across foci.

items.title: Subpages
items.text:
• Async Multi-Transducer Mode: for transducers that fire in separate, non-overlapping windows; covers configuration, the physical model, grid modes, outputs and constraints.

See also: doc_calibration.md, doc_multiintensity.md, doc_sequential.md, doc_modules.md, doc_transducer.md

items.title: Async Multi-Transducer Mode
items.text:
When transducers fire in separate, non-overlapping windows, their fields never interfere, so the coherent sum of Multi-Transducer Modelling would misstate the exposure. Async mode simulates each transducer on its own, scales each field to its own ISPPA target, and combines them: acoustic safety metrics take the per-voxel maximum and heating uses the sum of intensities.

On this page:

  • Async Configuration: switching on async mode, per-transducer targets and ISPPA sweeps.
  • Physical Model: how the fields are combined for safety metrics and heating.
  • Grid Geometry Mode: one shared grid or one grid per transducer.
  • Output Files: per-transducer, combined and joint outputs, resumption and HPC stages.
  • Constraints: required grid, head model and regime.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Transducers fire with non-overlapping duty cycles or alternating pulses, or you want an ISPPA sweep across several transducers.
  • Before you start: A multi-transducer layered setup as in Configuration; a 3-D grid.

Experimental

For transducers that fire with non-overlapping duty cycles or alternating pulses, so their fields never superpose coherently. Configure it only with a clear view of the intended exposure and the linear-regime assumptions below.

items.title: Async Configuration
items.text:
Async mode runs when transducer_coupling is 'async' and there is more than one transducer. prestus_pipeline_start(parameters) dispatches to it; no other entry point is needed.

simulation:
  transducer_coupling: async

transducer:
  - name: CTX500-A
    target_isppa_wcm2: 5.0
    freq_hz: 500000
    trans_pos: [x1, y1, z1]
    focus_pos: [fx1, fy1, fz1]
    annular:
      elem_p_amp: 100000

  - name: CTX500-B
    target_isppa_wcm2: 3.0
    freq_hz: 500000
    trans_pos: [x2, y2, z2]
    focus_pos: [fx2, fy2, fz2]
    annular:
      elem_p_amp: 100000

The per-transducer acoustic runs always record a free-water baseline, which the combine step needs for scaling.

Multi-ISPPA sweep. A vector target_isppa_wcm2 triggers a sweep.

Multi-ISPPA sweep

Every transducer carries either a scalar (held fixed) or a vector of the same length:

transducer:
  - name: CTX500-A
    target_isppa_wcm2: [3.0, 5.0, 10.0]   # swept across 3 points

  - name: CTX500-B
    target_isppa_wcm2: 2.0                  # fixed across all 3 sweep points

This gives three combine + thermal pairs (A→3.0, 5.0, 10.0; B→2.0 each time).

items.title: Physical Model
items.text:
Acoustic safety metrics (ISPPA, MI, peak pressure) use the per-voxel maximum of the scaled fields. Thermal heat deposition uses the sum of the transducers' intensities, applied during the pulses of the one timing block: each transducer is assumed to fire with that block's pulse timing, in windows that do not overlap.

Limitation

The thermal model does not represent the firing schedule. The time-averaged heating is exact when every transducer fires with the timing block's duty cycle (DC) in its own window, which requires \(N \cdot \mathrm{DC} \le 100\,\%\). If the transducers share the block's on-time between them (\(\mathrm{DC}_1 + \mathrm{DC}_2 = \mathrm{DC}\)), heating is overestimated by up to \(N\) for \(N\) transducers, also at each focus. Within a pulse, all intensities are applied at once, which slightly raises the short-term temperature peak but not the average.

Equations

Acoustic safety metrics:

\[p_\mathrm{safety} = \max_i\bigl(p_{i,\mathrm{scaled}}\bigr)\]

where \(p_{i,\mathrm{scaled}} = p_i \cdot \sqrt{I_{i,\mathrm{target}} / I_{i,\mathrm{baseline}}}\). This is sensor_data.p_max_async in the combined cache.

Thermal heat deposition:

\[Q_\mathrm{total} \propto \sum_{i=1}^{N} I_i = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{p_{i,\mathrm{scaled}}^2}{2\rho c}\]

This is sensor_data.p_max_all, passed to the bioheat solver as:

\[p_\mathrm{thermal} = \sqrt{2 \cdot I_\mathrm{total} \cdot \rho c}\]

items.title: Grid Geometry Mode
items.text:
simulation.async_grid_mode Grid Use when 'shared' (default) One grid for all transducers, aligned and cropped as in Grid alignment and Grid cropping. Default. 'per_transducer' Each transducer gets the grid a solo run would use. combine_async_intensity resamples every field onto transducer(1)'s grid via each run's planimg sidecar. Per-transducer focal distance, ISPPA or focal volume must match a solo run, or the transducers are widely separated or steeply angled. Grid mode choice and accuracy 
simulation:
  transducer_coupling: async
  async_grid_mode: per_transducer   # default: 'shared'

In shared mode an off-axis beam is voxelised at an angle, so its per-transducer results can differ from a solo run. The difference shrinks with resolution; at 2 mm (2.5 points per wavelength at 300 kHz) a beam 41° off axis lost 16% of its free-water ISPPA. In per_transducer mode the resampling (linear interpolation; parts outside transducer(1)'s grid are dropped) costs accuracy instead. per_transducer scales better with N: each grid stays sized to its own transducer, at the cost of N preproc jobs.

items.title: Output Files
items.text:
Two transducers, one target each:

cache/sub-001_layered_results_trans-01.mat
cache/sub-001_layered_results_trans-02.mat
cache/sub-001_layered_results_desc-asyncCombined.mat
sub-001_layered_desc-asyncJoint.csv
sub-001_layered_report_desc-asyncJoint.html
Sweep and affix naming

A 3-point sweep writes ..._desc-asyncCombinedS01.mat to S03 and sub-001_layered_desc-asyncJointS01.csv to S03.

With io.output_affix (e.g. run1), every affix starts with it: _desc-run1_trans-01, _desc-run1_desc-asyncJoint. The per-transducer runs also write their own CSV and acoustic NIfTIs at the simulated drive level; the Nexus Results tab shows them under the joint result.

Resumption. Re-running prestus_pipeline_start with the same config resumes from the last incomplete stage. With io.overwrite_files: always (default), preproc, acoustic and combine resume from their caches; the joint and water-validation stages always re-run. force re-runs every stage. See Overwrite behaviour.

Pipeline stages, HPC options and provenance Stage Count Affix Preproc 1 (shared) or N (per_transducer, parallel) _desc-asyncPreproc-t01, …, -tNN (per_transducer) Acoustic, at configured elem_p_amp, with water baseline N (parallel) _trans-01, …, _trans-NN Combine: scale each field to target, write p_max_all and p_max_async M sweep points _desc-asyncCombined (M=1) or _desc-asyncCombinedS01… Thermal (kWaveDiffusion) and report M _desc-asyncJoint (M=1) or _desc-asyncJointS01…

On HPC, each acoustic job depends on its preproc job, each combine job on all N acoustic jobs (afterok), and each thermal job on its combine job. prestus_pipeline_start returns the job IDs per stage, so later runs can wait on them:

[~, jobs] = prestus_pipeline_start(parameters);   % jobs.preproc, .acoustic, .combine, .thermal, .water
next.hpc.depend_job_ids = [jobs.preproc, jobs.acoustic];
prestus_pipeline_start(next);

HPC options:

options.acoustic_timelimit   = '06:00:00';   % per acoustic job
options.combine_timelimit    = '00:30:00';   % per combine job (CPU-only, lightweight)
options.thermal_timelimit    = '04:00:00';   % per thermal job
options.acoustic_memorylimit = 60;           % GB
options.thermal_memorylimit  = 40;           % GB
options.acoustic_partition   = 'gpu';
options.combine_partition    = 'cpu';        % combine stage needs no GPU

The combined cache records in acoustic_provenance:

Field Description combined_from Cell array of source cache file paths combination_mode 'async_dual_field': p_max_all holds the thermal intensity sum; p_max_async holds the per-voxel pressure maximum for acoustic safety combination_targets Per-transducer target ISPPAs used for scaling [W/cm²] combination_baselines Per-transducer free-water baselines at the simulated drive level [W/cm²] combination_time Timestamp of the combination step

items.title: Constraints
items.text:
• 3-D grid required. Axisymmetric (2-D) simulations are not supported.
  • Shared head model. All transducers use the same segmentation (same subject_id, simulation.medium and output directory).
  • Linear regime. The validity conditions of single-transducer ISPPA scaling apply (see doc_calibration.md).
  • Uncertainty mode. With simulation.uncertainty: true, each variant runs its own async pipeline (preproc included), and one uncertainty report is written per sweep point. See doc_uncertainty.md.

items.title: PRESTUS Nexus (GUI)
items.text:
The Nexus is a desktop app to set up, check and run a PRESTUS study, and to look at its placements and results. You fill in forms, the Nexus checks them as you type and writes the study config, and MATLAB runs the simulation. The config is an ordinary PRESTUS YAML that holds only the values that differ from the defaults, so it also runs without the Nexus; the Nexus replaces the deprecated MATLAB GUI prestus_gui.

On this page:

  • Installation: the prestus-nexus conda environment and other ways to install.
  • Starting the Nexus: opening the Nexus from MATLAB or a terminal, with a study config and project defaults.
  • A First Simulation: from a T1 image to results in six steps.
  • Beyond the First Simulation: where to go for studies, protocols, calibration, Localite and remote runs.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To build a study config without editing YAML, check it before it runs, and run it locally or on a cluster.
  • Before you start: The prestus-nexus conda environment (Installation) and MATLAB, which runs the simulations.

Subpages:

  • Tabs and Pages: every tab and page with the config keys it writes, for anyone changing settings beyond the QuickStart tab, running a study of many subjects, or following runs and results.
  • Calibration and Localite Pages: the MATLAB session and the Calibration and Localite pages, for anyone calibrating a transducer to hydrophone profiles or ingesting Localite recordings.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
System Run in the PRESTUS folder macOS, Linux bash nexus/install.sh Windows nexus\install.bat (or double-click it)

The installer creates the conda environment prestus-nexus from nexus/environment.yml. If conda is missing, it offers to install Miniforge into your home folder first. Run it again after a PRESTUS update: it then updates the environment. With conda already set up, conda env create -f environment.yml in PRESTUS/nexus does the same. Installing without conda, the standalone app and the cache folder are described under Installation options.

items.title: Installation Options
items.text:
pip, Qt and h5py

Without conda, pip install -e . in PRESTUS/nexus installs the same packages into any Python ≥ 3.10 environment; the list lives in nexus/pyproject.toml.

Install Qt from pip only (as environment.yml does). conda's pyqt together with pip's PyQt6-WebEngine fails to load (Library not loaded: …QtPrintSupport). In an older environment built with conda's pyqt, run conda remove pyqt and then pip install -e ..

Reading -v7.3 HEAT files on the Heating sub-tab also needs h5py (not installed by default; PRESTUS saves -v7 unless MATLAB's preference says otherwise).

Cache folder

The Nexus runs from a local copy of its own code in the user's cache folder (~/Library/Caches/prestus_nexus on macOS, ~/.cache/prestus_nexus on Linux); on the Donders project drive this halves the start-up time. The parsed config/equipment files are cached in the same folder while they are unchanged. Set PRESTUS_NEXUS_CACHE to use another cache folder.

Local copy of the code

On start the Nexus copies the files of nexus/prestus_nexus that changed since the last start into the cache folder and runs from there, so Python does not read its modules from a network drive. The checkout stays the source: an edit there is copied on the next start. Set PRESTUS_NEXUS_LOCAL_COPY=0 to run from the checkout directly.

nexus/packaging/prestus_nexus.spec builds a standalone app with PyInstaller (pip install -e . pyinstaller, then pyinstaller packaging/prestus_nexus.spec in nexus/). The app does not contain PRESTUS: on first start it asks for the PRESTUS folder (or use --prestus-root / PRESTUS_ROOT) and remembers it.

items.title: Starting the Nexus
items.text:
From MATLAB:

prestus_nexus                                  % untitled study (File > New / Open)
prestus_nexus('config_study.yaml')             % open a study config
prestus_nexus(Python='/path/to/env/bin/python')

From a terminal:

conda activate prestus-nexus
prestus-nexus [config_study.yaml]

From MATLAB, prestus_nexus finds the environment's Python by itself: $PRESTUS_NEXUS_PYTHON if set, the Python of the last start, the conda environment prestus-nexus, then python3. It uses the first that can start the Nexus and remembers it. If none can, the error lists what it tried; pass Python= to choose one.

items.title: Opening a Study Config
items.text:
The Nexus opens a given config, or an untitled one. File ▸ New study… creates a config and can copy config_default.yaml into its folder, which pins the defaults as prestus_config_init does. Open… and Open recent switch to another config. The subject, paths, T1/T2 patterns and SimNIBS folder are set on the Setup tab. The Issues panel checks them as you type: the T1 must resolve, and the m2m_sub-XXX folder must exist or SimNIBS must be set.

Compatibility with MATLAB's YAML loader

PRESTUS reads configs with yaml.loadFile (SnakeYAML, YAML 1.1). The Nexus:

  • quotes all strings (unquoted yes/no/04:00:00 would change type);
  • reads floats such as 2.17e-3 the way SnakeYAML does;
  • writes every element of a transducer list with the same top-level keys, which yaml.loadFile requires.

A round-trip test writes configs with the Nexus, loads them with load_parameters, and compares every value. It covers both a serial-based and a fully inline transducer.

Config schema and overlay

The schema is derived from config_default.yaml at startup. nexus/prestus_nexus/overlay.yaml adds only widget kinds, allowed values, units, visibility rules, keys the code reads that the default omits, deprecated keys, readable field labels where a key does not read as words (display; other labels are derived in labels.py), and the schematic icons shown with drop-down choices. Quote a value that contains a comma ({label: "a, b"}): unquoted, YAML splits it, and the drift test reports the stray key. nexus/tests/test_schema.py fails when the overlay no longer matches the default config or the code. See nexus/README.md for running the tests.

items.title: Project Defaults
items.text: When the study folder holds a copy of config_default.yaml (from File ▸ New study… or prestus_config_init), the Nexus merges it onto the toolbox default exactly as load_parameters does: the copy's values win, keys added to PRESTUS since the copy was made keep their toolbox defaults. The Review YAML page names both files. Tools ▸ Update project defaults… replaces the copy with the toolbox default (keeping a dated backup), optionally after writing the values the copy pinned differently into the study config so the simulation settings stay the same; prestus_config_upgrade(folder) does the same from MATLAB.

items.title: A First Simulation
items.text: The steps below take one participant from a T1 image to results. The screenshots show the demo subject sub-009.

items.title: 1. Fill In the QuickStart Tab
items.text:
The Nexus opens on QuickStart, which asks for four things and keeps every other setting at its PRESTUS default:

  1. Head image: the participant's T1-weighted NIfTI. The Nexus finds the T2, the SimNIBS segmentation and the subject number from it.
  2. Transducer: the device and driving system from the equipment library, the focal depth and the free-water intensity. The calibration PRESTUS will use is shown below.
  3. Target: where to focus, in MNI coordinates. Give the target alone and PRESTUS finds a transducer position, or give both.
  4. Check and run: where the simulation runs, and any errors still to fix.

Each step shows Done once it is complete. Continue to Run saves the study and opens the Run tab. The other tabs hold every setting, with the same values the QuickStart tab wrote.

items.title: 2. Check the Transducer
items.text: The Transducer tab shows what the library knows about the device. The device panel gives its focal range and the calibration entry PRESTUS will use; green values mean your focal depth lies inside that range. The cross-section draws the transducer and the focal depth you set (✕). The Calibration sub-tab (Transducer ▸ Calibration) plots how well the calibration fits at each depth, with your study's depth as a vertical line.

items.title: 3. Check the Placement
items.text:
Placement ▸ Viewer draws the transducer, the beam and the simulated field of view on the participant's T1 and segmentation. The readout on the right reports the placement: how deep the target lies, how far the transducer sits from the scalp, and how much skull the beam crosses. Red values need attention. In the example, the target lies 2.2 mm short of the focal depth setting, which Set focal depth to target corrects.

To change a manual placement, choose under Click sets whether a click moves the focus or the transducer, then click a slice. Snap to scalp moves the transducer onto the scalp along the beam. Placements from Localite, the heuristic search or PlanTUS are shown read-only.

items.title: 4. Clear the Issues
items.text: The error and warning counts in the header open the Issues panel. It lists what MATLAB would otherwise report only when the run starts: misspelt keys, missing files, intensities that cannot be reached, and the placement viewer's red flags. Clicking an issue opens the field it refers to. Fix the errors; read the warnings and notes.

items.title: 5. Run the Simulation
items.text:
The Run tab lists the pipeline stages, which you can switch off for partial runs, and where to run. Run locally runs MATLAB on this computer and streams its log. Submit to cluster submits from a cluster login node; Submit over SSH submits from a laptop with the project drive mounted. Submitted jobs appear under Jobs. Review YAML shows the exact config that will be written.

The first run on a participant also creates the segmentation, so it takes longest.

items.title: 6. Look at the Results
items.text:
The Results tab reads what the runs wrote to the subject's output folder. Run picks a run when the folder holds several. Acoustic and Thermal show the maps on the T1, centred on their peak; clicking a slice reads the value there. Report opens the HTML report, Data table the metrics, and Compare runs puts the key metrics of all runs side by side.

Heating plots the temperature of each tissue over the sonication and the cool-down after it.

items.title: Beyond the First Simulation
items.text:
To Go to Details Run many subjects or conditions Study tab Study tab, Group analysis Set the sonication protocol, or exchange it with the TUS calculator Sonication tab Timing diagram and TUS calculator Calibrate a transducer to your hydrophone profiles Transducer ▸ Calibration Calibration page Ingest Localite neuronavigation recordings Placement ▸ Localite Localite page Submit from a laptop over SSH Run tab Run tab Rerun with another intensity, timing or placement, or chain a sequential run Results ▸ Follow-up… Follow-up runs Undo a change, find a tab's docs, or export a figure Edit and Help menus, a figure's download button Menus and shortcuts See settings hidden as advanced Advanced on any tab, or the advanced icon on a card Advanced options Pin the defaults for a project File ▸ New study… Project defaults

Tabs and Pages describes every tab, page and control, with the config keys each one writes; Calibration and Localite Pages describes the pages that compute in MATLAB.

items.title: Nexus Calibration and Localite Pages
items.text:
The Calibration and Localite pages bring calibration_gui and neuronav_gui into the Nexus. Both compute in a MATLAB session that the Nexus starts when an action first needs it, so their first step waits for MATLAB to start. This page describes that session, the two pages, and the standalone MATLAB GUIs that the Tools menu opens.

On this page:

  • MATLAB Session: when the shared MATLAB session starts and ends.
  • Calibration Page: calibrating the study's transducers to hydrophone profiles.
  • Localite Page: ingesting Localite neuronavigation recordings.
  • Standalone MATLAB GUIs: opening neuronav_gui and calibration_gui from the Nexus.

At a glance

  • When you need it: You calibrate a study's transducer to hydrophone profiles, or ingest Localite neuronavigation recordings.
  • Before you start: MATLAB (the binary set on the Run tab); for calibration, a hydrophone profile CSV; for Localite, the recordings under path.localite_raw.

items.title: MATLAB Session
items.text:
The Calibration and Localite pages compute in MATLAB, with the same functions as calibration_gui and neuronav_gui.

When the session starts and ends

The Nexus keeps one MATLAB session open, started the first time an action needs it, e.g. Load, Predict or Fit on the Calibration page or Detect series on the Localite page; showing a page does not start it. The MATLAB binary is the one set on the Run tab. The first call takes as long as MATLAB needs to start (15–60 s); later ones take only the computation. The pages show the session's state (starting, ready, working), and Stop ends it.

  • The session ends by itself after 30 min without use, since it holds a MATLAB licence, and when the Nexus quits or stops answering. The next call starts a new one, and the pages open their transducer or session again.
  • Long work does not use the session: batch ingestion and the k-Wave drive check are written as scripts and run on the Run tab, where the log streams and Stop works.
How the session exchanges data

The session is nexus_bridge, started with matlab -batch. The Nexus and MATLAB exchange JSON files in a temporary folder. MATLAB runs only nexus_calibration, nexus_neuronav and nexus_ping from it.

items.title: Calibration Page
items.text:
Transducer ▸ Calibration is the transducer-calibration GUI for the study's own transducers. It does what calibration_gui does (Transducer library), computed by the same functions (calibration_desired_profiles, calibration_evaluate, calibration_fit, calibration_save_entry).

The controls are grouped in three steps: 1 Data (profile CSV, measured and desired depths), 2 Fit (where to calibrate, reference ISPPA, Fit, Evaluate) and 3 Save (save, Export, k-Wave drive check). The fitter's settings (ring profile, free parameters, forward model, near-field skip, loss, Huber δ, starts) are under Fit options, collapsed by default, because the defaults suit most fits.

The plots

Until MATLAB has answered, the right-hand side shows the current library entry from its YAML alone:

  • Quality: the global model's R² per calibrated depth, with the geometric and per-depth-fit medians as reference lines.
  • Drive: the drive amplitude per depth.
  • Phases: each ring's phase correction per depth, unwrapped; steps over 30° between neighbouring depths are marked.

The calibrated range is shaded and this study's depths are drawn as lines, coloured by whether the entry covers them. The same plot sits under the transducer drawing on the Settings sub-tab. After Predict, Evaluate or Fit, the Profiles view shows the profiles with a bar per depth coloured by R² (green ≥ 0.9, amber ≥ 0.8, red below); clicking a bar shows that depth.

The controls
  • Transducer lists the config's transducers that use a device from config/equipment; the driving system and transducer.library_path are taken from the config. The current library entry is the one PRESTUS would use (the user folder first, then config/calibration).
  • Profile CSV defaults to the combination's char_data_path under local/profiles. Loading it shows the geometric model and the library entry against the measured profiles (R² per depth).
  • Desired depths and Predict model any depths through the runtime library path, with the measured, interpolated or (within extrapolate ≤) extrapolated profile at each depth. The desired depths are prefilled with the depths this study uses with the device: the focal depth settings (focal_distance_ep or _bowl of every matching transducer, and the manifest's transducer[(i)].focal_distance_ep columns) and each matching transducer's target depth in the placement viewer (exit plane → focus_pos, 0.1 mm). They follow the config and placement each time the page is shown, until you type your own; Study depths fills them in again. Without either, the depths of the entry's meta.fit, then the device's defaults, are used. The plot then shows focus against target per depth, and the table the phases and drive each depth resolves to.
  • Ring profile (keep the entry's / fit / uniform rings) selects the within-ring velocity profile (Within-ring velocity profile); fit fits it on the measured profiles before the per-depth fits. Options… sets the profile fit and a plane-scan file (off-axis data) fitted with the axial profiles.
  • Fit calibrates per-depth refinements at the ticked measured depths or at the desired depths. Reference ISPPA defaults to transducer.target_isppa_wcm2. Advanced… holds the fitter's further options (as in calibration_gui; see Calibration), the desired-profile tolerance and the k-Wave drive check's grid and correction, and loads a preset.
  • Save entry writes <serial>[_<ds>].yaml to transducer.library_path. If that is not set, it asks for a folder and sets it in the config. The entry records how it was fitted (meta.fit), and opening it later restores those settings. The device panel on the Settings sub-tab then shows the new entry as the one PRESTUS will use.
  • k-Wave drive check… (per-depth fits) writes the unsaved fit and calibration/kwave_drive_<combo>.m next to the config. The script runs kwave_calibrate_drive with the study config's grid and platform, then saves the drive-corrected entry. Run it on the Run tab, or yourself (e.g. on the cluster); it takes minutes per depth.
  • Export profiles… and Export settings… write the same CSVs as calibration_gui.

Matrix transducers and new equipment entries (calibration_gui's View geometry and New…) are only available in calibration_gui.

items.title: Localite Page
items.text:
Placement ▸ Localite ingests Localite recordings with the study config's settings (path.localite_raw/_post, placement.localite.*, io.overwrite_files, neuronav.*). These are edited on the Settings sub-tab (Edit settings), not on the page. The config is saved before each step, because MATLAB reads it with load_parameters as a run does. The steps are those of neuronav_gui (doc_placement_neuronav.md).

Detect series and write outputs
  1. Detect series (neuronav_detect_series, neuronav_name_series) lists the series of the chosen subject and session with their QC (pulses, position and rotation deviation, tracking flags). Each series is named after the coil table, the planned target nearest its beam axis, or series_<k>. Tabs show the pulse positions in 3-D (with the beam direction and the planned targets), the deviation per pulse, the marker files found and the log.
  2. Write outputs (neuronav_check_target_map, neuronav_ingest_markers) writes the ticked series under their (editable) names and colours to path.localite_post/sub-XXX/ses-XX/. When the inputs or the settings change after detection, the page asks you to detect again.
Using the written outputs, batch ingestion and MNI view
  • Use in this study sets placement.localite.session and .target to the written session and target(s) (one per transducer).
  • Import into study… builds manifest rows from all ingested sessions (Study tab).
  • Ingest all sessions… scans every session (neuronav_scan_sessions) and lists the planned-target labels found, whose target names you can edit (Group labels by stem, Use labels as found). Save label map and run batch writes the map to neuronav.target_labels and the write mode to neuronav.batch_write, then runs ingest_<study>.m (neuronav_ingest_batch on the ticked sessions) on the Run tab.
  • MNI view… maps neuronav_ingest_summary.csv to MNI space with each subject's SimNIBS warp (neuronav_summary_to_mni, needs path.seg). It plots transducer, focus and beam axis over the MNI152 head outline, with filters per subject, session and target.

items.title: Standalone MATLAB GUIs
items.text:
The Tools menu opens the Localite and Calibration pages, and also opens PRESTUS's standalone MATLAB GUIs in an interactive MATLAB session (they need the MATLAB desktop):

  • neuronav_gui in MATLAB… (Localite ingestion). The study config is saved first and passed to the GUI.
  • calibration_gui in MATLAB… saves entries to transducer.library_path when that is set. It also offers View geometry and New… (adding a transducer to config/equipment), which the Calibration page does not.

items.title: Nexus Tabs and Pages
items.text:
The QuickStart tab sets up a first simulation and leaves every other setting at its PRESTUS default; the other tabs hold all of those settings. This page describes each tab and page of the Nexus, what its controls do and which config keys they write, so you can find a setting, read a check, and follow a run to its results.

On this page:
