  • File Mode: A Single XML File: reading one TriggerMarkers, GUMMarkers or InstrumentMarker file.
  • Several Transducers (Bilateral Setups): one pose per transducer.
  • Many Subjects and Sessions: manifest rows from the Nexus, and the functions for standalone use.

At a glance

  • When you need it: You set placement.mode: 'localite' for a run.
  • Before you start: transducer.focal_distance_ep set (see Placement from a Recorded Pose), and either sessions ingested as in Localite Ingestion or a single Localite XML file. Folder layout and path keys: Localite File Layout.

items.title: Automatic Mode: Ingested Markers
items.text:
Leave placement.localite.file empty. The ingested pair under path.localite_post is read. If it does not exist yet and path.localite_raw is set, ingestion runs first (with neuronav.coil_map if configured, otherwise for the requested series only, named series_<position> or target).

path:
  localite_raw:  '/data/localite_raw'
  localite_post: '/data/derivatives/localite'
placement:
  mode: 'localite'
  localite:
    session: 2          # -> ses-02
    target: 'L_M1'      # ingested target name, or leave '' and use:
    position: 2         # detected-series index, matched against series_index in the JSON sidecar

To choose series and names interactively, ingest with neuronav_gui first; placement then only reads the result. A raw series that was not ingested is an error (PRESTUS:localite:noSeries), and an untracked series (position at the origin) is refused.

items.title: File Mode: A Single XML File
items.text:
Set placement.localite.file. TriggerMarkers, GUMMarkers and InstrumentMarker files are accepted; the type is detected from the content.

placement:
  mode: 'localite'
  localite:
    file: '/path/to/TriggerMarkers_Coil0_20240820122011842.xml'
    position: 2        # detected series in the file (1-based, after the pulse-count filter), or:
    target: ''         # description of an InstrumentMarker / GUMMarkers entry

items.title: Several Transducers (Bilateral Setups)
items.text:
target and position take one entry per transducer; transducer i uses entry i, and each gets its own pose. A single value applies to every transducer. A list of the wrong length is an error (PRESTUS:localite:listLength).

placement:
  mode: 'localite'
  localite:
    session: 2
    target: [L_M1, R_M1]   # transducer(1) -> L_M1, transducer(2) -> R_M1

items.title: Many Subjects and Sessions
items.text:
For a study, the Nexus's Study tab turns the neuronav_gui outputs into manifest rows (Import from Localite…). It reads neuronav_ingest_summary.csv and the per-session InstrumentMarker_*.json files under path.localite_post, and makes either one run per target, or one run per session with the targets assigned to transducers 1, 2, … (left first, alphabetical, or a given order). The runs use placement.mode: localite, so PRESTUS reads the ingested markers itself. See Group analysis.

Entry points and standalone use

Placement runs in preproc_transducer_placement; the older placement.localite.enabled = 1 switch in preproc_head uses the same code. Both go through neuronav_localite_pose, and the pose's column 4 (position) and column 1 (beam direction) go to localite_matrix_to_positions. All paths share the same XML parser and position math.

For multi-position or multi-session workflows outside the pipeline, call neuronav_ingest_markers → neuronav_select_localite → neuronav_compute_series_statistics → neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels directly (see examples/demo_localite.m and Target coordinates from several sources). Average transducer and target locations can be provided in several coordinate spaces; native image space is the one PRESTUS uses. Standard-space definitions (experimental) allow e.g. plotting average transducer positions in standard space.

items.title: Named Target Coordinates
items.text:
When a session has several named targets, each simulated focus needs a coordinate and a record of how far that coordinate can be trusted. neuronav_resolve_target takes each target's coordinate from the best source available, from a pre-hoc lookup table down to a projection along the tracked transducer axis, and reports which source it used.

On this page:

  • Target Coordinates from Several Sources: what the functions resolve and when to use them.
  • Inputs You Provide: the recordings, the target_map and the optional sources.
  • Resolution Order: the four tiers and their confidence.
  • Worked Example: a loop over subjects and sessions.
  • Exported Session CSV: the per-session output and the function reference.

At a glance

  • When you need it: A study has more than one named target per subject and session, or needs a documented answer to where each target coordinate came from.
  • Before you start: The raw Localite exports and the planning T1 per subject; ingestion as in Localite Ingestion.

items.title: Target Coordinates from Several Sources
items.text: When a session has several named targets, your own extraction script resolves named, per-session brain-target coordinates (e.g. this subject's L_V1 on ses-03) from whichever raw Localite export the operator recorded, with a logged account of how confident each resolved coordinate is. The resolved coordinate is what a simulation uses as focus_pos. This is not a pipeline mode: the functions read the ingested files and add to the single-target placement pipeline rather than replacing it. Use them when a study needs more than one named target per subject, or a documented answer to where each reported coordinate came from. Localite file formats are in Neuronavigation read-in and coordinate spaces in Localite Files, Offset and Coordinates.

items.title: Inputs You Provide
items.text:
1. Raw entry-point recordings per subject and session, in any supported format (TriggerMarkers, GUMMarkers or InstrumentMarker). This supplies the transducer/coil position, always read from the current session's own recording.

  2. A target_map naming your targets, built by neuronav_build_target_map from the neuronav.coil_map you construct per subject and session:

    coil_map(1).coil   = 0;              % hardware coil index (0-based)
coil_map(1).target = 'L_V1';        % target_name -- your convention
coil_map(2).coil   = 1;
coil_map(2).target = 'R_V1';
target_map = neuronav_build_target_map(coil_map);
parameters.neuronav.coil_map = coil_map;   % ingest reads one file per coil

    A coil that records several position blocks in one session lists them as coil_map(i).sequences(j).target; ingest then takes that many series from the coil's file, in order (untracked blocks with every pulse at the origin are skipped), matching the series_index that neuronav_build_target_map assigns.

The following inputs are optional. Each one you provide moves more targets up the confidence ranking (see Resolution order).

  • EntryTarget exports, for at least some sessions, if your operator uses Localite's target-confirmation feature. target_map(i).localite_key is matched (case-insensitive substring) against each EntryTarget description. Set it whenever your description convention differs from target_name, and pass a cell array of candidates if more than one convention is in use across sessions:

    coil_map(1).localite_key = {'LEFT V1', 'L_V1', 'LEFT V', 'L_V'};

  • A pre-hoc target lookup table, if your study establishes targets before the session (e.g. a placement or optimisation step run ahead of time). This is the highest-confidence source when present and is cross-checked against EntryTarget wherever both exist. neuronav_read_target_lookup.m documents the CSV schema (subject_id, target_name, space, x, y, z). Build this file with your own per-study script from whatever your planning step produces.

Why several sources

Across one study, the same target was confirmed in different ways for different subjects and sessions: an operator-confirmed EntryTarget export for the exact session; an EntryTarget export only from an earlier session; no EntryTarget export at all (workflows that only used GUMMarkers, which has no separate target confirmation); two label conventions in the EntryTarget description across sessions ("LEFT V" and "L_V"); and a pre-hoc planned coordinate from individual anatomical segmentation, independent of Localite. neuronav_resolve_target resolves each target from the best source available for that target and reports which one it used.

items.title: Resolution Order
items.text:
neuronav_resolve_target tries these in order per target and returns which one supplied each row (target_source). Check this before treating a coordinate as ground truth.

Tier target_source value What it is Confidence 1 target_lookup Your pre-hoc lookup table (see above) Highest: established before the session 2 entrytarget_current This session's own EntryTarget export, label-matched High: operator-confirmed, same day 3 entrytarget:<session> Another session's EntryTarget export (nearest prior session tried first) Medium: operator-confirmed, different day 4 projected Transducer-axis geometric projection from the tracked entry pose Estimate only: no operator confirmation exists for this target

Because of tier 4, the resolved coordinate is never NaN: every target gets a value, but tier-4 rows are not confirmed. In one cross-check, tier-4 estimates differed from the tier-1 target by 3-5 voxels for a subject without any EntryTarget export, while tier-1 and tier-2 values matched to within 0-1 voxel. If a study needs sub-voxel target accuracy and some subjects stay on tier 4, provide a lookup table (tier 1) for those subjects.

items.title: Worked Example
items.text:
for i_sub = 1:numel(all_subjects)
    sub_id = all_subjects{i_sub};
    for i_ses = 1:numel(sessions)
        session = sessions{i_ses};

        coil_map = build_my_coil_map(sub_id, session);   % your own logic
        target_map = neuronav_build_target_map(coil_map);
        parameters.neuronav.coil_map = coil_map;

        [xml_path, ~, results] = neuronav_ingest_markers(parameters, sub_id, session, target_map);
        active_sides = find(~cellfun(@isempty, results));

        [trans_ras, trans_pos, target_ras, target_pos_projected] = ...
            neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels(sub_id, active_sides, results, parameters);

        t1_header = niftiinfo(my_planning_t1_path(sub_id));   % see doc_placement_neuronav_coordinates.md

        [target_vox, target_mm, target_source] = neuronav_resolve_target( ...
            parameters, sub_id, session, sessions, target_map, t1_header, ...
            target_pos_projected, my_target_lookup_csv_path);

        % target_vox is what you feed into PRESTUS as focus_pos.
        % target_source tells you, per row, whether that's confirmed or estimated.

        neuronav_export_session_csv(sub_id, session, {target_map.target_name}, ...
            outputs_folder, trans_pos, target_vox, trans_ras, target_ras, ...
            [], [], [], [], 0, target_mm, target_source);
    end
end

items.title: Exported Session CSV
items.text:
neuronav_export_session_csv writes one row per target with, among other columns:

  • trans_native_vox_x/y/z: transducer/coil position, always from the current session's own recording.
  • target_native_vox_x/y/z: the resolved target (target_vox above). A simulation script reads this as focus_pos.
  • target_localite_mm_x/y/z: the EntryTarget-matched mm coordinate, tiers 2-3 only. NaN for tier 1 and tier 4 rows, so it stays a reliable operator-confirmed signal independent of target_source.
  • target_projected_mm_x/y/z: the tier-4 geometric estimate, always computed whichever tier was used, kept for comparison.
  • target_source: see the resolution-order table above.
Function reference

The ingestion functions (neuronav_ingest_markers, neuronav_ingest_batch, neuronav_scan_sessions) are listed under GUI workflow; the naming functions under Series naming.

Function Role neuronav_build_target_map Expands your coil_map into the flat target_map every other function here consumes neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels Converts ingested marker positions to native voxel/mm space; also computes the tier-4 axis-projected target neuronav_read_entry_target Reads the latest EntryTarget*.xml snapshot for one subject/session neuronav_match_entry_targets Label-matches target_map entries against EntryTarget descriptions (tiers 2-3's matching step) neuronav_read_target_lookup Reads your pre-hoc lookup CSV (tier 1) neuronav_resolve_target The orchestrator: runs all four tiers in order for one subject/session and returns the resolved coordinate + provenance per target. Call this one function rather than the matching/lookup functions individually. neuronav_export_session_csv Writes the per-session summary CSV, including a target_source column neuronav_plot_placement QC plot of every target_map entry's entry/target pair on the segmented head neuronav_get_group_mean_mni / neuronav_apply_inverse_deformation Group-mean-MNI fallback for subjects missing trigger data entirely (a more severe gap than a missing target confirmation; see Coordinate transforms)

items.title: Localite Ingestion: GUI and Script Workflows
items.text:
Localite placement simulates the transducer pose the operator recorded, and ingestion decides which recorded series become simulated targets and what each is called. A series kept by mistake, or a name given to the wrong series, puts the simulated focus on another target than the one stimulated. This page turns raw Localite exports into the named, averaged targets that placement.mode: localite reads.

On this page:

  • Shared Settings File: the config keys that the GUI and scripts share.
  • Series Naming: the naming rule and the label map for inconsistent operator labels.
  • GUI Workflow: single sessions, batches and the MNI view in neuronav_gui.
  • Script Workflow: batch ingestion with neuronav_ingest_batch and the summary CSV.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Once per session (or in batch for a whole study) before simulating recorded poses.
  • Before you start: The raw Localite exports (path.localite_raw).

Ingestion turns recorded Localite positions into named, averaged targets per subject and session (folder layout and output files: Localite file layout). Run it in neuronav_gui, on the PRESTUS Nexus's Placement ▸ Localite page (settings from the study config; see Localite page), or scripted with neuronav_ingest_batch. All three run the same functions on the same settings:

GUI (neuronav_gui) Script (neuronav_ingest_batch) Best for Checking a session, choosing series by eye, setting up the label map Many subjects and sessions, reproducible re-runs, HPC Session selection Single session, or tickboxes in the Batch window (All / None / Not yet ingested) A table or {sub, ses} list, e.g. rows of neuronav_scan_sessions Settings Form fields, ⬆ Load settings… / ⬇ Save settings… (YAML) The same YAML via load_parameters Output InstrumentMarker_<sub>_<ses>.xml/.json + neuronav_ingest_summary.csv identical

Resolving the coordinates of several named targets per session in your own script is described in Named Target Coordinates.

items.title: Shared Settings File
items.text:
Every setting that affects ingestion and naming is a config key. Keep them in the study YAML (or a separate neuronav_settings.yaml saved from the GUI) and use that file in both workflows:

path:
  localite_raw:  '/data/localite_raw'          # <raw>/sub-XXX/ses-XX/[loc/]…
  localite_post: '/data/derivatives/localite'  # ingested outputs + summary CSV
  localite_t1:   '/data/localite_raw'          # planning T1s (for voxel coordinates); default = localite_raw

placement:
  localite:
    loc_folder: 'loc'              # '' if the export sits directly under ses-XX/
    expected_segment_length: 80    # pulses per TriggerMarkers series ([] = keep all)

io:
  overwrite_files: 'always'        # 'never' keeps existing ingested files

neuronav:
  coil_map: []                     # multi-coil setups, see doc_placement_neuronav_targets.md
  suggest_names: true              # name series after the planned target on their beam axis
  axis_tolerance_mm: 10
  target_depth_mm: [0, 150]
  target_labels:                   # planned-target labels as recorded -> study target names
    - target: 'L_V1'
      labels: ['LEFT V1', 'L_V1*']
    - target: 'R_V1'
      labels: ['RIGHT V1', 'R_V1*']
  batch_write: 'all'               # or 'named'

A file saved with ⬇ Save settings… contains exactly these keys and is a valid PRESTUS config: load_parameters('neuronav_settings.yaml') merges it with the defaults. Settings the GUI has no field for (for example transducer geometry, needed for focus coordinates) come from a config loaded with ⬆ Load settings…; load the study config first, then adjust.

items.title: Series Naming
items.text:
Each detected series gets a name by one rule (neuronav_name_series), the same in the GUI and the batch:

  1. Coil table / neuronav.coil_map: a target name given there for that coil/block.
  2. Planned target on the beam axis (if suggest_names is true). The session's named planned targets (the latest EntryTarget export and the EntryTargetPairs of its GUMMarkers exports, each label at its most recent position) are collected by neuronav_read_label_candidates. A recorded series takes the target closest to its beam axis if it lies within axis_tolerance_mm and at a depth inside target_depth_mm. A GUMMarkers EntryTargetPair series uses its own label. The label is then passed through target_labels.
  3. Default: series_<k>.

Repeated names get _rep2, _rep3, …; a planned pair that shares its label with a recorded pose in the same file becomes <label>_target.

items.title: The Label Map (neuronav.target_labels)
items.text:
Operators label planned targets inconsistently across sessions (LEFT V1 in one session, L_V1_1 in the next). target_labels maps recorded labels to the names your study uses. Each entry lists label patterns (* and ? wildcards, case-insensitive); the first matching entry wins; a label that matches no entry is kept as recorded. neuronav_map_label('L_V1_1', map) shows the result for a single label. When target_labels is empty, labels are used as found.

To see which labels the data contain, scan all sessions:

parameters = load_parameters('study.yaml');
[sessions, labels] = neuronav_scan_sessions(parameters);
labels(:, {'label', 'stem', 'target', 'n_subjects', 'n_sessions'})

labels.target is the name each label gets with the current map; labels.stem groups numbered variants (the label without a trailing _<number>, e.g. L_caudateV2_1, L_caudateV2_2 → L_caudateV2). Turn either into a map and store it:

map = neuronav_label_map_from_scan(labels, 'stem');   % or edit labels.target, then 'target'
parameters.neuronav.target_labels = map;
yaml.dumpFile('target_labels.yaml', struct('neuronav', struct('target_labels', map)));

In the GUI, the Batch window shows the same label table: Group labels by stem fills the target column of unmapped labels from their stems (existing mappings are kept), Use labels as found resets all of them, and any cell can be edited. Only labels whose target differs from the label end up in the saved map. The map applies to single-session naming too.

Check the name sources afterwards: the GUI's Name from column and the summary's rule, label, axis_dist_mm and depth_mm columns show where each name came from. A match far from the usual focal depth usually means the intended target is missing from the export; narrow target_depth_mm to reject such matches.

items.title: GUI Workflow
items.text:
neuronav_gui                   % empty form
neuronav_gui('study.yaml')     % pre-fill from a study config
neuronav_gui(parameters)       % pre-fill from a parameter struct

items.title: Single Session
items.text:
1. Set the raw root (containing <sub>/<ses>/<loc folder>/…; leave Localite folder empty if the export sits directly under <ses>/) and the output root. The full layout is in Localite file layout. The subject and session dropdowns list the sub-* / ses-* folders found; they can also be typed (a bare number 2 means ses-02).
  2. ▶ Detect series detects the series into a temporary folder; nothing is written yet. Check the series table and the plots.
  3. Tick the series to keep, check each target name (and optionally set a #rrggbb colour), then ✓ Write outputs. Changing any input after detection disables writing until series are detected again.
Settings read from a config, the series table and the pulse filter

Settings read from a config (all optional): path.localite_raw (falls back to path.localite), path.localite_post, placement.localite.loc_folder / voxel_size / expected_segment_length / session, io.overwrite_files, neuronav.coil_map.

The series table lists every detected series with pulse count, position deviation (mm from the series mean position), rotation deviation (rad from the mean orientation) and a flag for untracked series (all positions at the origin). The tabs show a 3-D plot of every pulse position (small dot = one pulse, ring = series mean, arrow = beam direction; no arrow for GUMMarkers), per-pulse deviation traces (one dot per pulse), all raw marker files found with the one used marked, and the captured log/warnings.

The Pulses per series filter (expected_segment_length, default 80) drops TriggerMarkers series whose pulse count differs from it by more than 20; leave it blank to keep all series.

items.title: Suggested Target Names
items.text:
With Suggest from planned targets ticked (default), detection also names each series after the planned target it was aimed at. The Name from column shows the source and the off-axis distance and depth of each match (or the nearest miss), and the 3-D plot marks the candidates (×) and the axis to each matched target. Names typed into the coil table are kept. ↻ Re-apply to series re-runs the naming after changing the tolerance or depth window.

A pose aimed at a target missing from the export takes the nearest remaining one, so check depth and distance: a match far outside the usual focal depth is suspect. Narrow Target depth around the focal distance to reject it. On the example data, all recorded poses whose planned target was in the export matched it, 0.7–4 mm off-axis.

How series are matched to planned targets

The naming runs neuronav_read_label_candidates and neuronav_suggest_target_names:

  • Candidates are the named, set targets of the session's latest EntryTarget export and of the EntryTargetPairs in its GUMMarkers exports. Each label is kept once, at its most recent position.
  • A recorded pose (TriggerMarkers series, or a GUMMarkers InstrumentMarker) takes the candidate closest to its beam axis (the line from the mean position along matrix column 1), provided it lies within Axis tolerance (default 10 mm) and at a depth inside Target depth (default 0–150 mm).
  • A GUMMarkers EntryTargetPair series uses its own label; when a pose in the same file matched that label, the pair becomes <label>_target and the pose keeps the bare name. Repeated blocks on one target get _rep2, _rep3, ….
Single-coil and multi-coil

With the coil table empty, ingest uses the newest non-duplicate TriggerMarkers_Coil0 file (falling back to GUMMarkers) and every detected series becomes a row. With one row per coil, ingest uses neuronav.coil_map: it reads one file per coil and keeps one series per target listed for that coil, skipping untracked blocks. For a coil that recorded several blocks, enter comma-separated target names (e.g. L_M1, L_M1 → L_M1_1, L_M1_2).

items.title: Many Sessions
items.text:
▦ Batch… opens a window that scans the raw root and lists every session with its marker files, planned labels and whether it is already ingested.

  1. Tick sessions (All, None, Not yet ingested, or individually).
  2. Check the label table on the right; group or rename targets.
  3. Choose Write all or named, then ▶ Run batch. Each session's status updates as it is processed; written targets are listed below and in the summary CSV.

⬇ Save settings… writes the settings (including the label map) as YAML for scripts or later GUI sessions.

The Batch window calls neuronav_ingest_batch with the main window's settings, so a saved settings file reproduces a GUI batch run in a script:

p = load_parameters('neuronav_settings.yaml');
neuronav_ingest_batch(p, {'sub-001', 'ses-01'; 'sub-002', 'ses-01'});

items.title: MNI View
items.text:
◎ MNI view… (in the Batch window) maps the summary CSV to MNI space and plots transducer, focus and beam axis of every subject and session over an MNI head outline.

Loading, filtering and saving the MNI view

MNI view reads the summary CSV (default <output root>/neuronav_ingest_summary.csv, i.e. every session ingested so far) and, on ▶ Load & map to MNI, maps each target's transducer, focus and Localite pose to MNI mm. Set SimNIBS root (path.seg); the planning T1 is found as in the main window (path.localite_t1). Subjects without a warp or planning T1 are listed in the status line and left out. The 3-D plot shows transducers (●), foci (◆), the beam axis between them and optionally the tracker pose (▲) over a head outline. Tick or untick subjects, sessions and targets in the three tables, colour by target, subject or session, and hover a point for its subject, session and target. ⬇ Save CSV… writes the summary with the MNI columns.

Warp and head outline

The mapping uses neuronav_summary_to_mni: planning T1 → m2m_<sub>/final_tissues.nii.gz → m2m_<sub>/toMNI/Conform2MNI_nonl.nii.gz. The outline is taken from Head template: SimNIBS's MNI152_T1_1mm.nii.gz when a SimNIBS installation is found (startup.simnibs_bin_path, or the default install folder); left empty, it is taken from the first mapped subject's final_tissues_MNI.nii.gz.

Functions Function Role neuronav_scan_sessions Inventory: sessions, marker files, planned labels, label table with stems neuronav_label_map_from_scan Label table → neuronav.target_labels neuronav_map_label Apply the label map to one label neuronav_detect_series Detect the series of one session without writing neuronav_name_series Naming rule (coil table > planned target > default) neuronav_ingest_batch Loop: detect, name, write, summary CSV neuronav_ingest_markers Write one session's ingested XML/JSON for a given target map neuronav_summary_to_mni Add MNI coordinates (pose, transducer, focus) to the summary via the SimNIBS nonlinear warp

items.title: Script Workflow
items.text:
parameters = load_parameters('study.yaml');   % paths, ingestion, naming, transducer

% 1. Inventory: which sessions exist, which labels they contain
[sessions, labels] = neuronav_scan_sessions(parameters);

% 2. Optional: set or refine the label map (see above)
% parameters.neuronav.target_labels = neuronav_label_map_from_scan(labels, 'stem');

% 3. Ingest all sessions with marker files, or a subset
todo = sessions(sessions.n_trigger + sessions.n_gum > 0, :);
% todo = todo(ismember(todo.sub, {'sub-001', 'sub-004'}), :);
% todo = todo(~todo.ingested, :);          % only sessions not ingested yet
summary = neuronav_ingest_batch(parameters, todo);

neuronav_ingest_batch(parameters) without a selection processes every session found. For a single session, neuronav_ingest_batch(parameters, {'sub-001', 'ses-02'}). Per session, the batch detects the series (nothing is written yet), names them, writes every tracked series (batch_write: 'all') or only the named ones ('named'), and adds one summary row per written target. Untracked series and coil dropouts are never written. Sessions that fail or have nothing to write get one row whose status says why; the batch continues with the next session.

items.title: Summary CSV
items.text:
<path.localite_post>/neuronav_ingest_summary.csv collects all sessions. Re-running a subset replaces that subset's rows and keeps the others. Columns:

Column Meaning sub, ses, target Session and target name (empty when nothing was written) series_index, coil Detected series (as in placement.localite.position) and coil index rule coil_map, heuristic or default (see naming) label, label_source Planned-target label as recorded, and the file it came from axis_dist_mm, depth_mm Distance of that target from the beam axis, and its depth along it n_pulses, pos_dev_mm, rot_dev_rad Series QC (as in the JSON sidecar) markertype, source_file Raw file the series came from pose_x/y/z, beam_x/y/z Mean instrument position and beam direction (Localite planning-image mm) trans_ras_*, focus_ras_* Transducer (bowl rear centre) and focus [mm], via localite_matrix_to_positions trans_vox_*, focus_vox_* The same in planning-T1 voxels xml, status Ingested file and outcome

Transducer, focus and voxel coordinates need the transducer focal distance (transducer.focal_distance_ep or _bowl) and the planning T1 (path.localite_t1, pattern path.localite_t1_pattern); when either is missing they are NaN and status says why. The pose columns are always filled.

placement.mode: 'localite' reads the ingested files for simulation.

items.title: PlanTUS Placement
items.text:
The entry point decides which part of the skull the beam crosses and whether the focus can reach the target. Given a T1-weighted image, a SimNIBS head mesh, a target-ROI mask and a transducer configuration, PlanTUS (placement.mode: 'plantus') scores every skin vertex as a candidate transducer position on skin–target distance, skin and skull angles, skull thickness and beam–target overlap. PRESTUS places the transducer at the vertex with the best weighted score, or at a vertex you choose on the maps on the Nexus PlanTUS page (or in Connectome Workbench).

On this page:

  • Running PlanTUS: the steps of a placement run.
  • Choosing the Position: automatic, on the Nexus PlanTUS page, or in Workbench.
  • Step-by-Step Pipeline: inputs, criteria, composite score, evaluation and placement geometry.
  • Coordinate Conventions: the frames PlanTUS and PRESTUS exchange.
  • External Dependencies: the tools each mode needs.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you want an optimised, documented choice of entry point, or to compare focal depths.
  • Before you start: The full SimNIBS mesh and a PlanTUS installation, 2.0 or later (Installation). PlanTUS 1.x also works but needs Connectome Workbench, FSL and FreeSurfer.

Experimental

PlanTUS placement is under active development. Verify results manually before use in a study.

Limitations

  • The Nexus PlanTUS page needs the maps of an earlier run (save_metrics: true) and draws them where the Nexus runs; the run itself can be headless.
  • Choosing in Workbench needs a display (desktop or VNC), Connectome Workbench wb_view and pynput. On macOS, the terminal or MATLAB needs Accessibility permission for pynput. Without a display (Linux), PlanTUS runs headless.
  • The Workbench review dialog needs PyQt5 in the SimNIBS Python. It ships with SimNIBS; without it, the last clicked vertex is placed without review.
  • With PlanTUS 1.x, the avoidance mask needs FSL, FreeSurfer and Workbench tools. Without them, all skin vertices are eligible (step 3).
  • To see errors from the launcher directly, run prestus_plantus_gui_launcher.py from a terminal (step 5b).

items.title: Running PlanTUS
items.text:
1. Set placement.mode: plantus, the placement.plantus paths and target, and the calibrated focal_distance_list / flhm_list.
  2. In the Nexus, click Compute maps on the Placement card (or on Placement ▸ PlanTUS). PlanTUS computes the criterion maps (a few minutes) and places the transducer at the composite-score optimum; no simulation runs. In MATLAB, run the pipeline with placement.plantus.vertex: [].
  3. Open Placement ▸ PlanTUS. The skin is coloured by the composite score; choose a criterion under Map to see one map. Click a skin position: the panel lists its criteria, composite score and rank, and the view shows the beam axis and the transducer there, in the housing Placement ▸ 3D draws.
  4. Click Place here. The Nexus sets placement.plantus.vertex and places the transducer at that vertex on the same maps, without recomputing them. The config keeps the choice, so a later simulation run uses it.
  5. Check the placement report and the Viewer. Section 5a explains the evaluation it contains.

items.title: Choosing the Position
items.text:
placement.plantus.vertex and placement.plantus.interactive ([], the default, follows simulation.interactive) select how the vertex is chosen:

Setting Script Vertex selection Automatic (vertex: [], interactive: 0) prestus_plantus_launcher.py Weighted composite score; no display required Chosen vertex (vertex: N) prestus_plantus_launcher.py --do_only_trajectory N Vertex N (0-based) of the maps of an earlier run in the same placement run folder, chosen on the Nexus PlanTUS page; the maps are not recomputed Workbench (vertex: [], interactive: 1) prestus_plantus_gui_launcher.py The five criterion maps in Connectome Workbench; you click a vertex, close wb_view, see the transducer there and confirm it in a review dialog

Automatic and Workbench runs compute the same maps and composite score (steps 2 to 5a) and write the same files. A chosen vertex is placed only while the target is where the maps were computed for: if the target moved more than 1 mm, the run stops and asks you to clear placement.plantus.vertex and compute the maps again. A chosen vertex belongs to one subject's maps; for a study, give it per run in a manifest column. Only Workbench runs need pynput, wb_view and PyQt5.

Both modes share all code except vertex selection (plantus_common.py). The scripts replicate PlanTUS_wrapper.py (Mainz group, at placement.plantus.script_path) but take CLI arguments instead of hard-coded paths.

items.title: 1  Parse Inputs
items.text:
PRESTUS writes a flat transducer YAML for PlanTUS.

The skin–target distance window

position_transducer_plantus.m derives the skin–target distance window from the transducer calibration, unless placement.plantus.min_distance_mm, max_distance_mm and optimal_distance_mm are set:

Field Value written by PRESTUS (when not set) min_distance max(0, min(focal_distance_list) − max(flhm_list)) max_distance max(focal_distance_list) + max(flhm_list) optimal_distance mean(focal_distance_list), the desired skin–target distance

If max(flhm_list) is NaN or ≤ 0, a 10 mm margin is used instead. For a steerable array, list the steering depths in focal_distance_list and set the window to the steering range. The default margin (the largest FLHM, often > 50 mm) otherwise admits skin spots the focus cannot reach.

Launcher inputs and the FLHM fit Input Description t1_filepath Subject T1.nii.gz (SimNIBS output) simnibs_mesh_filepath Head mesh sub-XXX.msh (CHARM output) target_mask_filepath Binary NIfTI sphere centred on the target tx_config_yaml Transducer + placement parameters (written by PRESTUS)

The YAML is flat. Key fields: max_distance, min_distance, optimal_distance, transducer_diameter, plane_offset, additional_offset, focal_distance_list, flhm_list, five weight_* scalars. Without optimal_distance in the YAML, the launcher uses (min_distance + max_distance) / 2.

PlanTUS fits FLHM against focal distance with a cubic, which needs at least 4 points. With fewer (e.g. the single O'Neil estimate when no axial profile CSV is given), the launchers (plantus_compat.py) interpolate linearly and hold FLHM constant outside the calibrated range. Non-finite pairs are dropped.

items.title: 2  Convert SimNIBS Mesh to Surfaces
items.text:
PlanTUS.convert_simnibs_mesh_to_surfaces (convert_simnibs_mesh_to_surface in PlanTUS 1.x) extracts .surf.gii surfaces from the .msh mesh. With PlanTUS 2.0 or later, the skin surface is smoothed with placement.plantus.skin_smoothing_iterations Taubin passes (default 2, as in PlanTUS) before any criterion is computed; this reduces mesh noise in the normals and so in the angle maps.

Surfaces extracted Surface SimNIBS tags File Skin 1005 skin.surf.gii Skull 1007, 1008 skull.surf.gii

SimNIBS also produces skull.stl, used for the skull-entry angle (4d).

items.title: 3  Build the Avoidance Mask
items.text:
Skin vertices over air cavities and near the eyes and ears are excluded from the composite score.

Excluded vertices and required tools

Skin vertices over air cavities and sinuses, within 30 mm of each eye centre and within 15 mm of the tragus are excluded from the composite score (avoidance == 0), and the mask is eroded by transducer_radius mm as a safety margin. The step needs final_tissues.nii.gz and eeg_positions/Fiducials.csv from the m2m folder; PlanTUS 2.0 builds the mask in Python, PlanTUS 1.x also needs fslmaths, wb_command, mri_tessellate and mris_convert. If any is missing, the step is skipped with a warning and all vertices remain eligible.

How the mask is built (create_avoidance_mask)
  1. Air cavities / sinuses: vertices whose outward normal ray hits air in final_tissues.nii.gz (holes filled and the air surface extracted in Python in PlanTUS 2.0; with wb_command -volume-fill-holes and mri_tessellate in 1.x).
  2. Eyes: vertices within 30 mm of each eye centre (tag 1006, centres by k-means on x).
  3. Ears (tragus): vertices within 15 mm of LPA/RPA from eeg_positions/Fiducials.csv, shifted 1.5 cm posterior.
  4. Erosion: the mask is eroded by transducer_radius mm.

items.title: 4  Score Each Vertex
items.text:
PlanTUS scores every skin vertex on five metrics: 4a to 4d here, 4e below.

Metrics 4a to 4d Metric Definition Better 4a Skin–target distance d_i Euclidean distance from vertex i to the target mask's centre of mass (PlanTUS.roi_center_of_gravity). The score uses the absolute deviation from optimal_distance; vertices outside [min_distance, max_distance] are excluded (see 5a). Lower deviation 4b Skin–target angle α_i Angle (degrees) between the skin normal and the vector to the target centre. Lower 4c Skin–target intersection x_i Path length of the 200 mm outward-normal ray inside the target mask STL (PlanTUS.stl_from_nii); chords are summed for several entry–exit pairs. Higher 4d Skin–skull angle β_i Angle between the skin normal and the skull normal where the 40 mm ray meets the skull. NaN (worst) where it meets no skull. Lower

items.title: 4e  Skull Thickness
items.text:
Bone path length (mm) along the 4d ray.

Sampling and missing values

final_tissues.nii.gz (next to the SimNIBS mesh) is sampled every 0.25 mm (nearest voxel) up to 50 mm from the skin. Bone samples (labels 4, 7, 8: bone, compact, spongy) are counted until the first intracranial sample (labels 1–3: WM, GM, CSF). Lower is better.

t_i is NaN (worst) where the ray meets no bone or reaches no intracranial tissue within 50 mm (face, neck, skull base). Without final_tissues.nii.gz, t_i is NaN everywhere, a warning is logged and weight_skull_thickness is ignored.

A few vertices get implausibly thin values (≤ 1 mm): neck rays reaching the spinal canal, and skin next to the ear where CHARM places bone or CSF directly under the skin. These vertices also have large skin–target angles and are rarely chosen unless thickness dominates the weights.

items.title: 5a  Combine and Evaluate Scores
items.text:
PlanTUS combines the normalised metrics into a weighted composite score; headless mode places the vertex with the minimum score.

The composite score

Each metric is min–max normalised to [0, 1] over its finite values. NaN or infinite values are set to 1 (worst), also for the inverted intersection metric.

score_i = ( w_dist  × norm(|d_i − optimal_distance|)
          + w_ang   × norm(α_i)
          + w_inter × (1 − norm(x_i))
          + w_skull × norm(β_i)
          + w_thick × norm(t_i) )
        ÷ (w_dist + w_ang + w_inter + w_skull + w_thick)

If t_i is unavailable (all NaN, or an older plantus_metrics.mat without it), w_thick is dropped from numerator and denominator. Vertices with avoidance == 0, d_i < min_distance or d_i > max_distance get score = inf. Headless mode places the vertex with the minimum score. Interactive mode reports that optimum before wb_view opens, and the score and rank of each placed vertex. A few outlying vertices (e.g. 40 mm skull-base rays for t_i) compress the spread and weaken that criterion below its nominal weight.

Criteria evaluation (placement.plantus.evaluate) re-scores the placement under 12 weight sets and flags settings under which a criterion cannot discriminate.

Criteria evaluation

Criteria evaluation (placement.plantus.evaluate, default true; needs save_metrics) re-scores the placement under 12 weight sets (configured, equal, one criterion at 0.55 with the rest sharing 0.45, and each criterion alone) and writes, next to the metrics file:

File Contents plantus_evaluation.json Placed vertex (rank, each criterion's value and % of eligible vertices that are better), per-criterion ranges over eligible vertices, the weight sweep and diagnostics; read by the placement report plantus_weight_sensitivity.csv One row per weight set: chosen vertex, its criteria, distance to the placed vertex plantus_criteria_maps.png Each criterion and the composite score on the skin (4 views) plantus_weight_sensitivity.png Criteria at the placed spot and at each weight set's choice; all chosen spots on the skin

Diagnostics flag settings under which a criterion cannot discriminate between positions:

Code Condition distance_range_unconstrained [min_distance, max_distance] excludes < 5% of the skin outside the avoidance mask (e.g. a large flhm_list value) intersection_sparse Beam–target intersection non-zero at < 2% of eligible vertices (small target mask) <criterion>_unavailable / _nan Criterion undefined at all / > 25% of eligible vertices placed_ineligible Placed vertex excluded under the configured scoring (interactive selection) placed_not_optimum Placed vertex is not the composite optimum (interactive selection) tradeoff_<criterion> At the placed vertex a weighted criterion is worse than at > 50% of eligible vertices weight_sensitive A single-criterion-heavy weight set moves the chosen spot > 20 mm

Warnings also go to the placement log. Evaluation failures never abort a placement.

plantus_metrics.mat and offline re-scoring

plantus_metrics.mat (placement.plantus.save_metrics, default true) is written to <output_dir>/plantus_metrics.mat. It holds skin coordinates, normals and faces, the target centre, d_i, α_i, x_i, β_i, t_i (skull_thickness), the avoidance mask, the composite score, best_vertex (composite optimum), selected_vertex (vertex placed), selection_mode (auto headless, gui interactive, manual after --do_only_trajectory), min_distance, max_distance, optimal_distance and the weights. Vertex indices and faces are 0-based. Each run deletes an existing plantus_metrics.mat first, even with save_metrics: false.

Use compute_composite_score in plantus_common.py to re-score under other weights without new ray casts. The evaluation runs plantus_evaluation.py on the metrics; to evaluate an existing metrics file, run python functions/neuronav/plantus_evaluation.py <plantus_metrics.mat>.

items.title: 5b  Select a Vertex Interactively
items.text:
With placement.plantus.interactive = 1, wb_view opens a scene with the maps 4a–4d, one per tab. The skull-thickness map (skull_thickness_skin.func.gii) is loaded too and can be chosen as an overlay in any tab. Each click replaces the selection and prints the vertex's criteria, composite score and rank (and the composite optimum) to the log.

Review dialog and requirements

Closing wb_view places the last selected vertex (step 6) and opens its placement scene (transducer and focus on skin and T1) in a second wb_view. A review dialog then offers Use this position, Choose another vertex (the planning scene reopens; metrics are not recomputed) or Cancel (the launcher exits non-zero and PRESTUS stops). Closing the planning scene without a click reviews the previous vertex, or aborts if there is none.

Interactive mode requires:

  • A graphical display (desktop or VNC session; not a batch/HPC job). The MATLAB desktop is not needed: placement.plantus.interactive = 1 also works under matlab -batch and from the Nexus
  • pynput (mouse listener); on Linux it needs an X display, on macOS Accessibility permission for the terminal/MATLAB
  • Connectome Workbench wb_view, on PATH or via placement.plantus.connectome_wb_path
  • PyQt5 for the review dialog (part of SimNIBS)
The --selection launcher option

--selection sets how a vertex is confirmed: review (the dialog above; PRESTUS uses it), prompt (Generate transducer placement for vertex N? (yes/no) after each click, for a terminal), last_click (no review) and auto (default: prompt when stdin is a terminal, else review if PyQt5 is available, else last_click). If no vertex is confirmed, the launcher exits non-zero. If wb_view exits at once without a click, the planning scene is reopened without the skull-thickness map.

items.title: 6  Compute the Placement Geometry
items.text:
For the selected vertex, PlanTUS computes the beam direction and the transducer centre (prepare_acoustic_simulation) and writes a 4 × 4 Localite position matrix (RAS mm).

Output files

Outputs go to <output_dir>/vtx<N>/, where <output_dir> is the per-target placement run folder <path.placement>/sub-XXX/plantus/<target_name>/:

File Contents *_Localite.mat position_matrix (4×4, RAS mm), used by PRESTUS *_Localite.txt Plain-text copy *_kPlan.mat Same matrix in k-Plan convention (m, axes permuted) *_Localite_XML.txt, *_Localite_dummyXML.txt (2.x) Fake Localite XML snippet (rewritten on each run) *_Trajectory_Brainsight.txt, *_Trajectory_BabelBrain.txt Trajectory for Brainsight and BabelBrain (PlanTUS 2.0) *Focus*, *TransducerModel*.surf.gii Focus and transducer surface models at the position scene.scene Workbench placement scene (all modes; opened only by the Workbench picker)

PlanTUS 2.0 names the files <mask>_vtx<N>_…, PlanTUS 1.x position_matrix_<mask>_vtx<N>_….

<output_dir> itself holds the skin/skull surfaces, the metric maps (distances_skin, distances_skin_thresholded, angles_skin, target_intersection_skin, skin_skull_angles_skin, skull_thickness_skin, avoidance_skin; .func.gii), the planning scene.scene and plantus_metrics.mat.

Beam direction and transducer centre

For the selected vertex v:

  1. Beam direction: PlanTUS 2.0 aims from the skin vertex at the target centre (its default target_centered orientation); the PlanTUS page draws this axis. PlanTUS 1.x uses the negated skin normal if it intersects the target (x_v > 0), otherwise the negated skin-to-target vector. All are unit vectors pointing into the head.
  2. Transducer centre: transducer_centre = skin_coordinate_v − (plane_offset + additional_offset) × beam_direction. plane_offset is the distance from the bowl apex to the exit plane (curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm); additional_offset is placement.skin_gap_mm, the gap between skin and exit plane.
  3. Localite position matrix (PlanTUS.create_Localite_position_matrix): column 3 = transducer_centre, column 0 = beam_direction, columns 1–2 by Gram–Schmidt.

items.title: 7  Read the Output into PRESTUS
items.text: position_transducer_plantus.m loads the most recent *Localite.mat under <path.placement>/sub-XXX/plantus/<target_name>/ written during the current run. If there is none, it errors (PRESTUS:plantus:noOutput). localite_matrix_to_positions converts position_matrix into trans_pos and focus_pos in voxel coordinates. A T1 overlay plot (plot_placement_t1_overlay) of the transducer and target is written to the subject output folder.

items.title: Coordinate Conventions
items.text: Frame Units Description Voxel / grid integer indices PRESTUS simulation grid RAS+ (subject) mm T1 image world space; used by Localite matrix MNI mm Template space; target specified here, mapped to RAS via SimNIBS k-Plan m, permuted axes Not used by PRESTUS

items.title: External Dependencies
items.text:
Tool Automatic / chosen vertex Workbench Used in step SimNIBS Python (nibabel, scipy, nilearn, vtk, h5py), see installation guide ✓ ✓ All steps PlanTUS Python library (PlanTUS.py) ✓ ✓ All steps trimesh, pandas (PlanTUS 2.0) ✓ ✓ Surfaces, avoidance mask, target model PyYAML (or built-in fallback) ✓ ✓ YAML config loading FSL fslmaths (PlanTUS 1.x) ✓ ✓ Avoidance mask: tissue binarisation Connectome Workbench wb_command (PlanTUS 1.x) ✓ ✓ Surface metrics, avoidance mask FreeSurfer mri_tessellate / mris_convert (PlanTUS 1.x) ✓ ✓ Avoidance mask: air mesh Connectome Workbench wb_view – ✓ Interactive scene display pynput Python package – ✓ Mouse click listener for wb_view PyQt5 (part of SimNIBS) – ✓ Review dialog

The launchers detect the PlanTUS version from code/PlanTUS.py and check for the tools that version needs before they start.

Install trimesh (PlanTUS 2.0), potpourri3d and pynput (Workbench picker) in the SimNIBS conda environment. PlanTUS 2.0 uses potpourri3d for exact geodesic distances when it shrinks the avoidance mask; without it, PlanTUS falls back to an approximation, so the mask can differ slightly between installs:

conda activate simnibs_v4.6.0
pip install trimesh potpourri3d pynput

items.title: TUS_entry Transducer Placement
items.text:
A simulated transducer position is useful only if the real transducer can be placed there with good contact on the scalp. placement.mode: 'tus_entry' runs the TUS_entry R toolbox, which selects the scalp entry point with the smallest coupling geometry error (the standard deviation of the transducer-disk-edge to scalp distances), subject to an optional depth constraint. TUS_entry optimises mechanical fit (how perpendicular the transducer disk sits on the scalp); PlanTUS optimises acoustic objectives (beam–target overlap, skull thickness).

On this page:

  • Installation: R, its packages and TUS_entry in a conda environment.
  • Required Configuration: the two paths PRESTUS needs and the head mask it builds.
  • Optional Configuration: masks, depth window and other settings.
  • Candidate List: the full ranked candidate list.
  • Coordinate Conventions: voxel and world frames, and how the exit plane and focus are set.
  • Output Files: the files written per run.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When good mechanical contact of the transducer is the main concern.
  • Before you start: R with TUS_entry in a conda environment, and a SimNIBS segmentation (or another head mask).

Experimental feature

TUS_entry placement is under active development and is not yet covered by the PRESTUS test suite. Check the placement report before simulating.

placement:
  mode: tus_entry
  tus_entry:
    script_path: /path/to/TUS_entry/TUS_entry.R
    env_path:    /home/user/.conda/envs/tus_entry
    mni_target_mm: [-40, 20, 50]     # DLPFC example
    minimal_distance_cm: 4.24
    maximal_distance_cm: 7.46
    transducer_size_cm:  6.4
    target_name: DLPFC
How TUS_entry selects the entry point
  1. Distance filter: candidate entry points on a sphere of radius maximal_distance around the target centroid. Only trajectories that cross the scalp surface and avoid the exclusion zone are kept.
  2. Spatial decimation: candidates are thinned by resolution.
  3. Angle scoring: for each candidate, a circular transducer footprint (diameter transducer_size) perpendicular to the trajectory is scored by the SD of disk-edge-to-scalp distances. A lower SD is a better-coupled placement.
  4. Final selection: the angle-ranked candidates are fine-tuned in turn; the first that satisfies minimal_distance ≤ depth ≤ maximal_distance is returned.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
TUS_entry requires R and four CRAN packages. Use a dedicated conda environment:

conda env create -f examples/environment_tus_entry.yml
conda activate tus_entry

environment_tus_entry.yml is in examples/ (run the command there or give its path). Then clone TUS_entry:

git clone https://github.com/CyrilAtkinson/TUS_entry /path/to/TUS_entry

Point placement.tus_entry.script_path to TUS_entry.R and placement.tus_entry.env_path to the conda env prefix (e.g. ~/.conda/envs/tus_entry).

items.title: Required Configuration
items.text:
Field Type Description placement.tus_entry.script_path string Full path to TUS_entry.R placement.tus_entry.env_path string Path to conda env containing Rscript

TUS_entry needs a solid head mask. It walks each candidate ray from outside the head towards the target and takes the last voxel outside the mask as the scalp entry. With a hollow skin shell the head interior counts as outside, every candidate collapses onto the target, and TUS_entry fails (replacement has 1 row, data has 0). PRESTUS therefore builds the head mask itself: it reads placement.tus_entry.scalp_mask (default: the SimNIBS m2m_sub-<ID>/final_tissues.nii.gz), treats every nonzero voxel as head, fills it (3D and slice-wise, which also closes a skin shell open at the neck) and writes the result to the work directory. The source file is only read.

items.title: Optional Configuration
items.text:
Field Default Description placement.tus_entry.scalp_mask (SimNIBS final_tissues.nii.gz) NIfTI head or scalp mask in the T1 grid (nonzero = head); filled into a solid head mask in the work directory placement.tus_entry.target_mask (auto) Path to binary NIfTI target mask. When empty, a sphere is generated from focus_pos or mni_target_mm. placement.tus_entry.target_mask_radius_mm 5 Radius [mm] for the auto-generated spherical target mask placement.tus_entry.mni_target_mm (from focus_pos) [1×3] MNI target coordinate [mm]; converted to subject RAS via SimNIBS placement.tus_entry.exclu_mask '' Path to binary NIfTI exclusion zone (e.g. ventricles, vessels) placement.tus_entry.minimal_distance_cm 4.24 Minimum scalp-to-target depth [cm] placement.tus_entry.maximal_distance_cm 7.46 Maximum scalp-to-target depth [cm] placement.tus_entry.transducer_size_cm 6.4 Transducer outer diameter [cm] placement.tus_entry.voxel_size_cm (T1 voxel size) Voxel size [cm/voxel]; by default the mean T1 voxel size (the masks are on the T1 grid). TUS_entry assumes isotropic voxels placement.tus_entry.resolution_cm 0.33 Spatial decimation step [cm] placement.tus_entry.return_candidates false Save the full ranked candidate list as RDS (see below) placement.tus_entry.target_name 'target' Label for output filenames placement.tus_entry.work_dir (auto) Override output directory (default: <path.placement>/sub-<ID>/tus_entry/<target_name>/)

Units

TUS_entry uses centimetres internally. PRESTUS converts distance outputs to millimetres, as for all other PRESTUS coordinates.

All keys are also listed in Parameters.

items.title: Candidate List
items.text:
By default, TUS_entry returns a single selected entry point. With return_candidates = true, the runner script saves the full angle-ranked candidate list to tus_entry_candidates.rds in the working directory. Inspect it in R:

cands <- readRDS("tus_entry_candidates.rds")
head(cands)

MATLAB cannot read RDS files directly. To filter ranked candidates in PRESTUS (e.g. the entry with the lowest skull thickness among the top-10 coupling candidates), load the RDS in R, export to CSV and load that in MATLAB. The candidates output argument of position_transducer_tus_entry is reserved for a future native implementation and returns an empty struct array.

items.title: Coordinate Conventions
items.text:
Space What TUS_entry provides PRESTUS convention Voxel 1-based array indices (same as MATLAB) trans_pos, focus_pos: 1-based World NIfTI affine applied to voxel indices trans_pos_ras, focus_pos_ras: RAS mm

TUS_entry operates in the native voxel space of the input masks. Use the same T1 as the reference for both SimNIBS segmentation and PRESTUS placement.

The exit plane lies placement.skin_gap_mm (default 5 mm) outward from the Scalp_coordinates returned by TUS_entry, along the trajectory. trans_pos lies a further curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm outward, the offset used by all placement modes. focus_pos is derived by stepping inward from the exit plane by transducer.focal_distance_ep (or focal_distance_bowl minus the apex-to-exit-plane offset, as focal_distance_calculation converts it; if neither is set, the geometric focus dist_geom_ep_mm).

items.title: Output Files
items.text:
All outputs are written to the placement run folder, <path.placement>/sub-<ID>/tus_entry/<target_name>/ (override with placement.tus_entry.work_dir):

File Content run_tus_entry.R Auto-generated runner script (for reproducibility / debugging) tus_entry_report.csv Selected entry: voxel coords, distance [mm], angle score tus_entry_candidates.rds Full ranked candidate list (only if return_candidates = true) sub-<ID>_tus_entry_head_mask.nii.gz Solid head mask passed to TUS_entry as scalp placement_run.json Run record: resolved positions and the settings they depend on (reused per placement.reuse) sub-<ID>_<target_name>_trajectory.txt Brainsight trajectory export sub-<ID>_<target_name>_target_mask.nii.gz Auto-generated spherical target mask (if no target mask was provided) References

When using TUS_entry placement, cite: Atkinson C, et al. TUS_entry: A tool for optimising transducer entry point selection in transcranial ultrasound stimulation. GitHub: https://github.com/CyrilAtkinson/TUS_entry

items.title: Segmentation and Head Preprocessing
items.text:
The skull reflects, attenuates and refracts ultrasound, so how the head is represented in the simulation shapes the predicted focus and intensity. This step turns an MRI into that representation: SimNIBS labels the tissues, and PRESTUS orients, resamples, smooths and crops the labels into the simulation grid.

On this page:

  • Segmentation: running SimNIBS charm and reusing its result.
  • From Segmentation to Grid: orientation, scaling, layer mapping, cropping and smoothing of the property maps.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Rarely: the defaults suit most studies. Read it when the skull looks wrong in the report, or to understand why the grid has the size it has.
  • Before you start: A layered simulation with a SimNIBS segmentation.

items.title: Segmentation
items.text:
For a layered medium, the first run segments the T1 (and the T2, when path.t2_pattern is set) with SimNIBS charm into <path.seg>/m2m_sub-XXX/. This takes an hour or more. Later runs reuse final_tissues.nii.gz from that folder unless io.overwrite_simnibs: 1.

  • modules.segmentation_only: 1 segments and stops, e.g. to segment all subjects before simulating them.
  • segmentation.use_qform: 1 when charm reports a qform/sform mismatch; segmentation.debug: 1 passes --debug to charm.
  • segmentation.noneck: 1 passes --noneck for a scan without a neck.

items.title: SimNIBS Version and charm Settings
items.text:
startup.simnibs_bin_path selects the SimNIBS install, and with it the version; PRESTUS needs SimNIBS 4 or later. While they are empty, hpc.ld_library_path (the install's libraries for SimNIBS tools) and placement.plantus.env_path (the Python PlanTUS runs in) follow it; a value set there overrides it. To change charm's settings, copy the install's charm.ini (in its simnibs package folder), edit the copy and set segmentation.settings_file to it; keep it outside the m2m folder. Report the settings you changed.

An existing segmentation is reused even when another version or other settings are selected. PRESTUS then warns, comparing the version in charm_log.html and the settings in settings.ini of the m2m folder with the selection. Set io.overwrite_simnibs: 1 to segment again, which deletes the m2m folder first, or point path.seg to a separate folder per version to keep both. What was built from the old segmentation is detected on reuse: grid, medium, acoustic and head-model caches, placement runs and pseudo-CTs record the segmentation's checksum (Cache reuse checks), and a defaced copy is made again.

In the Nexus, the Segmentation card (Medium tab) lists the SimNIBS installs on this computer, shows the version and the existing segmentation, opens charm_report.html, and has the re-run switch. When runs are submitted to a cluster over SSH (Run tab), Scan cluster lists the installs there: conda environments, ~/SimNIBS*, /opt/simnibs* and the bin folders of the simnibs environment modules. The Nexus keeps the result per host, so it can check a cluster path that does not exist on this computer.

items.title: Defaced Copy for Sharing
items.text:
segmentation.deface: 1 writes a copy of the m2m folder, m2m_sub-XXX_defaced/, with the face removed from the anatomical images by pydeface (install it in the SimNIBS environment). Tissue labels, surfaces, warps and meshes are copied unchanged, and the original folder is not modified. The copy is made once and again after the segmentation changes. Figures are defaced separately, with io.deface_plots (on by default).

Installing SimNIBS: Installation. Errors: Troubleshooting.

items.title: From Segmentation to Grid
items.text: PRESTUS turns a layered segmentation into a simulation grid in three steps: a single resample that rotates and rescales each image (Orientation and Scaling), layer mapping with mask smoothing and skull hole filling, and cropping with padding. Optional smoothing of the property maps runs later, when the medium is set up. Each step has one or two settings; the defaults are listed with them.

items.title: Orientation
items.text:
grid.mode sets how the head is rotated before cropping, so that the beam runs along the grid's z axis:

Mode What it does focal_axis (default) Rotates the volume so that the mean beam axis of all transducers aligns with z. With one transducer this is its beam axis. transducer_axis Rotates so that the beam axis of transducer(1) aligns with z. Use it when other transducers are secondary. ras_plus No rotation; only isotropic rescaling to the grid resolution. Keeps the world-space (RAS+) orientation. principal_axis Removed; errors. Use focal_axis. How the mean beam axis is formed

Beams are averaged as axes, not directions (mean_beam_axis): a beam pointing against transducer(1)'s is reversed first. Beams converging from the same side give their bisector; opposed (bilateral) beams give the bisector of the two axes, so each beam is tilted from z by about half the angle between their axes (two beams 41° off exactly opposed: 21° each). z points along transducer(1)'s beam. If the mean axis vector is shorter than grid.focal_axis_min_norm (default 0.5), transducer(1)'s axis is used instead; for two transducers this cannot happen (minimum 0.71). Implemented in preproc_align_to_mean_focal_axis (focal_axis) and preproc_align_to_focal_axis (transducer_axis). In all modes the returned scale_rotate_recenter_matrix encodes the full T1-space to grid transform, used to map every transducer and target position into the simulation space.

items.title: Scaling
items.text: The planning image, the segmentation and the bone mask (or (pseudo-)CT) are resliced to grid.resolution_mm by isotropic scaling and centred regridding, in the same resample as the rotation. Images with fewer than 20 distinct values, such as masks and segmentations, use nearest-neighbour interpolation; all others, such as the planning image or a (pseudo-)CT, use linear interpolation.

items.title: Layer Mapping and Smoothing
items.text:
The SimNIBS segmentation (10 tissues) is mapped onto the layers in layers. The default lists six: water, brain, skin, skull (label 4), skull_cortical and skull_trabecular. Labels not assigned to another layer become water, which by default includes CSF (label 3), eyes, blood and muscle. A requested layer without a segmentation label is dropped. A charm segmentation has no label 4, so the default skull layer is dropped and the head consists of brain, skin, cortical and trabecular bone in water; with a pseudo-CT the skull layers are merged into one skull layer. Each layer index corresponds to its position in medium_properties, so layers can be added or removed without changing the ids of the others.

Each layer mask is smoothed and binarised. Settings:

Setting Default Options headmodel.smooth_method gaussian gaussian (isotropic blur, smooth edges, moderate erosion), box (uniform kernel, fastest, blocky, prone to skull holes), off (raw mask, no filtering or binarisation) headmodel.smooth_fwhm_mm 1 mm Kernel size in mm, converted to voxels at the grid resolution (not the T1 resolution) headmodel.smooth_threshold_skull, headmodel.smooth_threshold_other 0.5 Binarisation threshold after smoothing; higher gives a thinner mask headmodel.skull_fill_method rubberwrap rubberwrap (skull inflation) or imclose; holes become cortical skull

With a two-layer skull, cortical and trabecular bone are first combined and smoothed as one skull, which becomes cortical bone; the trabecular layer is then smoothed and added inside it. Holes in the combined skull are filled afterwards and become cortical bone.

items.title: Cropping
items.text:
The grid is cropped tightly around the head and every transducer bowl, with a 1-voxel margin; k-Wave adds the PML outside the grid. This keeps the simulation as small as possible. Two settings change the crop:

  • headmodel.csf_expansion [mm]: how far beyond the CSF segmentation the head region extends. Voxels outside become water and are eligible for cropping.
  • headmodel.head_pad_mm: symmetric padding added to the rotated volume before the CSF expansion and the crop. The crop box already contains every bowl, and the volume is padded automatically (with a warning) if a bowl centre falls outside it, so this setting is rarely needed. Padding beyond the head and bowls is cropped away, so it does not slow the simulation.
Crop bounds and FFT-friendly sizes

The crop box encloses the layered medium mask and the bowl geometry of every transducer, plus a 1-voxel margin; the PML lies outside the grid. With several transducers all bowls count, which matters for bilateral set-ups: without the contralateral bowl, that side of the grid would be bounded only by the CSF-expanded head and would carry unused space. Rotation follows the mean beam axis in the default focal_axis mode and transducer(1)'s axis in transducer_axis mode; all transducers are mapped into the same space before the bounds are computed. The box is then enlarged by up to grid.max_expand voxels per dimension to sizes with small prime factors (find_min_factor), which makes k-Wave's FFTs faster. The medium stays anchored at its origin, so transducer and target do not move relative to the head. All transformations are concatenated and applied to the transducer and target positions.

items.title: Property Map Smoothing
items.text:
Sharp transitions between tissues reflect sound. headmodel.smooth_properties: true smooths the acoustic and thermal property maps themselves during medium setup, with the same smooth_method and smooth_fwhm_mm as above. It is off by default. Pseudo-CTs made with PRESTUS already smooth the skull edges (pseudo-CT), so property smoothing is usually not wanted with them. Recommended settings are an active area of investigation.

Which property each tissue gets is described in Medium properties.

items.title: CT-Based Skull Mapping
items.text:
By default each skull layer of a layered simulation takes one value per property, although skull bone properties can vary within and between individuals. A CT gives the skull subject-specific properties instead. With pct.enabled: 1, PRESTUS maps the Hounsfield units (HU) of a CT to density, sound speed and attenuation within the skull layer. The CT is one of two images:

  • a measured CT of the subject (path.ct_pattern), or
  • a pseudo-CT that PRESTUS generates from a UTE/PETRA MR image, used when path.ct_pattern is empty.

Both feed the same HU-to-property mapping; only the pseudo-CT needs the UTE-to-HU step first.

On this page:

  • Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run: the scan, the tools, the minimum config and the outputs.
  • Using a Measured CT: the CT's requirements and the minimum config.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you want skull properties that follow the individual skull, and have a CT or a UTE/PETRA scan.
  • Before you start: A CT co-registered to the T1w, or a UTE/PETRA image per subject plus FSL and ANTs.

Subpages:

  • From UTE to Pseudo-HU: for choosing pct.skull_mapping and the matching pct.density_calibration; read it whenever you change either from the default.
  • Skull Property Mappings: for choosing how pHU become skull density, sound speed and attenuation, with the equations and references.

Experimental

(pseudo-)HU mapping is an experimental feature in active development. The most suitable mapping remains an active area of research; treat all mappings as experimental. See this issue.

items.title: Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run
items.text:
1. Acquire an MR sequence with detailed bone contrast (PETRA UTE; example parameters below).
  2. Run SimNIBS with the T1w and the PETRA UTE scan (instead of the T2w) as inputs, either in PRESTUS (default) or in the SimNIBS GUI. The UTE image is the one in path.t2_pattern, which SimNIBS registers to the T1 as m2m_sub-XXX/T2_reg.nii.gz (UTE_reg.nii.gz is also read).
  3. Set pct.enabled: 1. PRESTUS runs pct_create_pseudoCT.sh after segmentation if pseudoCT.nii.gz does not exist yet. This needs FSL (fslmaths), ANTs (N4BiasFieldCorrection, SmoothImage) and MATLAB on PATH; set startup.fsl_bin_path and startup.ants_bin_path so PRESTUS can prepend them. On HPC, also set startup.matlab_bin_path.

Minimum config:

path:
  t2_pattern: 'sub-%1$03d_UTE.nii.gz'  # UTE image (used for both SimNIBS and pseudoCT)

startup:
  fsl_bin_path: '/opt/fsl/bin'           # prepended to PATH for fslmaths
  ants_bin_path: '/opt/ants/bin'          # prepended to PATH for N4BiasFieldCorrection, SmoothImage
  matlab_bin_path: '/opt/matlab/R2024a/bin/matlab'  # required on HPC; local falls back to matlabroot

pct:
  enabled: 1
  skull_mapping: 'kosciessa' # UTE→HU linear mapping algorithm
  debug: 1                   # keep intermediate images in the debug_pct/ subfolder
  mapping_density: 'k-plan'
  density_calibration: ''    # HU->density table for k-plan; '' = k-Plan default (see Matching the CT Calibration)
  mapping_soundspeed: 'k-plan'
  mapping_attenuation: 'k-plan'

Outputs go to <path.pct>/sub-XXX/, or to <parent of path.seg>/pct/sub-XXX/ when path.pct is empty:

File / folder Content pseudoCT.nii.gz, tissues_mask.nii.gz pseudo-CT and tissue mask pseudoCT.json sidecar: skull mapping, segmentation folder, PRESTUS version debug_pct/ intermediate images and the log log_hpc/ cluster job logs

Reuse. An existing pseudoCT.nii.gz is used and not regenerated. Its pseudoCT.json must record the current pct.skull_mapping; otherwise the run stops with prestus:cache:signatureMismatch (see io.cache_signature_check). To regenerate, move the folder aside or set path.pct to another folder. A pseudo-CT without a sidecar is used with the warning prestus:cache:unverified. A pseudo-CT inside m2m_sub-XXX/ is used with the warning PRESTUS:pct:legacyLocation; move it to the pseudo-CT folder. See Starting from earlier stage outputs.

Manual. You can also run pct_create_pseudoCT.sh in bash before starting PRESTUS. An example wrapper is at examples/createPseudoCT.sh. Required modules: SimNIBS, FSL, ANTs.

Example PETRA UTE parameters

From Carpino et al. (2024):

  • TR: 3.32 ms
  • TE: 0.07 ms
  • voxel size: 0.8 mm3
  • 352 sagittal slices
  • flip angle: 2°
  • FoV: 294 mm

items.title: Using a Measured CT
items.text:
Set path.ct_pattern to the subject's CT and pct.enabled: 1. The run then needs no UTE image and generates no pseudo-CT.

path:
  ct_pattern: 'sub-%1$03d_CT.nii.gz'  # relative to path.anat, like t1_pattern

pct:
  enabled: 1
  density_calibration: ''  # this CT's HU->density table; '' = k-Plan default
  mapping_density: 'k-plan'
  mapping_soundspeed: 'k-plan'
  mapping_attenuation: 'k-plan'
  • Units. The CT must hold Hounsfield units (NIfTI scaling is applied).
  • Registration. The CT must be co-registered to the T1w: PRESTUS resamples it onto the segmentation grid through both images' world coordinates and does not register it. Voxels outside the CT are set to air (-1000 HU). The run logs the median HU of the skull voxels and warns (PRESTUS:pct:ctMisregistered) when it is below 300 HU.
  • Skull voxels. The skull layer comes from the SimNIBS segmentation, built as for the pseudo-CT. No files are written to the pseudo-CT folder.
  • Calibration. HU depend on scanner, kVp and kernel. Set pct.density_calibration to this CT's HU-to-density table when you have one; with the k-Plan default, PRESTUS warns (prestus:pct:ctDefaultCalibration).
  • Reuse. Grid and medium caches record the CT's name, size and date, so replacing the CT rebuilds them.

items.title: From UTE to Pseudo-HU
items.text:
The pseudo-CT is only as good as the line that turns UTE intensity into pseudo-Hounsfield units (pHU), and that line returns HU on the scale of the CT it was fitted to. This page describes the available UTE-to-HU mappings, how PRESTUS generates the pseudo-CT, and how to pair each mapping with the HU-to-density calibration of the same CT.

On this page:

  • Choosing the UTE-to-HU Mapping: the pct.skull_mapping options and the generation steps.
  • Matching the CT Calibration: pairing pct.skull_mapping with pct.density_calibration.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you change pct.skull_mapping from the default, use your own UTE-to-HU line, or set pct.density_calibration.
  • Before you start: A pseudo-CT run set up as in Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run.

items.title: Choosing the UTE-to-HU Mapping
items.text:
pct.skull_mapping sets the linear UTE→pHU mapping of the skull. Soft tissue is set to 42 HU and air to -1000 HU for every mapping.

skull_mapping pHU kosciessa (default) individualised: a line fitted per subject through three UTE histogram points set to 1900, 700 and 300 HU (see below) miscouridou pHU = −2085 UTE + 2329 carpino (deprecated) pHU = -2194 UTE + 2236. Warns prestus:pct:deprecatedSkullMapping; the same line is custom with custom_slope: -2194, custom_intercept: 2236 wiesinger pHU = -2000 (UTE-1) + 42 treeby pHU = -2929.6 UTE + 3274.9 (ucl-bug/petra-to-ct; fitted to 80 kVp CT: use with density_calibration: ucl_lowdose_80kvp, see below) custom pHU = pct.custom_slope UTE + pct.custom_intercept (any other linear map) The generation steps
  • UTE: threshold at 0, bias field correction, then normalisation by the soft tissue peak (normalised UTE intensity = 1). pct_soft_tissue_peak finds the peak.
  • pHU soft tissue (normalised UTE intensity = 1): 42 HU (Wiesinger et al., 2018).
  • pHU air: -1000 HU (Wiesinger et al., 2018; Miscouridou et al., 2022).
  • pHU skull: the linear mapping set by pct.skull_mapping (table above).
  • kosciessa (pct_skullmapping_fit) fits a least-squares line through three points from the UTE histograms of charm cortical and trabecular bone: the lower quarter-max crossing of the cortical histogram → 1900 HU, the crossover of the two histograms → 700 HU, and the upper quarter-max crossing of the trabecular histogram around its x-weighted peak → 300 HU. Bins 0.9–1.1 are replaced by a spline against soft-tissue partial volume. The anchors, width level and interpolation window are options of pct_skullmapping_fit.
  • 3D Gaussian smoothing (σ=0.8 voxels via ANTs' SmoothImage) prevents abrupt tissue transitions in the simulation grid. Within an eroded skull mask, unsmoothed values are kept to limit partial volume effects.

items.title: Matching the CT Calibration
items.text:
A UTE→HU line returns HU on the scale of the CT it was fitted to. That scale depends on scanner, tube voltage (kVp) and reconstruction kernel: at 80 kVp, bone has about 1.35 times the HU it has at about 120 kVp. The simulation needs density, and turning HU into density needs the calibration of that same CT. Set pct.skull_mapping, pct.mapping_density: k-plan and pct.density_calibration together:

skull_mapping CT the line was fitted to mapping_density density_calibration kosciessa, miscouridou, carpino (deprecated), wiesinger clinical CT, about 120 kVp (assumed; for kosciessa the anchors 1900/700/300 HU are assumed on this scale) any '' (k-Plan default) treeby low-dose CT, 80 kVp, BONEPLUS kernel (UCL) k-plan ucl_lowdose_80kvp custom with petra2density's line (−2080.02, 2133.23) the cph2025 phantom calibration k-plan cph2025 custom with your own line your CT (any scanner and kVp) k-plan path to that CT's phantom table 
pct:
  skull_mapping: 'treeby'
  mapping_density: 'k-plan'
  density_calibration: 'ucl_lowdose_80kvp'   # the 80 kVp CT treeby was fitted to
  mapping_soundspeed: 'k-plan'               # follows from density
  mapping_attenuation: 'k-plan'

pct.density_calibration values:

Value Table '' (default) k-Plan default (config/ct_calibration/kplan_default.csv) 'ucl_lowdose_80kvp' UCL low-dose CT (GE Revolution, 80 kVp, BONEPLUS; CIRS 062M phantom): the CT behind skull_mapping: treeby. Bone has about 1.35× the default's HU for the same density 'cph2025' petra2density's phantom calibration, the CT behind its line −2080.02·UTE + 2133.23 (use skull_mapping: custom). Bone has about 0.85× the default's HU a path any CSV with two columns, HU and density [kg/m³] (lines starting with # are comments), e.g. a phantom scan of your own scanner or a table that goes with a study-specific custom line

Tables are applied piecewise linearly and extrapolated linearly beyond their end points. For a line fitted at another kVp, scan a density phantom with the same protocol and pass its table; no HU conversion between kVp is needed. medium_setup prints the resolved table and records it in the medium statistics.

Only k-plan reads the calibration; with another density mapping it is ignored, with a warning. The other mappings assume a fixed, clinical HU scale. Use them with lines on the clinical scale only; otherwise use k-plan with the matching calibration. PRESTUS warns when skull_mapping: treeby is used without mapping_density: k-plan and density_calibration: ucl_lowdose_80kvp.

HU scale assumed by the other mappings
  • k-wave: Schneider et al.; marsac: 300–2000 HU; air-tissue (needed by pichardo and mcdannold): about −1000 to 1000 HU.
  • webb sound speed and attenuation: GE 120 kVp, B kernel by default; scanner-specific values via pct.webb_*.
  • aubry and mueller rescale by the skull's own minimum and maximum HU. They are insensitive to the HU scale but remove between-subject differences in density level.

items.title: Skull Property Mappings
items.text:
The pseudo-CT holds pseudo-Hounsfield units, while the simulation needs density, sound speed and attenuation in each skull voxel. Several published mappings make this conversion, and they assume different HU scales and give different skull properties. This page lists the mappings PRESTUS offers for each property, their equations and prerequisites, and how to check the resulting skull properties before simulating.

On this page:

  • From Pseudo-HU to Acoustic Properties: how the mappings are applied.
  • Mapping Skull Density: the pct.mapping_density options.
  • Mapping Skull Sound Speed: the pct.mapping_soundspeed options.
  • Mapping Skull Attenuation: the pct.mapping_attenuation options.
  • Predicting the Modelled Skull Properties: the skull property distributions a run will model, and the references.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you change pct.mapping_density, pct.mapping_soundspeed or pct.mapping_attenuation from the k-plan default, or want the equations behind a mapping.
  • Before you start: A pseudo-CT (Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run) and a density calibration that matches its UTE-to-HU mapping (Matching the CT Calibration).

items.title: From Pseudo-HU to Acoustic Properties
items.text: With pct.enabled: 1, choose a mapping for each of density, sound speed and attenuation. The pseudo-CT is read from the pseudo-CT folder (see Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run).
