This is a subtype of a layered medium. Mappings apply only within the uniform skull mask. A property set to "none", or with its field missing, keeps the uniform skull value. Defaults below are those in config_default.yaml.

items.title: Mapping Skull Density
items.text:
Set by pct.mapping_density.

Value Mapping k-plan (default) 4-part piecewise linear fit based on k-Plan defaults; pct.density_calibration replaces the table (see Matching the CT Calibration) k-wave 4-part piecewise linear fit based on Schneider et al. (1996) marsac linear between HU_min = 300 and HU_max = 2000, Marsac et al. (2017) aubry porosity-based mixture of bone and water, Aubry et al. (2003) air-tissue linear air-to-bone calibration (BabelBrain-compatible); use with pichardo or mcdannold sound speed or attenuation Density equations

Several mappings use the porosity of Aubry et al. (2003), with the max. skull HU denominator from Guo et al. (2019):

\[ \phi_\text{skull} = 1 - \frac{\text{HU}}{\text{HU}_\text{max}} \]

k-plan. Piece-wise linear mapping between HU and mass density in kg/m^3 (k-Plan documentation):

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \text{fit_pairwiselinear}(\text{HU}, \text{density}) \] 
HU = [-990, 60, 1000, 1950]
density = [1.2, 1060, 1530, 2150]

The minimum is regularised to the configured water density. Sound speed and attenuation of the k-plan pipeline follow from density. k-Plan's bone segmentation starts at density values of 1150 kg/m3, which internally regularizes data ranges; PRESTUS does not enforce this. Thermal simulations use a fixed bone density:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = 1850 \, \text{kg/m}^3 \]

k-wave. Pseudo-CT values are shifted by +1000 and thresholded at 300 to align with hounsfield2density:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \text{hounsfield2density}(\text{HU} + 1000) \]

Density is regularised at the minimum to the configured water density and at a max. skull density rho_bone = 2100 kg/m3.

marsac. Skull pHU are clipped to HU_min = 300 and HU_max = 2000. Unlike Marsac et al., 2017, PRESTUS clips pHU < HU_min instead of excluding them from the skull mask, which would create skull holes.

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \rho_\text{water} + (\rho_\text{bone} - \rho_\text{water}) \cdot \frac{\text{HU} - \text{HU}_\text{min}}{\text{HU}_\text{max} - \text{HU}_\text{min}} \]

with max. skull density rho_bone = 2100 kg/m3.

aubry. Mixture of bone and water density, both from the configuration:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \rho_\text{water} \cdot \phi_\text{skull} + \rho_\text{bone} \cdot (1 - \phi_\text{skull}) \]

air-tissue. Linear HU→density between air (HU ≈ −1000) and cortical bone (HU ≈ 1000), as HUtoDensityAirTissue in BabelBrain's Pichardo and McDannold workflows:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = 1.01237293 \cdot \text{HU} + 1013.67 \]

The minimum is regularised to water density. pichardo and mcdannold need density from this calibration.

items.title: Mapping Skull Sound Speed
items.text:
Set by pct.mapping_soundspeed.

Value Mapping k-plan (default) density-based, k-Plan marsac density-based, Marsac et al. (2017) aubry porosity-based, Aubry et al. (2003) webb linear in HU, Webb et al. (2018); scanner-specific slope and intercept via pct.webb_sos_slope and pct.webb_sos_intercept pichardo frequency-dependent ρ→c, Pichardo et al. 2D interpolation map; needs pct.mapping_density: air-tissue mcdannold polynomial ρ→c, McDannold et al.; needs density first (air-tissue or marsac)

For k-plan, webb, pichardo and mcdannold, the minimum sound speed is regularised to water sound speed.

Sound speed equations

k-plan.

\[ c_\text{skull} = 1.33 \cdot \rho_\text{skull} + 167 \]

marsac.

\[ c_\text{skull} = c_\text{water} + (c_\text{bone} - c_\text{water}) \cdot \frac{\rho_\text{skull} - \rho_\text{water}}{\rho_\text{bone} - \rho_\text{water}} \]

with max. speed of sound in skull c_skull = 3360 m/s and max. skull density rho_bone = 2100 kg/m3. Water properties come from the configuration.

aubry.

\[ c_\text{skull} = c_\text{water} \cdot \phi_\text{skull} + c_\text{bone} \cdot (1 - \phi_\text{skull}) \]

Tissue sound speeds come from the configuration.

webb.

\[ c_\text{skull} = \text{slope} \cdot \text{HU} + \text{intercept} \times 1000 \]

Defaults (GE 120 kVp, B kernel, 0.5 × 0.6 mm resolution): slope = 0.75, intercept = 1.32 (c = 0.75 · HU + 1320 m/s). Set scanner-specific values from Webb et al. Tables I and II with pct.webb_sos_slope and pct.webb_sos_intercept.

pichardo. Reads MapPichardo.h5 from the BabelBrain submodule: longitudinal speed of sound [m/s] as a function of density [kg/m³] and frequency [MHz]. Interpolation is bilinear with nearest-neighbour extrapolation. MATLAB cannot read the Blosc-compressed H5 without the filter plugin, so PRESTUS uses the same table in functions/medium/MapPichardo.mat. Requires pct.mapping_density: air-tissue (or another density algorithm run first), the BabelBrain submodule initialised at external/BabelBrain, and the simulation frequency in parameters.transducer(1).freq_hz.

mcdannold.

\[ c_\text{skull} = \frac{1}{p(\rho_\text{skull})} \]

where \(p(\rho) = -2.79 \times 10^{-18}\,\rho^4 + 5.31 \times 10^{-16}\,\rho^3 + 1.69 \times 10^{-10}\,\rho^2 - 7.63 \times 10^{-7}\,\rho + 1.24 \times 10^{-3}\). Requires density first (pct.mapping_density: air-tissue or marsac).

items.title: Mapping Skull Attenuation
items.text:
Set by pct.mapping_attenuation.

Value Mapping k-plan (default) uniform: the skull alpha_coeff and alpha_power of medium_properties; to replicate k-Plan set alpha_coeff = 13.3 and alpha_power = 1 mueller HU-based, Mueller et al. (2017), bounds from Yaakub et al. (2023) aubry porosity-based, Aubry et al. (2003) webb exponential HU-based model, Webb et al. (2021); scanner-specific values via pct.webb_att_alpha0, pct.webb_att_beta and pct.webb_att_c pichardo frequency-dependent ρ→Att from Pichardo et al. 2D interpolation map; prerequisites as for pichardo sound speed mcdannold polynomial ρ→Att from McDannold et al. with linear frequency scaling; needs density first Attenuation equations

k-plan.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull} = \alpha_\text{coeff} \]

Reads alpha_coeff and alpha_power of medium_properties.skull from the config, and warns when they differ from k-Plan's fixed 13.3 and 1.

mueller.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull} = \alpha_\text{min} + (\alpha_\text{max} - \alpha_\text{min}) \left(1 - \frac{\text{HU} - \text{HU}_\text{min}}{\text{HU}_\text{max} - \text{HU}_\text{min}}\right)^{0.5} \]

with α_min = 4 and α_max = 8.7 (see Yaakub et al., 2023). These are 𝛼(f) at 500 kHz (see Aubry, J.-F., 2022 for benchmark simulations). PRESTUS converts them to alpha_0 in 𝛼(f) = alpha_0 x f[MHz] ^ y as alpha_0 = 𝛼(f)/0.5^y, with y the skull alpha_power.

aubry.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull} = \alpha_\text{min} + (\alpha_\text{max} - \alpha_\text{min}) \cdot \phi_\text{skull}^{0.5} \]

with α_min = 0.2 and α_max = 8 (Aubry et al., 2003).

webb.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull}(f) = \alpha_0 \cdot \left(\frac{f}{1\,\text{MHz}}\right)^{\beta} \cdot \exp(c \cdot \text{HU}) \]

Output is k-Wave alpha_coeff [dB/cm/MHz\(^\beta\)] with alpha_power = β. Defaults (GE 120 kVp, B kernel, 0.5 × 0.6 mm): α₀ = 26, β = 1.3, c = −0.0016. Set scanner-specific values from Webb et al. Table IV with pct.webb_att_alpha0, pct.webb_att_beta and pct.webb_att_c.

pichardo. Reads longitudinal attenuation [Np/m] from MapPichardo.h5 as a function of density [kg/m³] and frequency [MHz]. The value at the simulation frequency is converted to k-Wave alpha_coeff [dB/cm/MHz] with alpha_power = 1 (linear frequency scaling assumed). Prerequisites as for pichardo sound speed; density must be filled first.

mcdannold.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull}(f) = p(\rho_\text{skull}) \cdot \frac{f}{660\,\text{kHz}} \]

where \(p(\rho) = 1.36 \times 10^{-10}\,\rho^4 - 1.41 \times 10^{-6}\,\rho^3 + 5.40 \times 10^{-3}\,\rho^2 - 9.02\,\rho + 5.71 \times 10^{3}\) [Np/m]. Converted to k-Wave alpha_coeff [dB/cm/MHz] with alpha_power = 1. Requires density first.

items.title: Predicting the Modelled Skull Properties
items.text:
To see the skull properties a run will model before simulating, call pct_predict_skull_properties(parameters) or use Predict skull properties on the Nexus Pseudo-CT sub-tab. It applies the configured mappings to the pseudo-CT skull voxels and writes their distributions to cache/sub-NNN_<medium>_pct_prediction<affix>.json, alongside the skull values of the uncertainty bound variants. See Pseudo-CT runs.

References
  • Aubry, J.-F., et al. Experimental demonstration of noninvasive transskull adaptive focusing based on prior computed tomography scans. J Acoust Soc Am 113, 84–93 (2003).
  • Aubry, J.-F. et al. Benchmark problems for transcranial ultrasound simulation: Intercomparison of compressional wave models. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 152, 1003–1019 (2022).
  • Carpino et al. (2024). Transcranial ultrasonic stimulation of the human amygdala to modulate threat learning. MSc thesis.
  • Guo, S., et al. Feasibility of ultrashort echo time images using full-wave acoustic and thermal modeling for transcranial MRI-guided focused ultrasound (tcMRgFUS) planning. Phys. Med. Biol. 64, 095008 (2019).
  • Lim Fat, D. et al. The Hounsfield value for cortical bone geometry in the proximal humerus: an in vitro study. Skelet. Radiol. 41, 557–568 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00256-011-1255-7
  • Marsac, L. et al. Ex Vivo Optimisation of a Heterogeneous Speed of Sound Model of the Human Skull for Non-Invasive Transcranial Focused Ultrasound at 1 MHz. International Journal of Hyperthermia. 33. 635–645 (2017).
  • McDannold, N., et al. Transcranial magnetic resonance imaging-guided focused ultrasound surgery of brain tumors: initial findings in 3 patients. Neurosurgery 66(2):323–332 (2010).
  • Miscouridou, M., Pineda-Pardo, J. A., Stagg, C. J., Treeby, B. E. & Stanziola, A. Classical and Learned MR to Pseudo-CT Mappings for Accurate Transcranial Ultrasound Simulation. IEEE Trans. Ultrason., Ferroelectr., Freq. Control 69, 2896–2905 (2022).
  • Mueller, J. K., Ai, L., Bansal, P. & Legon, W. Numerical Evaluation of the Skull for Human Neuromodulation with Transcranial Focused Ultrasound. Journal of Neural Engineering. 14. 066012 (2017).
  • Pichardo, S., et al. Multi-frequency characterization of the speed of sound and attenuation coefficient for longitudinal transmission of freshly excised human skulls. Phys. Med. Biol. 56(1):219–250 (2011). DOI: 10.1088/0031-9155/56/1/014
  • Schneider, U., Pedroni, E., and Lomax A., "The calibration of CT Hounsfield units for radiotherapy treatment planning," Phys. Med. Biol., 41, pp. 111-124 (1996).
  • Webb, T. D., et al. Measurements of the Relationship Between CT Hounsfield Units and Acoustic Velocity and How It Changes With Photon Energy and Reconstruction Method. IEEE Trans Ultrason Ferroelectr Freq Control 65(7):1111–1124 (2018). DOI: 10.1109/TUFFC.2018.2827899
  • Webb, T. D., et al. Acoustic Attenuation: Multifrequency Measurement and Relationship to CT and MR Imaging. IEEE Trans Ultrason Ferroelectr Freq Control 68(5):1532–1545 (2021). DOI: 10.1109/TUFFC.2020.3039743
  • Wiesinger, F. et al. Zero TE-based pseudo-CT image conversion in the head and its application in PET/MR attenuation correction and MR-guided radiation therapy planning. Magn. Reson. Med. 80, 1440–1451 (2018).
  • Yaakub, S. N. et al. Pseudo-CTs from T1-Weighted MRI for Planning of Low-Intensity Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: An Open-Source Tool. Brain Stimulation. 16. 75–78 (2023).

items.title: Reading Your Results
items.text:
A finished run leaves a folder of files. Before you use its numbers, check that the run simulated the placement and intensity you intended, and compare its exposure with the safety reference levels. This page lists the files to open first, the checks in order, and how to read the safety summary; every file and column is described in Outputs & Reports, and terms in the Glossary.

On this page:

  • Files to Open First: the report, placement report, metrics table and maps to open first.
  • Checks Before Using Results: placement, intensity, safety reference levels and unusual results.
  • Uncertainty of the Estimate: how to see how much results depend on tissue properties.
  • Methods Text: the methods paragraph the report writes for you.

items.title: Files to Open First
items.text:
Results are in <path.sim>/sub-XXX/. Open these first:

File What it is sub-XXX_<medium>_report<affix>.html The simulation report: safety summary, key numbers, figures and the run log. Start here. sub-XXX_placement_<mode><affix>.html The placement report: where the transducer and the target ended up, drawn on the T1 (head simulations). sub-XXX_<medium><affix>.csv All metrics in one table, for your own analysis. nii/ 3D maps (intensity, pressure, MI, temperature) in the participant's T1 space and in MNI space, to view in any NIfTI viewer.

<medium> is water or layered, and <affix> is your io.output_affix (empty by default).

items.title: 1. Placement and Focus
items.text:
Open the placement report and the report's figures:

  • The transducer sits on the scalp, not inside the head or far from it, and points at the target.
  • The focus lies at the target. The report's intensity overlay should show the hot spot in the target region. In the table, compare real_focal_distance_mm (where the peak actually is) with your focal depth setting, and Ipa_target (intensity at the target) with Isppa_brain (the peak in the brain). A peak far from the target means the placement or the focal depth setting needs a second look.
  • The configuration summary in the report lists the transducer, focal depth, target intensity and medium that were used. Check that they are the ones you intended.

For many runs, the targeting analysis (sub-XXX_<medium><affix>_targeting.csv) measures the distance between the simulated and the planned focus (Targeting accuracy).

items.title: 2. Intensity in the Brain
items.text:
• transducer.target_isppa_wcm2 is the free-water intensity (30 W/cm² by default). The intensity in the brain (Isppa_brain, Ipa_target) is lower, mostly because the skull reflects and absorbs ultrasound. How much lower depends on the person, the skull thickness and the angle of incidence.
  • If the run log shows prestus:isppa:largeScale, the field was scaled by more than 4× (or less than 0.25×) from the simulated drive. The result is then an extrapolation; check that it is still realistic for your device.

items.title: 3. Safety Reference Levels
items.text:
The top of the report shows a safety verdict and one card per metric. Each card is coloured by how close the value is to its ITRUSST non-significant-risk (NSR) reference level (Aubry et al., 2025):

Colour Meaning Green below 50 % of the reference level Amber 50–100 % of the reference level Red above the reference level Grey not computed for this run (e.g. no thermal simulation, or a metric that does not apply to this medium) Metric Reference level Mechanical index, transcranial (MI_tc) or in free water (MI) 1.9 Peak pressure (Psptp) 2 MPa Temperature rise (riseT_*) 2 °C Maximum temperature (maxT_*) 39 °C Thermal dose (CEM43_*) brain 2, skull 16, skin 21 min

A red card does not by itself mean the protocol is unsafe, and the verdict then says inspect rather than fail. The ITRUSST thermal criteria are alternatives: an exposure qualifies as non-significant risk through the temperature rise, the maximum temperature or the thermal dose. Check the flagged values against the criteria that apply to your protocol, and read the original consensus for details. PRESTUS reports the comparison; it makes no safety recommendation of its own.

Thermal metrics only appear when a thermal simulation ran (modules.run_heating_sims: 1, with a sonication protocol in timing.*). The report shows the CEM43 form selected by thermal.cem43_iso (Thermal).

items.title: 4. Unusual Results
items.text:
What you see What it may mean The highest intensity is in the skin or skull rather than the brain Expected to some degree near the transducer; a hot spot at the scalp can also mean poor contact or a transducer placed into the head. Check the placement report. The focus is much shallower or deeper than the setting Strong skull refraction, or a target depth outside the transducer's range (min_foc–max_foc of the device). Warnings about points per wavelength (PPW) in the log The grid is too coarse for the frequency; results near the focus may be inaccurate (Spatial and temporal sampling). load_transducer_from_library:uncalibratedAmplitude in the log The transducer's drive at this depth was not checked in k-Wave; absolute intensities carry that uncertainty (Free-water k-Wave drive calibration).

More known messages and their fixes are in Troubleshooting.

items.title: Uncertainty of the Estimate
items.text: Simulated intensities and temperatures depend on assumed tissue properties, which are uncertain, especially for the skull. To see how much your results could change, run the uncertainty mode (default tissue properties and the ITRUSST bounds that maximise and minimise heating and intensity), or use subject-specific skull properties from a pseudo-CT.

items.title: Methods Text
items.text: The report contains an automatically written methods paragraph (with references) describing the software, transducer, grid, tissue properties, protocol and resulting exposure. Copy it with Copy methods text, and check it against your study before using it in a manuscript.

items.title: Sequential Simulations
items.text:
A sonication that follows another can start in tissue that is still warm from the first and adds to the thermal dose already accumulated. Run independently, each simulation starts from the baseline temperature and zero CEM43, so this carryover is missing. Sequential mode chains the runs so that each heating simulation starts from the end-of-run temperature and CEM43 maps of the previous one.

On this page:

  • Basic usage: passing follow-up configs to the pipeline.
  • Cache reuse: which stages a follow-up run reuses and which it recomputes.
  • Sequential simulation parameters: the settings that carry the thermal state forward.
  • Combining with uncertainty mode: chaining each uncertainty variant.
  • Output affix handling: how files of each run and variant are named.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you stimulate from different coordinates in sequence and want the cumulative thermal state (for stimulation in parallel, see Multi-Transducer Modelling).
  • Before you start: One config per sonication, loaded as structs.

items.title: Basic Usage
items.text:
Each config is a struct. Given config_1, config_2, and config_3 to run in sequence:

Without heat carryover, run each independently:

prestus_pipeline_start(config_1)
prestus_pipeline_start(config_2)
prestus_pipeline_start(config_3)

With heat carryover, pass the follow-up configs via options. The thermal end state is handed over as T1w-space NIfTIs (*_heating_end, *_CEM43_end, *_CEM43_iso_end). Each follow-up resamples them into its own grid with its own transform, so the start state is correct for a follow-up with a different beam axis. The NIfTI stage is enabled for every run in a chain, and dispatch stops with sequential_pipeline:missingThermalEnd if a map is missing. It never starts from the water baseline silently.

sequential_configs.config_2 = config_2;
sequential_configs.config_3 = config_3;
options.sequential_configs = sequential_configs;
prestus_pipeline_start(config_1, options);

Field names in sequential_configs must follow the pattern config_<N> where <N> is a non-negative integer (e.g. config_2, config_3, config_11). The dispatcher picks the field with the lowest numeric value first; only relative order matters. Non-numeric suffixes (e.g. config_abc) are silently ignored.

In the Nexus, Results ▸ Follow-up… with Sequential creates a follow-up config and adds it to the chain under Run ▸ Where to run ▸ Pipeline options, which the run script passes as options.sequential_configs (Run tab).

items.title: Cache Reuse
items.text:
When a follow-up simulation is dispatched, PRESTUS decides which results are reused and which are recomputed:

Stage Default behaviour How to override Grid & medium setup Reused from base run Set io.preproc_affix in the sequential config Acoustic simulation Re-run with the follow-up config Set io.acoustic_cache_affix to an existing affix to reuse prior acoustics Thermal simulation Re-run (cache file gets a unique name automatically) Set io.thermal_cache_affix explicitly to control the cache filename

The head geometry does not change between sequential targets, so preproc can always be shared. Acoustics default to a fresh run because the follow-up may target a different location or use different transducer settings.

To reuse the base run's acoustic results in the follow-up (e.g. same target, different timing protocol):

options.sequential_configs.config_2.io.acoustic_cache_affix = config_1.io.output_affix;

items.title: Sequential Simulation Parameters
items.text: Parameter Description io.adopted_heatmap Path to a temperature heatmap NIfTI (heating_end.nii.gz) used as the thermal starting point. Set automatically from the previous run's output; override to supply a custom starting temperature. io.adopted_cem43 Path to a CEM43 NIfTI (CEM43_end.nii.gz) carried forward for cumulative thermal dose. Set automatically; can be overridden. io.adopted_cem43_iso Path to the ISO-variant CEM43 NIfTI (CEM43_iso_end.nii.gz). Set automatically alongside adopted_cem43. io.preproc_affix Affix for grid/medium cache lookup (defaults to the base run's output_affix). io.acoustic_cache_affix Affix for acoustic cache lookup. Not set by default; acoustics are re-run unless you set this explicitly. io.thermal_cache_affix Affix for the thermal cache file (defaults to the run's own io.output_affix). options.sequential_configs Struct of follow-up configs to dispatch in order (see example above). options.sequential_cleanup_intermediate If true, per-run NIfTI and image files are deleted after the final summary report is successfully generated. Default: false.

items.title: Combining with Uncertainty Mode
items.text:
options.sequential_configs can be combined with parameters.simulation.uncertainty = true. Each follow-up run is executed once per uncertainty variant (default, Temp-H, Temp-L, Trans-H, Trans-L). The default and Temp variants inherit the thermal end-state from the matched variant of the prior run; the Trans variants re-run the acoustic simulation only:

parameters.simulation.uncertainty = true;

options.sequential_configs.config_2 = config_2;
options.sequential_configs.config_3 = config_3;

prestus_pipeline(parameters, options);

After all sequential runs complete, a sequential report is written for all variants. The base run appears as run 1; each follow-up adds a further run entry. The report shows temperature and CEM43 timeseries with the Temp-L to Temp-H band shaded around the default trajectory.

On HPC, job names are prefixed with r1- when sequential configs are present (e.g. PRESTUS-r1-u2-sim-default_sub-001) to keep scheduler job names unambiguous across chained submissions. See doc_uncertainty.md for the uncertainty pipeline.

items.title: Output Affix Handling
items.text:
Every PRESTUS output file embeds an affix, a short string appended to the subject/medium prefix, that distinguishes files produced by different simulation variants or pipeline modes. PRESTUS assigns affixes from the active modes; you rarely set one yourself.

  • A plain sequential run gets _seq<N> (e.g. _seq2 for the second run).
  • An uncertainty variant gets _desc-temphigh, _desc-templow, _desc-transhigh or _desc-translow.
  • Both combined: _desc-temphigh_seq2.
  • A custom io.output_affix on any sequential config is used as-is; no _seq<N> suffix is added.

Example filenames for subject 1, layered medium, two sequential runs with uncertainty:

sub-001_layered.csv                              ← base run, default
sub-001_layered_desc-temphigh.csv                ← base run, Temp-H
sub-001_layered_desc-templow.csv                 ← base run, Temp-L
sub-001_layered_desc-transhigh.csv               ← base run, Trans-H
sub-001_layered_desc-translow.csv                ← base run, Trans-L
sub-001_layered_seq2.csv                         ← sequential run 2, default
sub-001_layered_desc-temphigh_seq2.csv           ← sequential run 2, Temp-H
…                                                ← and so on for the other variants

If you see a warning that a variant output was not found but the file exists on disk, confirm that io.dir_output was set before calling the pipeline (i.e. path_log_setup has run), and that no custom options.affixes struct was passed with different values than those used during simulation.

Affix construction and report file lookup

Affix sanitisation. load_parameters sanitises the raw affix string before use: characters that are not alphanumeric, hyphens, underscores, or slashes are replaced with underscores, and the prefix _desc- is prepended if not already present. So "pilot" becomes "_desc-pilot".

Full affix table.

Pipeline mode io.output_affix value Single run, no user affix '' (empty) Single run, user sets io.output_affix = 'myreg' '_desc-myreg' Uncertainty, default variant base_affix Uncertainty, Temp-H / Temp-L variant base_affix + '_desc-temphigh' / '_desc-templow' Uncertainty, Trans-H / Trans-L variant base_affix + '_desc-transhigh' / '_desc-translow' Sequential run N, no uncertainty base_affix + '_seq<N>' Sequential run N, default variant base_affix + '_seq<N>' Sequential run N, other variants base_affix + '_desc-<variant>_seq<N>' (e.g. '_desc-temphigh_seq<N>') Sequential run N, custom affix supplied the supplied affix, unchanged

base_affix is whatever io.output_affix was on the parameters struct passed to uncertainty_pipeline or prestus_pipeline_start. For most studies it is empty.

How report functions locate files. generate_uncertainty_report reconstructs CSV paths as <io.dir_output>/sub-NNN_<medium><variant_affix>.csv rather than trusting io.filename_table, which may carry a stale value from an earlier pipeline stage. generate_sequential_report uses the explicit affix registry built by sequential_pipeline (one struct per run with output_affix and thermal_cache_affix) for all lookups; io.filename_table is a fallback only.

Thermal cache affix. io.thermal_cache_affix controls the filename of the heating .mat cache (sub-NNN_<medium>_heating_res<affix>.mat). It defaults to the run's own output_affix. Set it explicitly only if you need to point a follow-up run at a specific pre-existing cache file.

See also: doc_uncertainty.md, doc_multitransducer.md, doc_hpc.md

items.title: Acoustic Simulations
items.text:
The acoustic simulation computes the pressure field the transducer produces in the head. Every reported intensity, focus position and mechanical index comes from this field, so its settings decide how far the results can be trusted: how finely the grid samples the wave, how long the simulation runs, and which intensity the field is scaled to.

On this page:

  • Main Settings: the few settings most studies change.
  • Spatial and Temporal Sampling: grid resolution, time step and simulation duration.
  • Amplitude Ramping: how the source is switched on.
  • ISPPA Targeting: scaling the field to a free-water intensity.
  • Memory Use: fitting large runs into memory.
  • Axisymmetric Simulations: fast 2D runs for symmetric setups.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Read ISPPA targeting for every study. The rest matters when you change grid settings or run out of memory.
  • Before you start: Nothing; the defaults are a sound starting point.

items.title: Main Settings
items.text:
The defaults run a 3D simulation with k-Wave's kspaceFirstOrder3D (see the available simulation backends). The settings most studies touch:

grid:
  resolution_mm: 0.5        # spatial step; keep PPW >= 6 in the slowest medium
  source_cfl: 0.15          # time step relative to the stability limit
transducer:
  target_isppa_wcm2: 30     # free-water ISPPA the results are reported at
modules:
  run_water_baseline: auto  # free-water baseline for the ISPPA scaling

The simulation models compressional waves (P-waves) in isotropic media and computes pressure and velocity fields. Shear waves are not modelled explicitly; their scattering contributes to the bulk attenuation coefficient. This makes the run faster and less memory-intensive than an elastic simulation. An elastic skull model is available as a separate backend (kwave_elastic, draft).

Turning off acoustic simulations

With modules.run_acoustic_sims: 0, PRESTUS loads the existing acoustic results from the cache (subject to io.overwrite_files; see Overwrite behaviour). This lets a follow-up thermal simulation reuse an earlier acoustic run. Other modules behave differently: turning them off may skip the step without loading existing data.

items.title: Spatial and Temporal Sampling
items.text:
Accuracy depends on resolving the shortest wavelength in the domain. Two parameters govern this.

Grid resolution (grid.resolution_mm) sets the spatial step dx. With the medium sound speed c and the fundamental frequency f, the number of spatial samples per wavelength is

PPW = c / (f × dx)

The worst case is the slowest medium (water or brain, ~1500 m/s). Keep PPW ≥ 6; PRESTUS warns below grid.min_ppw (jwave stops), and the Nexus flags it before a run.

For head (layered) and phantom media, a grid coarser than 0.75 mm staircases the tissue transitions (skull, scalp), which may affect the results; PRESTUS and the Nexus warn above it.

CFL number (grid.source_cfl) sets the time step dt relative to dx and the fastest medium (skull, ~2800 m/s), which sets the stability limit:

dt  = CFL × dx / c_max
PPP = PPW / CFL

PPP is the number of time steps per wave period. resolution_mm and source_cfl are independent, so you can refine or coarsen the time step without changing the grid. Both must stay within the stability limit.

Rule of thumb: the coarsest grid that satisfies a minimum PPW at frequency f in the slowest medium is dx_max = c_min / (f × PPW_min). At 500 kHz in water (1500 m/s) with PPW = 6: resolution_mm = 0.50 mm.

PPW across tissues, the stability recheck and the CFL default

PPW varies across tissues. The check against grid.min_ppw uses the slowest medium. At 500 kHz with 0.5 mm resolution, water/brain (1500 m/s) gives PPW = 6 and skull (2800 m/s) PPW ≈ 11. The binding spatial constraint is always in the slow tissues.

The stability recheck can reduce dt below the CFL target. After source setup, prestus_pipeline calls checkStability. If the CFL-derived dt exceeds the estimated stability limit for the heterogeneous medium, source setup is rerun with a smaller time step scaled by grid.source_limit_fraction (default 0.9). The final dt can therefore be smaller than CFL × dx / c_max. The PPW check runs only on the first source setup call; the adjusted call receives dt explicitly and bypasses it.

Overriding source_ppw decouples temporal from spatial resolution. A manual grid.source_ppw only affects the time step (PPP = source_ppw / CFL). The spatial check against grid.min_ppw still uses the actual PPW from c_min / (f × dx). A coarser source_ppw increases dt and reduces runtime without suppressing the spatial warning.

The default CFL of 0.15 is conservative. k-Wave's own default is 0.3. PRESTUS uses 0.15 for extra stability margin in heterogeneous skull simulations, where the theoretical stability limit is an approximation (checkStability). This roughly doubles the number of time steps and the acoustic runtime. If simulations are stable, source_cfl can be raised towards 0.3; validate this against the checkStability output for your medium.

items.title: Simulation Duration
items.text:
With the default grid.steady_state_transits: 1, the simulation lasts long enough for the wave to cross the domain diagonal once, so the steady-state field is established everywhere:

t_end   = steady_state_transits × grid_diagonal / c_min
N_steps = round(t_end / dt)

where grid_diagonal = sqrt(x_size² + y_size² + z_size²) and c_min is the minimum sound speed across all media (water or brain, ~1500 m/s). Request more transits for compact, reflective domains, or set a fixed duration with grid.sim_time_us. The sensor records p_max_all and p_final over the last grid.steady_state_num_periods (default 3) wave periods.

items.title: Amplitude Ramping
items.text:
A ramped pulse delivers less pulse-average intensity (ISPPA) than the temporal-peak intensity (ISPTP), because intensity scales with amplitude². When timing.pulse_ramp_dur > 0, acoustic_analysis scales the acoustic_Ipa map and every derived ISPPA value (per tissue, at target) by

f = ISPPA / ISPTP

before further analysis. With pulse_ramp_dur absent or zero, f = 1. The factor can also be computed directly with compute_ramp_factor(pd, ramp_dur, shape):

Parameter Description pd Pulse duration [s] ramp_dur Ramp duration per edge [s]; applied at onset and offset, so the ramped interval per pulse is 2 × ramp_dur shape 'linear': linear amplitude taper (intensity integral factor k = 1/3); 'tukey': raised-cosine taper (k = 3/8)

Example: 20 ms pulse, 2 ms ramp per edge (10 % of pd per edge, 20 % total):

Shape k f (ISPPA/ISPTP) linear 1/3 ≈ 0.867 tukey 3/8 ≈ 0.875 Ramp factor formula 
t_flat = pd - 2 × ramp_dur
f      = (k × ramp_dur + t_flat + k × ramp_dur) / pd

Ramping reduces spectral splatter by smoothing the transducer drive at pulse onset and offset instead of switching abruptly.

items.title: ISPPA Targeting
items.text:
The acoustic simulation runs at the drive elem_p_amp (from the study config or the transducer library). transducer.target_isppa_wcm2 (default 30 W/cm²) sets the free-water ISPPA the results are reported at. Pressure is linear in drive, so PRESTUS scales the simulated field by

scale_p = sqrt(target_isppa / baseline_isppa)

where baseline_isppa is the free-water peak ISPPA of the same drive. All pressure fields used downstream (p_max_all, p_min_all, p_final) are scaled, so intensities, MI and heating are consistent. A scalar target scales one run; a vector runs one thermal job per value; an empty target ([]) reports the field at an inline elem_p_amp. A transducer resolved from the library (transducer.serial) needs a target, because its drive is resolved at that ISPPA.

The baseline comes from one of two sources (isppa_baseline):

  1. a free-water simulation with the same grid, source and backend (acoustic_water_baseline; BabelBrain runs its own), recorded as acoustic_provenance.freefield_isppa_wcm2 with its origin in freefield_source; or
  2. the transducer's calibration ISPPA (tx_calibration.isppa_wcm2, from the library or a calibration file), used only when it matches the target to within 1 %. No scaling is then needed.

modules.run_water_baseline decides when the free-water simulation runs (needs_water_baseline):

Value Runs the baseline when auto (default) a target is set and the transducer has no calibration ISPPA, or the target differs from it by more than 1 % 1 always 0 only when the target differs from a calibration ISPPA

A target is never reported unscaled. When a rescale is needed but no simulated baseline exists (for example run_water_baseline: 0 with an uncalibrated transducer, or a cached result from a run without baseline and run_source_setup: 0), the run stops with prestus:isppa:noBaseline or prestus:isppa:unsimulatedBaseline (isppa_scale_factor). Scale factors above 4 or below 0.25 warn (prestus:isppa:largeScale): check that the target is in the linear regime of the simulated drive.

Check what a run models. The parameter summary at the start of the log and the HTML report (row Modelled intensity) state the free-water ISPPA the results report and how it relates to the calibration ISPPA of the drive. A target that differs from the calibration ISPPA, or the default target on a drive without calibration ISPPA, is marked ⚠️ and warns prestus:isppa:targetVsCalibration. A calibration file (<equipment>-F<focus>mm-I<isppa>wpercm2.yaml, calibration) sets both target_isppa_wcm2 and tx_calibration.isppa_wcm2 to its calibrated intensity. If you copy only its annular drive into a config, also set target_isppa_wcm2 to that intensity; otherwise the results are rescaled to the default 30 W/cm².

Several transducers. target_isppa_wcm2 is set per transducer and refers to that transducer alone. Coherent runs set each transducer's drive to its own target before the simulation; async runs scale each field before combining (Multi-transducer: ISPPA targets). The older calibration.target_isppa_wcm2 is read and moved to transducer(1).target_isppa_wcm2 with a deprecation warning.

Axial profile plot

The baseline run also stores the free-water intensity along each transducer's beam axis (bowl apex to grid edge) as acoustic_provenance.freefield_axial. The axial profile plot (sub-XXX_<medium>_axial_profile<affix>.png / .csv, 3D grids) compares the simulated intensity with the free-water intensity of the simulated transducer settings: the k-Wave baseline profile when the baseline ran, and the analytical O'Neil profile for a single annular transducer (always), both at the drive level of the plotted field after scaling. The plot is omitted for combined async / FOV fields (scaled per source) and for the BabelBrain backend.

items.title: Memory Use
items.text:
Two components dominate acoustic memory:

  • Grid fields: pressure, velocity and medium maps, proportional to the number of voxels. A 0.5 mm head grid takes roughly 7–8 GB; this scales with resolution, not transducer size.
  • Source signal matrix: one waveform per active source voxel over all time steps. Negligible for a focused single-element transducer; for a large multi-element phased array it can exceed the grid fields.

PRESTUS compresses the source matrix automatically per backend (details below). A coarser grid or a limited acoustic FOV reduces the grid fields; the cpp_* backends stream the source matrix from disk.

How PRESTUS reduces source memory by backend

The source signal matrix has size num_source_voxels × Nt. For a kHz-range aperture at 0.5 mm resolution with the standard CFL of 0.15, Nt is on the order of several thousand, so the dense matrix reaches several gigabytes for large transducers.

matlab_cpu / matlab_gpu: lazy rank-2 factorisation for CW sources. For continuous-wave (CW) stimulation every source voxel's time signal has the form

p(voxel, t) = A_voxel · cos(ω t + φ_voxel)

which two real numbers per voxel describe (amplitude and phase, or the real and imaginary part of a complex amplitude). PRESTUS stores only those two numbers per voxel (CWSourceMatrix.m) and evaluates each time column on demand during the simulation. Memory scales with num_source_voxels only, a reduction by a factor of ~2 000–5 000 for typical parameters. This path is used when code_type is matlab_cpu or matlab_gpu and all transducer elements share a single frequency; otherwise the dense matrix is used. k-Wave's own source scaling (kspaceFirstOrder_scaleSourceTerms), including the per-voxel loop for heterogeneous media, is applied to the stored amplitudes, so no dense matrix is built at any point.

cpp_cpu / cpp_gpu: HDF5 streaming from disk. The source matrix is written to an HDF5 file before the simulation and the C++ binary reads it in blocks during execution. Peak memory is bounded by the block size rather than the full matrix, at the cost of I/O throughput.

Backend Simulation device Source signal representation Peak additional RAM / VRAM matlab_gpu GPU Lazy rank-2 (CW) or dense single 2 × (num_src + Nt) × 4 B (CW) matlab_cpu CPU Lazy rank-2 (CW) or dense single 2 × (num_src + Nt) × 4 B (CW) cpp_cpu / cpp_gpu CPU / GPU HDF5 file, streamed Bounded by I/O block size

For a 10 000-voxel source at Nt = 9 000 time steps: dense = 360 MB; CW lazy = 0.08 MB.

items.title: Axisymmetric Simulations
items.text:
For symmetric media (a 2D phantom or water medium), a 3D axisymmetric problem can be modelled on a 2D grid with kspaceFirstOrderAS (grid.axisymmetric: 1; see k-Wave's focused bowl example). This reduces the computational cost markedly compared with a full 3D simulation. kspaceFirstOrder2D is not a substitute: it models an infinite cylinder, not a focusing shell.

What applies in axisymmetric mode:

  • Specify the grid as [radial x 2, axial]. The (2x) radial axis is assumed to be shorter than the axial axis.
  • Only a single transducer is supported; several transducers with axisymmetric == 1 raise an error.
  • Only annular transducers explicitly support axisymmetric kWaveArray mode. Other transducer types are untested in this configuration.
  • A 3D phantom is cut along its second dimension at the transducer's trans_pos when that is given in 3D, else at the centre slice. Output NIfTIs of phantom runs are written in the phantom file's voxel order and world space.
  • The source keeps every grid point with a non-zero band-limited-interpolation weight, as the 3D path and k-Wave do.

Axisymmetric 2D vs. 3D output

Axisymmetric simulations are 3D simulations performed on 2D input grids. grid.axisymmetric_output sets the form of the results: 'auto' (default) expands them to 3D for phantom media and when heating follows, and keeps the 2D plane otherwise; '2d' keeps the mirrored plane (no heating); '3d' always expands.

items.title: Backend Compatibility
items.text:
Backend (simulation.code_type) Axisymmetry support Notes matlab_cpu ✓ Uses kspaceFirstOrderAS matlab_gpu ✓ Uses kspaceFirstOrderAS with RadialSymmetry option cpp_cpu ✓ Uses the C++ OMP binary kspaceFirstOrderASC cpp_gpu (CUDA) ✗ No CUDA binary supports axisymmetric geometry. PRESTUS falls back to the matlab_gpu path (kspaceFirstOrderAS with gpuArray data cast) with a warning. GPU acceleration is preserved; only the CUDA binary is bypassed. Axis mapping and PML in axisymmetric mode

kspaceFirstOrder2D uses a 2D Cartesian grid with X and Y axes, mapped onto the second and first dimensions of input matrices and coordinates ([y, x]). This mirrors 3D image voxel coordinates [i, j, k], which map onto [Y, X, Z]. kspaceFirstOrderAS uses axial and radial axes, mapped onto the first and second dimensions. Internally, [radial x 2, axial] is remapped onto [axial, radial] and only the columns from the beam axis (the transducer's lateral position) onward are retained. With the axis off centre, the expanded output repeats the outermost simulated value beyond the simulated radius. Medium, source and sensor are set up in [axial, radial] dimensions. After the simulation, values are either mirrored into a Cartesian 2D grid ([radial x 2, axial] again, as for kspaceFirstOrder2D) or radially expanded into a Cartesian 3D grid.

PML. With PMLInside=false (the PRESTUS default) the PML is applied asymmetrically: the axial dimension receives pml_size voxels on both sides, the radial outer edge pml_size voxels on one side only. The inner radial boundary at r = 0 is a symmetry axis and needs no PML. k-Wave handles this; no configuration change is needed.

items.title: Thermal Simulations
items.text:
Tissue absorbs part of the ultrasound and heats up, and temperature rise and thermal dose (CEM43) are the measures safety guidelines use for this effect. PRESTUS computes both from the acoustic field and the sonication protocol, so the predicted heating depends on the timing, step sizes and absorption settings described here. The report compares the results with published reference levels; PRESTUS does not make an independent safety recommendation.

On this page:

  • Protocol Timing: describing pulses, pulse trains, repetitions and the post-stimulation period.
  • Step, Temperature and Sensor Settings: step sizes and starting temperature.
  • Heat Deposition: how tissue absorption turns the acoustic field into heat.
  • Thermal Dose (CEM43) Calculation: the two CEM43 formulations and their outputs.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Whenever you simulate heating (modules.run_heating_sims: 1).
  • Before you start: A working acoustic simulation, and the timing of your protocol.

Thermal simulations use the output of the acoustic simulation; they cannot run without one. They run in k-Wave by default. With acoustic_backend: babelbrain, BabelBrain's own Pennes solver can be used instead (thermal_backend: babelbrain). See Simulation backends for valid combinations and how the results compare, and BabelBrain thermal for the timing mapping and tissue-property differences. Known limitation: BabelBrain thermal uses its own built-in tissue thermal properties, so the thermal fields in medium_properties apply only to the k-Wave thermal backend.

items.title: Protocol Timing
items.text:
Protocol timing follows the nomenclature of the TUS Calculator, which you can use to specify the protocol. All three levels of nesting (pulse, pulse train, pulse train repetition) must be set. For a single pulse train without repetitions, set ptri and ptrd equal to ptd.

Example: a 20 s, 5 Hz, 10 % duty-cycle protocol as a single pulse train repetition:

timing:
  pd: 0.02               # pulse duration (PD) [s]
  pri: 0.2               # pulse repetition interval (PRI) [s]
  ptd: 20                # pulse train duration (PTD) [s]
  pt_timestep: 0.02      # modelling time step inside a PT, with equal_step_duration: 1 [s]
  ptri: 20               # pulse train repetition interval (PTRI) [s]
  ptrd: 20               # pulse train repetition duration (PTRD) [s]
  post_ptri_dur: 20      # steady-state duration following the PTRD [s]
  post_pt_timestep: 1    # modelling time step between PTs and after the PTRD [s]
  equal_step_duration: 0 # 0: one step per on and off period; 1: fixed step duration pt_timestep

Continuous pulse train protocols can be modelled either as a single pulse train repetition with multiple pulse trains (as above) or as multiple pulse train repetitions of a single pulse train.

A coarser protocol neglects the heating dynamics between pulses and models one longer pulse per train. Collapsing the off period lets the simulation use a coarser step size there:

timing:
  pd: 2
  pri: 2
  ptd: 2
  pt_timestep: 0.02
  ptri: 20
  ptrd: 20
  post_ptri_dur: 0
  post_pt_timestep: 1

Post-stimulation period. Heat dissipation continues after the final pulse. Run the simulation until a steady state is reached by setting timing.post_ptri_dur; its time step is timing.post_pt_timestep, separate from pt_timestep. For a continuous pulse train, a steady-state phase can also be part of an extended PTR interval; post_ptri_dur also gives protocols with repetitions a steady-state phase. For long intervals between pulse trains, a coarser post_pt_timestep may be sufficient.

items.title: Step, Temperature and Sensor Settings
items.text: Parameter Role timing.pt_timestep Step size for the on and off periods of each pulse within a pulse train. Used only with equal_step_duration: 1; PD and PRI − PD must be integer multiples of it. timing.equal_step_duration 1: every on and off period is split into steps of pt_timestep. In the first example above (PD 20 ms, PRI 200 ms, PTD 20 s, pt_timestep 20 ms), each of the 100 pulses takes 1 step with stimulation and 9 without (10 × 100 = 1,000 steps). 0 (default): every on and off period is one simulation step (2 × 100 = 200 steps), which reduces the computational load. timing.post_ptri_dur Duration of the post-stimulation period after the PTRD. thermal.temp_0 Starting temperature in degrees, per tissue.

items.title: Heat Deposition
items.text:
The acoustic field deposits heat at the rate Q = 2·α_abs·I = α_abs·p²/(ρc), with the absorption coefficient α_abs [Np/m] at the source frequency. Each tissue in medium_properties specifies α_abs in one of two ways (see Medium properties):

  • absorption_fraction: a fraction of the attenuation coefficient. The defaults use this for every tissue, so a change of alpha_coeff also changes absorption.
  • absorption_coeff [dB/(cm·MHz^y)]: a fixed coefficient, with the tissue's attenuation power law y (alpha_power). It does not follow changes of alpha_coeff.

A tissue sets one of the two; the other stays empty. When a config layer (a study YAML file, a struct passed to load_parameters, or an override) sets one of them for a tissue, load_parameters empties the other one inherited from earlier layers, such as the default absorption_fraction. One run can combine both. For example, brain absorption as a fraction and skull absorption as a coefficient:

medium_properties:
  brain:
    absorption_fraction: 0.77
  skull:
    absorption_coeff: 3.78   # clears the default skull absorption_fraction

A layer that sets both for one tissue stops with the error medium_absorption_layer:bothSet. If you change the struct in MATLAB after loading, empty the other field yourself (parameters.medium_properties.skull.absorption_fraction = [];); otherwise the medium setup stops with thermal_absorption_model:bothSet. Empty and NaN values count as not set; a tissue with neither uses a fraction of 1.

A pseudo-CT skull with mapped attenuation has no matching absorption map. A skull absorption_coeff is then applied as the fraction absorption_coeff / alpha_coeff of the mapped attenuation, with a warning (medium_setup:absorptionModelForced).

The log, the run summary and the HTML methods text give each tissue's model with its effective coefficient and fraction (α_abs/α) at the configured attenuation. The medium log gives the mapped range for a pseudo-CT skull. With io.save_property_maps, both are written as absorption_np [Np/m at the source frequency] and absorption_fraction maps.

items.title: Thermal Dose (CEM43) Calculation
items.text:
PRESTUS computes both CEM43 formulations in every k-Wave thermal simulation. Both are written to the CSV output, exported as NIfTI volumes and shown as separate figures. The HTML report (dashboard, safety verdict, methods text) uses the formulation selected by thermal.cem43_iso. With the BabelBrain thermal backend only BabelBrain's own dose is available (R = 0.25 below 43 °C, 0.5 at or above 43 °C): the ISO maps are NaN, and load_parameters sets cem43_iso to 0 with a warning, so the report uses BabelBrain's dose.

Both forms are based on the thermal isoeffective dose of Sapareto & Dewey (1984), CEM43 = Σ Δt · R^(43 − T).

items.title: k-Wave Form (Default)
items.text:
CEM43 as implemented in k-Wave's kWaveDiffusion: R = 0.25 for 37 ≤ T < 43 °C, R = 0.5 for T ≥ 43 °C, and no dose below 37 °C.

cem43 = cem43 + ...
        dt ./ 60 .* ...
        (0.25 .* (T >= 37 & T < 43) + ...
         0.5  .* (T >= 43)).^(43 - T);

items.title: ISO Form
items.text:
Set thermal.cem43_iso: 1 to use this form in the HTML report. It is computed by cem43_iso_increment and combines:

  • ISO 14708-3:2017, Clause 17.1, Formula (1): R = 0.25 for T < 43 °C and R = 0.5 for T ≥ 43 °C, "valid for temperatures between 39 °C and 57 °C". Table 101 gives the tissue thresholds brain 2, bone 16 and skin 21 CEM43, which ITRUSST adopts (Aubry et al., 2025) and PRESTUS uses as reference levels (get_risk_limits).
  • ITRUSST biophysical safety consensus (Aubry et al., 2025): dose is accumulated over the whole time the tissue is above 39 °C, including cooling; and because thermotolerance "is not maintained beyond 43 °C, nor does it return upon cooling", R = 0.5 is used for all time steps after 43 °C has been reached (citing Sapareto & Dewey, 1984). PRESTUS tracks this with T_max.
  • PRESTUS choice: voxels that reach 57 °C (current T or T_max) are set to CEM43 = ∞. ISO 14708-3 only states that the formula is not valid above 57 °C; ∞ is a conservative flag for that range, not taken from either source.
cem43_iso = cem43_iso + ...
        dt ./ 60 .* ...
        (0    .* (T < 39  & T_max < 43) + ...
         0.25 .* (T >= 39 & T < 43 & T_max < 43) + ...
         0.5  .* (T >= 43 | T_max >= 43)).^(43 - T);
cem43_iso(T >= 57 | T_max >= 57) = Inf;

items.title: Output Naming
items.text:
Suffix Description CEM43 / CEM43_end kWave form (max over protocol / at end of last pulse) CEM43_iso / CEM43_iso_end ISO form (max over protocol / at end of last pulse)

Both suffixes apply to NIfTI filenames (sub-XXX_<medium>_T1w<affix>_CEM43_iso.nii.gz, etc.) and to CSV columns (CEM43_brain, CEM43iso_brain, etc.).

References
  • Sapareto SA, Dewey WC (1984). Thermal dose determination in cancer therapy. Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 10:787–800. https://doi.org/10.1016/0360-3016(84)90379-1
  • ISO 14708-3:2017. Implants for surgery. Active implantable medical devices. Part 3: Implantable neurostimulators. Clause 17.1, Formula (1), Table 101. https://www.iso.org/standard/60539.html
  • Aubry J-F, Attali D, et al. (2025). ITRUSST consensus on biophysical safety for transcranial ultrasound stimulation. Brain Stimul 18:1896–1905. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brs.2025.10.007
  • Martin E, et al. (2024). ITRUSST consensus on standardised reporting for transcranial ultrasound stimulation. Brain Stimul 17:607–615 (Eq. 5: Sapareto & Dewey form only). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brs.2024.04.013

items.title: PRESTUS Telemetry
items.text:
PRESTUS can send anonymous usage statistics, one event per pipeline run, so the developers can see which features and platforms are in use. Participation is voluntary, and no data is sent without an explicit opt-in. This page shows how to give or change your decision, how batch and cluster runs handle it, and every field an event may contain.

On this page:

  • Opt-In and Opt-Out: the prompt, how to record or change your decision, the PRESTUS_TELEMETRY override and batch or cluster runs.
  • Collected Data: every field of an event, grouped by topic.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To decide whether to opt in, to change your decision, or to silence the prompt on a cluster.
  • Before you start: Nothing; your decision lives in ~/.prestus/telemetry.json.

items.title: Opt-In and Opt-Out
items.text:
On each pipeline run PRESTUS prints a short notice and asks whether to enable telemetry. How the prompt appears depends on the session:

  • Interactive console session: a y/n prompt that blocks until you answer.
  • GUI session (prestus_gui, deprecated): a modal Allow / Decline / Ask me later dialog shown once at startup, before the "Run Simulation" button can be pressed.
  • Non-interactive session (matlab -batch, deployed app, SLURM/PBS job, or a session with neither desktop nor display; see below): no prompt is shown and the run never waits for an answer.

The prompt repeats every run until you give an explicit answer. Your decision is stored in ~/.prestus/telemetry.json. To change it:

  • Opt out: run telemetry_set_consent(false) in MATLAB, or set "opt_in": false in that file.
  • Opt in: run telemetry_set_consent(true), or set "opt_in": true in the same file.
  • Undecided again: telemetry_setup_reset() deletes the file, so the next run asks again.

items.title: Per-Process Override (PRESTUS_TELEMETRY)
items.text:
The PRESTUS_TELEMETRY environment variable sets the decision for one MATLAB process, without a prompt and without writing ~/.prestus/telemetry.json:

Values and precedence Value (case-insensitive) Effect for this process off, 0, false Opted out: no prompt, nothing sent. on, 1, true Opted in if no decision is recorded: no prompt, run_end/run_error events are sent. A recorded opt-out still applies. The random ID in ~/.prestus/uuid.txt is created on the first send, as for a recorded opt-in. unset or empty No override: the recorded decision applies, or the prompt/notice described above. anything else Warning prestus:telemetry:invalidEnv (once per value per MATLAB session), then treated as unset.

PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=off takes precedence over a recorded decision: it sends nothing even after an opt-in. PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=on never overrides a recorded opt-out; it only applies when no decision is recorded. The variable never changes the recorded decision; use telemetry_set_consent for a lasting choice. Set the variable before MATLAB starts (PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=off matlab -batch "...", or export PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=off in a job script) or with setenv('PRESTUS_TELEMETRY', 'off') in the session.

items.title: Batch and Cluster Runs
items.text:
PRESTUS never prompts, and never waits for an answer, in these sessions:

How these sessions are detected
  • matlab -batch runs (detected with batchStartupOptionUsed, R2019a and later), whether or not a display is attached: cron jobs, CI runners and scripts started from a terminal;
  • deployed applications and jobs under SLURM (SLURM_JOB_ID) or PBS/Torque (PBS_JOBID);
  • sessions with neither the MATLAB desktop nor a display (e.g. matlab -nodisplay -r ... from cron). An interactive matlab -nodisplay terminal session is also treated this way; record a decision there with telemetry_set_consent.

The full notice is printed to stdout (visible in job logs) on every run, but no decision is recorded and no data is sent unless consent was already recorded or PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=on is set. The notice reappears on every run until you record a decision or set PRESTUS_TELEMETRY.

To opt in from an HPC environment, either:

  1. Run PRESTUS once interactively (e.g. on a login node) and answer y,
  2. Run telemetry_set_consent(true) (or false to opt out) in MATLAB,
  3. Set PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=on (or off) in the job script, for that job only, or

  4. Create ~/.prestus/telemetry.json by hand:

    {"opt_in": true, "decided_on": "YYYY-MM-DD", "prestus_ver": ""}

items.title: Technical and Deployment Runs
items.text: Test and CI runs that exercise prestus_pipeline are tagged run_type: technical automatically, so their pass/fail rate can be tracked separately from real deployment usage on the usage statistics page. Set PRESTUS_RUN_TYPE=technical yourself when running PRESTUS purely to validate an install or a pipeline change; leave it unset for real runs (default: deployment).

items.title: Collected Data
items.text:
Each pipeline run emits one event: run_end (on clean exit) or run_error (if the pipeline throws an unhandled exception). The tables below list every field that may be sent. Subject IDs, file paths and directory names are not collected, because they could contain identifiable information.

In short: system resources, software versions, a random installation ID, the execution environment, simulation and transducer settings, and the run outcome (an error identifier, never the message text).

items.title: System Resources
items.text:
Fields Field Description os_version OS version string (macOS: sw_vers -productVersion; Linux: kernel release; Windows: ver output). Returns 'unknown' on error. cpu_model CPU model name (e.g. Apple M2 Pro). Returns 'unknown' on error. n_cpu_cores Number of logical CPU cores via feature('numcores'). ram_gb Total physical RAM in GB (rounded). Returns NaN on error. gpu_model GPU device name from gpuDevice(). Returns 'no_pct' when the Parallel Computing Toolbox is not licensed; 'none' when no GPU is found; otherwise the device name string. toolboxes Cell array of installed MATLAB toolbox names (MATLAB itself excluded).

All system resource fields are collected inside try/catch blocks and fall back to 'unknown' or NaN on any error, so they never cause the telemetry payload to fail.

items.title: Run Identity and Versions
items.text: Fields Field Description event Event type: run_end or run_error run_type technical (test/CI run) or deployment (default). See Technical and Deployment Runs. timestamp_utc POSIX timestamp (seconds since epoch, UTC) uuid Random UUID generated locally on first run; stored in ~/.prestus/uuid.txt. Not linked to your identity or machine. run_id Random UUID generated per pipeline run, so the events of one run can be told apart. Not linked to your identity or machine. prestus_ver Version string of the running PRESTUS checkout (from git describe or the VERSION file, e.g. v0.5.1) prestus_hash Short git commit hash of the running PRESTUS checkout (e.g. 628edd0) matlab_ver MATLAB release string (e.g. R2024a) kwave_ver k-Wave toolbox version string as reported by getComputerInfo platform CPU architecture string from computer('arch') (e.g. maci64, glnxa64)

items.title: Execution Environment
items.text: Fields Field Description sim_platform Execution platform: matlab, slurm, qsub, etc. code_type k-Wave code variant: matlab_cpu, matlab_gpu, cpp_cpu, cpp_gpu precision Floating-point precision: single or double hpc_name HPC cluster name if running on a known cluster; unknown otherwise use_gpu Boolean: whether a GPU device is configured

items.title: Simulation Configuration
items.text: Fields Field Description medium Medium type: water, layered or phantom layers List of tissue layer names (e.g. ["skin","skull","brain"]) pct_enabled Boolean: whether pseudo-CT is enabled pct_density Name of the density mapping used for pCT (string, not values) pct_speed Name of the sound-speed mapping used for pCT pct_atten Name of the attenuation mapping used for pCT modules_enabled Names of the modules.* flags set to 1 (e.g. ["run_acoustic_sims","run_heating_sims"]) pipeline_mode Pipeline mode of the run: single, async (asynchronous multi-transducer), multi_isppa or sequential

items.title: Transducer Settings
items.text: Fields Field Description transducer_type Transducer geometry type (e.g. focused_bowl) transducer_name Transducer model name from the config freq_hz Nominal operating frequency in Hz n_transducer_elements Number of transducer elements (elem_n from the transducer config)

items.title: Run Outcome
items.text: Fields Field Description duration_s Total pipeline wall-clock time in seconds status "success" or "error" error_id MATLAB error identifier string (e.g. MATLAB:badsubscript); no message text is transmitted

items.title: Usage Statistics
items.text: See the Usage Statistics page for live charts populated from the anonymised telemetry database.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
PRESTUS is tested at five levels, from checks that take seconds and run on every change to benchmarks that need a GPU or a real subject and run before a release. This page tells you which level a change needs, what data, hardware and time each level takes, and how to add a test.

On this page:

  • Level 0: Static Checks: the doc, parameter, link and Nexus checks that run on every push.
  • Level 1: Unit Tests: data-free tests of each function's logic, grouped by area.
  • Level 2: Physics Benchmarks: free-water fields against the O'Neil solution and the ITRUSST benchmarks, with their tolerances.
  • Level 3: Pipeline Tests: the whole pipeline on synthetic water, a segmented subject and the demo subject, with golden metrics.
  • Level 4: Backends and the Nexus Round Trip: jwave and BabelBrain against k-Wave, and Nexus configs loaded in MATLAB.
  • Release Checklist: the tests to run before tagging a release.
  • Rules for New Tests: where a new test goes and the rules it follows.

The MATLAB tests use matlab.unittest and live in tests/; the Nexus tests use pytest and live in nexus/tests/. run_all_tests(level) runs a MATLAB level and fails (non-zero exit under matlab -batch) when any test fails.

Level What it guarantees Command Needs Time Runs 0 Static Docs match the code, the site builds, the Nexus works see Level 0 Python ~2 min CI, every push 1 Unit Every function's logic, incl. config, placement, scaling, caches, HPC parsing, reports run_all_tests('unit') MATLAB ~15 min (macOS, checkout on a network drive; less on a local disk) CI, every push 2 Physics The solver path reproduces analytic and published reference fields run_all_tests('physics'), ('itrusst') MATLAB (+ ITRUSST data) ~5 min CPU (2D), plus the unit tests, which run_all_tests('physics') also runs CI weekly; 3D on a GPU node before a release 3 Pipeline Whole pipeline on synthetic and real data, numbers stable against a reference run_all_tests('water') … ('demo_golden') k-Wave CPU; SimNIBS outputs; demo data 10 min – hours before a release 4 Backends jwave / BabelBrain agree with k-Wave; Nexus ↔ MATLAB round trip runtests('tests/test_jwave.m') etc. conda envs, GPU, MATLAB 10–60 min after backend or environment changes

items.title: Level 0: Static Checks
items.text:
python tests/docs/gen_function_index.py --check   # doc_functions.md lists every function
python tests/docs/check_param_docs.py             # every config key documented; defaults match
python tests/docs/check_links.py                  # relative links and anchors resolve
mkdocs build --strict -d /tmp/prestus-site        # site builds without warnings (mkdocs < 2)
(cd nexus && python -m pytest -q -m "not matlab")

gen_function_index.py without --check regenerates doc/doc_functions.md (it keeps written descriptions and takes new ones from each file's help line). check_param_docs.py compares the Default column of doc_parameters.md with config_default.yaml. The Nexus tests include the schema drift test (test_schema.py: overlay vs. config_default.yaml and functions/), which also guards the list of extra config keys MATLAB uses for its unknown-key check.

items.title: Level 1: Unit Tests
items.text:
cd tests
run_all_tests          % same as run_all_tests('unit')

No data, SimNIBS, k-Wave simulation or GPU is needed. A failed test prints its full diagnostic; a skipped test prints why it was skipped.

Area Files Configuration test_load_parameters, test_config_layering (toolbox → project → study layering, stale project defaults, unknown keys, non-interactive warnings, prestus_config_upgrade), test_config_upgrade (keys from v0.5.0 on converted to current names), test_study Intensity scaling test_isppa_policy (needs_water_baseline, isppa_baseline, isppa_scale_factor, apply_isppa_scaling), test_focal_reference, test_focal_fwhm Caches test_cache_signature Transducers & calibration test_transducer_library, test_transducer_model (tag model), test_library_conditions, test_matrix_transducer, test_cw_source_matrix, test_calibration_session (the GUI/Nexus calibration steps, meta.fit) Placement & neuronavigation test_transducer_placement (tag manual), test_plantus_placement (tags validation, dispatch), test_neuronav_io, test_neuronav_batch, test_placement_report, test_placement_positions Coordinates test_transform Head model test_head_preprocessing, test_integration_headpreproc, test_deface_m2m Thermal test_thermal_parameters, test_thermal_dose (ISO CEM43 against Sapareto & Dewey values) Backends (logic only) test_babelbrain_insitu_isppa, test_babelbrain_thermal_timing, test_babelbrain_air_regions (needs Python with numpy/scipy/nibabel; skipped otherwise) HPC test_hpc_job_report, test_parse_memory_tags, test_hpc_submit Security test_shell_quote_arg, test_r_quote_string, test_run_command, test_command_injection Nexus MATLAB session test_nexus_bridge (nexus_bridge protocol and allow-list, nexus_neuronav and nexus_calibration on synthetic data) Helpers, reports, suite wiring test_helper, test_reports, test_suite_wiring

items.title: Level 2: Physics Benchmarks
items.text:
These check numbers, not just that code runs. Both use a focused bowl in lossless water (the ITRUSST BM1 source: ROC 64 mm, aperture 64 mm, 500 kHz, 60 kPa) run through prestus_pipeline.

test_physics_water: against the analytic O'Neil solution (k-Wave focusedBowlONeil), no data needed:

Check Tolerance (2D axisymmetric) Focal position on axis 0.5 mm Focal peak pressure 2 % −3 dB (intensity) axial focal length 5 % Four-ring annular array in phase (CTX-500 ring diameters on the same bowl) against O'Neil summed over the rings: focal position / peak pressure / −3 dB length 1 mm / 2 % / 5 % (2026-10-08: 0.50 mm, +0.10 %, +0.04 %; the summed peak is flat, ±0.5 mm costs 0.08 % pressure) Doubling the drive doubles the pressure 1 % A target ISPPA on an uncalibrated transducer is met in water 2 % With run_water_baseline: 0, an unmet target stops the run error prestus:isppa:noBaseline

test_itrusst_benchmark: benchmarks PH1-BM1-SC1 (focused bowl) and PH1-BM1-SC2 (20 mm plane piston, a flat annular element) of Aubry et al. (2022): the pressure amplitude in the central plane against the published k-Wave reference (60 points per wavelength). Download INTERCOMPARISON-PH1-DATA-V1.0 from Zenodo and set PRESTUS_ITRUSST_DATA to it; the test skips otherwise.

Metric Bowl: tolerance (2D) Bowl: result 2026-10-02 Piston: tolerance (2D) Piston: result 2026-10-02 Focal pressure 2 % +0.2 % 2 % 0.0 % Focal position shift 0.5 mm 0.0 mm 0.5 mm 0.0 mm L∞ (max abs. difference / reference max) 4 % 2.1 % 3 % 1.6 % L2 (relative norm) 3 % 1.5 % 1 % 0.4 %

For the piston, every on-axis near-field maximum has the same amplitude (2 p₀), so the focal pressure and position are taken beyond half the near-field distance (a²/2λ), which leaves only the last axial maximum.

run_all_tests('physics')       % unit + test_physics_water (2D axisymmetric, ~5 min CPU)
setenv('PRESTUS_ITRUSST_DATA', '/path/to/INTERCOMPARISON-PH1-DATA-V1.0')
run_all_tests('itrusst')       % 2D BM1 bowl + piston, 3D BM1 bowl
run_all_tests('physics_3d')    % 3D O'Neil check

The 3D variants (tags physics_3d, itrusst_3d; ~6 M voxels at 0.5 mm) belong on a GPU node: set PRESTUS_PHYSICS_CODE_TYPE (e.g. cpp_gpu) and submit the MATLAB call as a job. Their tolerances are provisional (focal pressure 5 %, position 1 mm; ITRUSST L∞ 10 % and L2 6 %; O'Neil focal length 10 %) until their first run on the reference node.

Tolerance policy. A benchmark's tolerances are set from its first passing run on the reference machine plus a margin, recorded with that run's values in the test file, and then kept fixed. Loosen a tolerance only together with an explanation in the changelog; a benchmark that starts failing after a change is a finding, not a test to adjust.

items.title: Synthetic Water Pipeline
items.text:
run_all_tests('water')     % unit + slower unit checks + 3D water pipeline + multi-ISPPA

test_integration_water runs the full pipeline with simulation.medium: water on a small 3D grid (CPU k-Wave), test_isppa_rescaling the multi-ISPPA pipeline. The level also runs the slower data-free checks: test_transducer_model tag fit (optimiser) and test_plantus_placement tag integration (mocked PlanTUS subprocess; needs Python 3). Fixture: fixtures/make_minimal_parameters.m (single-element bowl, drive level, no target ISPPA), fixtures/make_synthetic_segmentation.m.

items.title: Subject Smoke Tests
items.text:
test_integration_pipeline reaches checkpoints on a SimNIBS-segmented subject; each level includes the ones above it:

Level Coverage Duration run_all_tests('head') smoke_config, smoke_head (head preprocessing to medium masks) 1–5 min run_all_tests('acoustic') + smoke_acoustic 10–60 min run_all_tests('all') + smoke_thermal 10–60 min 
export PRESTUS_TEST_DATA=/path/to/demo/data      # folder containing m2m_sub-001/
export PRESTUS_DEMO_CONFIG=/path/to/config.yaml   # optional; default config/config_tutorial.yaml

items.title: Demo Subject (All Placement Modes)
items.text:
test_integration_demo uses demo subject sub-009 (SimNIBS segmentation, UTE-derived pseudo-CT, Localite data) in a folder outside the repository, PRESTUS_DEMO_DATA (check its layout with setup_demo_data('/path/to/prestus_testdata')):

prestus_testdata/
├── bids/sub-009/anat/           sub-009_T1w.nii.gz, sub-009_UTE.nii.gz
├── simnibs/m2m_sub-009/          SimNIBS output (incl. pseudoCT, MNI transforms)
├── localite/sub-009/ses-02/localite/Session_*/TMSTrigger/TriggerMarkers_Coil0*.xml
├── coords/sub-009_heuristic_target.json   {"target_name": "MD_thalamus", "mni_target_mm": [-6,-16,4]}
├── configs/config_demo_{manual,localite,heuristic}.yaml
├── golden/sub-009_manual_metrics.json     reference metrics (see below)
└── sim_outputs/                  written by the tests
Level Checks Duration demo_inputs input files exist ~1 s demo_config the three placement configs load ~1 s demo_localite Localite XML → finite voxel positions ~1 s demo_pct pseudo-CT readable ~1 s demo_head head preprocessing (manual, pseudo-CT) 1–5 min demo_acoustic full acoustic pipeline (3D) 10–60 min (GPU) demo_thermal thermal on the cached acoustics 10–60 min demo_golden key metrics vs. the stored reference seconds

Golden metrics. test_demo_golden reads the result table of the manual-placement demo run and compares Isppa_brain (5 %), Psptp_brain and MI_brain (3 %), the focus position I{x,y,z}_brain_vox (1 voxel), maxT_brain (0.2 °C) and CEM43iso_brain (20 %) with golden/sub-009_manual_metrics.json. Without a reference it writes …metrics.candidate.json and reports the test as incomplete: review the candidate (e.g. against the last release), then rename it. Update the reference only for intended changes and say so in the changelog. Run it after demo_acoustic and demo_thermal.

items.title: Level 4: Backends and the Nexus Round Trip
items.text:
File Checks Needs smoke_test_backends.m BabelBrain and jwave importable, bridge scripts present (<30 s) conda envs test_babelbrain.m staged: paths, input writing, transducer mapping, dry run, full FDTD (tags quick, nogpu, full) BABELBRAIN_PYTHON, GPU for full test_jwave.m jwave (Helmholtz) vs k-Wave on the same water simulation: peak, FWHM, field correlation (tag quick without the timing sweep) JWAVE_PYTHON nexus/tests/test_matlab_roundtrip.py configs written by the Nexus load in load_parameters with identical values MATLAB (PRESTUS_MATLAB) nexus/tests/test_real_configs.py every study config in $PRESTUS_REAL_CONFIG_DIR round-trips real configs nexus/tests/test_bridge.py (matlab-marked part), test_bridge_pages_matlab.py the real nexus_bridge; the Localite and Calibration pages end to end (synthetic Localite study; CTX_250_001 profiles from local/profiles) MATLAB 
runtests('tests/test_babelbrain.m', 'Tag', 'nogpu')
runtests('tests/test_jwave.m', 'Tag', 'quick')

cd nexus && python -m pytest -q      # includes the MATLAB round trip when MATLAB is found

items.title: Release Checklist
items.text:
1. CI green (levels 0–1, and the latest weekly physics run).
  2. run_all_tests('itrusst') and run_all_tests('physics_3d') on the GPU node.
  3. run_all_tests('demo_acoustic'), run_all_tests('demo_thermal'), run_all_tests('demo_golden').
  4. test_babelbrain (full) and test_jwave if a backend or its environment changed.
  5. Nexus round trip (cd nexus && python -m pytest -q).

items.title: Rules for New Tests
items.text:
• New function or fix → a methods (Test) block in the test_*.m of the function's area; a new file only for a new area. run_all_tests finds every test class in tests/ and runs a test at the levels its level tag belongs to (prestus_test_levels.m). Give each class the shared path fixture and one level tag, and add no addpath of its own:

    classdef (SharedTestFixtures = {prestus_paths}, TestTags = {'unit'}) test_x < matlab.unittest.TestCase

    A file that spans levels tags each methods (Test, TestTags = {...}) block instead; standalone marks tests no level runs. test_suite_wiring fails for a test without exactly one level tag. - Anything that changes numbers → extend a physics benchmark, or the golden metrics, so the change is visible. - New pipeline stage → a tagged method in test_integration_pipeline.m and, if it warrants it, a level in prestus_test_levels.m. - New demo subject or placement mode → extend test_integration_demo.m with a private loader like load_demo_config. - Tests write only to tempdir (or PRESTUS_DEMO_DATA/sim_outputs) and skip, not fail, when optional data or tools are missing (assume*).

items.title: Time Reversal: Refocusing, Aberration Report and Pose Search
items.text:
The skull delays and attenuates the parts of the beam differently, so the waves from different parts of the transducer no longer arrive at the target in phase: the focus weakens and shifts. With time_reversal.enabled: true, PRESTUS measures this with one extra simulation per target, using acoustic reciprocity, and uses it to report the aberration, give refocusing phases for arrays and score alternative transducer poses.

On this page:

  • Main Settings: the switches and the files they write.
  • Phases by Transducer Type: the phases each transducer type can use, and the summary metrics.
  • Applying the Phases: running the acoustic simulation with the refocusing phases.
  • Pose Search: scoring poses around the planned one from the same reverse run.
  • Pose Workflow: search, forward verification and final run in one call.
  • Run Time and Memory: run time and memory of the reverse run.
  • Assumptions and Limits: where the method does not apply.

Draft

This feature is new and not yet validated against forward simulations. Treat its predictions as a ranking signal and check any pose or phase set you intend to use with a regular acoustic simulation.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When the focus through the skull is weaker or shifted and you want to correct phases (arrays) or choose a better pose (single element or annular array).
  • Before you start: A working acoustic simulation of the planned pose on a 3D Cartesian grid.

items.title: Main Settings
items.text:
time_reversal:
  enabled: true          # reverse run: aberration report and refocusing phases
  apply_phases: false    # true: use the time-reversal phases in the acoustic run
  placement_search:
    enabled: false       # true: score poses around the planned one (curved annular transducers, 3D grid)
  pose_workflow:
    enabled: false       # true: search, forward verification and final run in one call

Outputs per transducer: <prefix>_timereversal_summary.csv (metrics), <prefix>_timereversal_elements.csv (relative transfer, current and time-reversal phase, and the phase error with which each element arrives at the target) and, with a pose search, <prefix>_timereversal_poses_T<i>.csv.

items.title: Phases by Transducer Type
items.text:
Transducer Phases it can use Report Matrix array One per element: full refocusing All metrics; apply_phases uses the per-element phases Annular array (elem_n > 1) One per ring: the axially symmetric part of the correction All metrics; apply_phases uses the ring phases Single element None Coherence and predicted focal shift; nothing to apply

The metrics in <prefix>_timereversal_summary.csv:

  • coherence_elements: |Σ contributions| / Σ |contributions| over the elements with the current phases. 1 means the elements arrive in phase; refocus_gain_pressure = 1 / coherence_elements is what refocusing gains at the target.
  • coherence_aperture: the same over the whole surface, including the phase spread within each element, which no element phase can correct.
  • **shift__mm*: predicted focal shift with the current drive (axial > 0: deeper than the target), and with the time-reversal drive (shift_refocused_*).
How the reverse run works

A point source is placed at the target and run as a continuous wave on the grid, medium and time axis of the acoustic simulation (reverse_point_source_field). By reciprocity, the pressure this source produces at a point x equals the pressure that a source at x would produce at the target (up to one constant common to all points). Recorded on the transducer surface, the reverse field therefore gives, for every element, the amplitude and phase with which it reaches the target through the skull (time_reversal_refocus):

G_e = sum over the element's grid points of (weight × reverse field)
pressure at the target = sum_e  A_e · exp(i·phi_e) · G_e

Driving each element with the phase −angle(G_e) (phase conjugation, i.e. time reversal) makes all elements arrive in phase: the largest target pressure the element amplitudes allow.

Predicted focal shift. Near the target the forward field is approximated by F(y) = Σ_j q_j · exp(−i·k·(|x_j − y| − |x_j − t|)): the skull aberration seen from the target is taken to be the same for points within a few millimetres of it (isoplanatic patch), and only the path through the tissue around the target changes.
